That is Allah, my Lord; in Him I have placed my trust, and to Him I turn in repentance﴾ ﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth, He made for you mates from among yourselves, and of the cattle mates too, multiplying you thereby. There is nothing like Him, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing﴾ ﴿To Him belong the keys of the heavens and the earth. He extends provision to whom He wills and restricts it; surely He has full knowledge of all things﴾

These verses are Meccan according to al-Hasan, 'Ata', 'Ikrimah and Jabir. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is Meccan except for four verses from His words, ﴿Say, I do not ask you any reward for it, except love for the near kin﴾ [al-Shura: 23] to the end of the four verses, for they were revealed in Madinah. Muqatil said: among it, a Madinan part is His words, ﴿That is what Allah gives as good news to His servants﴾ [al-Shura: 23] up to (al-Sudur). The connection between the beginning of the surah and what precedes it is that He said, ﴿Say: Have you considered, if it is from Allah...﴾ [Fussilat: 52], and in that was a judgment that they were in error.

When they disbelieved in it, He said here "thus" (kadhalika), meaning: like the earlier revelation of the Qur'an which these people disbelieved in. ﴿He reveals to you﴾: that is, His revelation to you, may He be exalted, is continuous and uninterrupted, attending to you from time to time.

The exegetes mentioned regarding ﴿Ha, Mim﴾ ﴿'Ayn, Sin, Qaf﴾ conflicting opinions, none of which is sound, as is their habit with these openings; we set aside mentioning them entirely.

Al-Jumhur read (yuhi) in the active voice; Abu Haywa, al-A'sha from Abu Bakr, and Aban read (nuhi) with the plural of majesty (nun of greatness).

Mujahid, Ibn Kathir, 'Abbas, and Mahbub, both of whom are from Abu 'Amr, read (yuha) in the passive voice; and (Allah) is nominative by a hidden verb whose implied sense is "He revealed," or by the subject, the implied sense being: Allah, the Almighty, the All-Wise, the Revealer.

On the reading (nuhi) with the nun, ﴿Allah, the Almighty, the All-Wise﴾ is subject and predicate.

(Yuhi) either means "obligated," so that His words ﴿and to those before you﴾ are coherently linked, or it is read in its own sense, and an implied governing verb connected to (ila alladhina) is assumed, its sense being: "and He revealed to those before you." The discussion of ﴿The heavens are almost torn apart﴾ has already been covered in Surah Maryam, both in reading and interpretation.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Yunus related from Abu 'Amr, and it is an Arabic reading, (tatafattarna) with two taʼs and a nun, and its parallel is a rare form transmitted in the Nawadir of Ibn al-A'rabi: "the camels tatashammamna." End of quotation.

The apparent meaning is that this is a mistake by al-Zamakhshari in transmission, because Ibn Khalawayh mentioned in his collection of irregular readings that Yunus related from Abu 'Amr a reading that put (tafattarna) with a ta and a nun. Ibn Khalawayh said: this is a rare form, because the Arabs do not combine the two markers of feminine gender.

It is not said: "al-nisa' taqumna," but "yaqumna," and "al-walidat yurdi'na." Abu 'Umar al-Zahid had indeed transmitted in the Nawadir of Ibn al-A'rabi "al-ibl tatashammamna," which we rejected, but he strengthened it, because this is Ibn Khalawayh's statement. If the copies of al-Zamakhshari all agree on his saying with two taʼs and a nun, then it is a mistake; and if in some of them it is with one ta and a nun, it agrees with Ibn Khalawayh's statement, and the two-ta version would be a scribal distortion.

Likewise their writing of (tatafattarna) and (tatashammamna) with two ta's. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in (min fawqihinna) returns to (al-samawat). Ibn 'Atiyyah said: from their upper parts. Al-Zamakhshari said: they are split apart from the exalted greatness of Allah, and the Most High and His majesty, and this is indicated by its coming after ﴿the Most High, the Great﴾.

It has also been said: from their attributing a child to Him, like His words: ﴿The heavens are almost torn apart because of it﴾ [Maryam: 90]. If you ask: why did He say "from above them"? I say: because the greatest signs and the most indicative of majesty and greatness are above the heavens, namely the 'Arsh (throne), the Kursi (footstool), and the ranks of angels reverberating with glorification and sanctification around the Throne, and what none knows the reality of except Allah, of the traces of His supreme dominion. Therefore He said: ﴿they are split apart from above them﴾, that is, the splitting begins from the upper direction.

Al-Hawfi and a group said: (from above them), and the ha' and nun are a reference to the earths. End of quotation.

(From above them) is connected to (yatafattarna), and the earlier mention of the earth supports this view.

'Ali ibn Sulayman al-Akhfash said: the pronoun refers to the disbelievers, and the meaning is: from above the sects and the heretical groups, that is, because of their sayings. End of quotation.

This verse is like the one in Surah Maryam. Makki considered this view unlikely, saying: it is not permissible for male sons of Adam, meaning the feminine pronoun, and what Makki mentioned is an inference. 'Ali ibn Sulayman said: above the sects and groups, and the apparent meaning of the angels is generality. Muqatil said: the bearers of the Throne and the glorification; it was said: their saying "Subhan Allah," and it was said: they say "La ilaha illa Allah." The apparent meaning of (yastaghfirun) is seeking forgiveness, and for the people of the earth is a general statement specified by His words: ﴿and they seek forgiveness for those who believe﴾ [Ghafir: 7], as said by al-Suddi. It was also said: it is general. The meaning of seeking forgiveness is seeking guidance which leads to forgiveness, as if they were saying: "O Allah, guide the people of the earth, and forgive them."

This is indicated by His being described with forgiveness, mercy and opening.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is possible that they intend by seeking forgiveness for them: asking for forbearance and pardon, as in His words: ﴿Allah holds the heavens and the earth lest they cease; surely He is Forbearing, Forgiving﴾ [Fatir: 41], and His words: ﴿Surely your Lord is full of forgiveness for mankind despite their wrongdoing﴾ [al-Ra'd: 6], and the meaning is forbearance towards them, and that He does not hasten to punish them, so it is general. End of quotation.

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi spoke about His words ﴿the heavens are almost torn apart﴾ with statements outside the usual meanings of Arabic, drawn from the words of the philosophers and those who follow their path; this can be consulted in his book.

﴿Those who take protectors other than Him﴾: that is, idols and images; ﴿Allah is Watchful over them﴾: that is, over their deeds and the One who will recompense them for them; ﴿and you are not a guardian over them﴾: that is, not one entrusted with their affair nor one responsible for them.

What is in this of conciliation has been abrogated by the verse of the sword. (And thus) that is: like this revelation and decree, you are not a guardian over them, ﴿We have revealed to you an Arabic Qur'an﴾.

(p-509) The apparent meaning is that (Qur'anan) is the object of (awhayna).

Al-Zamakhshari said: the kaf is the object, that is, We revealed it to you, and it is an Arabic Qur'an with no ambiguity upon you, since it came in your tongue. End of quotation.

I translate the passage as requested, with the Qur'anic quotations, technical terms, and the grammatical discussion handled according to the guidelines.

Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 42, verses 1–12 (part 2 of 2):

He used the kaf (كاف) as a noun within the speech, and this is the view of al-Akhfash (al-Akhfash, the grammarian).

﴿لِتُنْذِرَ أُمَّ القُرى﴾ ("that you may warn the Mother of Towns"): Makkah, i.e., the people of Umm al-Qura. Likewise, the first object is omitted, and the second is ﴿يَوْمَ الجَمْعِ﴾ ("the Day of Assembly"), i.e., the gathering of creatures. The thing warned of is what takes place on the Day of Assembly of recompense and the division of the gathering into two groups, or the gathering of spirits with bodies, or the people of the earth with the people of the heavens, or people with their deeds. These are four opinions.

(لِيُنْذِرَ) with the ya' of the third person, i.e., "that it may warn": the Qur'an is the subject.

﴿لا رَيْبَ فِيهِ﴾ ("there is no doubt in it"), i.e., there is no doubt about its occurrence.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿لا رَيْبَ فِيهِ﴾ is certainly a parenthetical clause (i'tiraḍ). End of quotation.

It does not appear that it is a parenthetical clause, in the technical grammatical sense, since it did not come between a speaker and what is spoken of.

The majority of readers read (فَرِيقٌ) with nominative case in both places, i.e., they are a group, or among them is a group. Zayd ibn 'Ali read both in the accusative, i.e., they separated, a group in such-and-such and a group in such-and-such; and the separation is indicated by the gathering understood from "the Day of Assembly."

﴿ولَوْ شاءَ اللَّهُ لَجَعَلَهم أُمَّةً واحِدَةً﴾ ("And if Allah had willed, He would have made them one community"): meaning, in faith or in disbelief. Al-Dahhak said this, and it is the view of the People of the Sunnah. This is consolation for the Messenger, for what he endured from his people's disbelief, and a reminder that this rests with His will; but whoever has been preceded by happiness, He admits into His mercy.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿لَجَعَلَهم أُمَّةً واحِدَةً﴾ means all of them believers by compulsion and coercion, like His saying: ﴿ولَوْ شِئْنا لَآتَيْنا كُلَّ نَفْسٍ هُداها﴾ (As-Sajdah 13), and His saying: ﴿ولَوْ شاءَ رَبُّكَ لَآمَنَ مَن في الأرْضِ كُلُّهم جَمِيعًا﴾ (Yunus 99).

The proof that the meaning is compulsion toward faith is His saying: ﴿أفَأنْتَ تُكْرِهُ النّاسَ حَتّى يَكُونُوا مُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ (Yunus 99). He mentioned what he thought was evidence for this, and it is in the manner of the Mu'tazilah.

Anas ibn Malik said: ﴿فِي رَحْمَتِهِ﴾ ("in His mercy") means: in the religion of Islam.

﴿أمِ اتَّخَذُوا مِن دُونِهِ أوْلِياءَ﴾ ("Or have they taken protectors besides Him?"): am here means "rather" (bal), for transition from one speech to another, and the hamzah is for denunciation of them for taking protectors besides Allah. It was said that am means only the hamzah, and the discussion of this kind was treated earlier where the disjunctive am appears. The meaning: they took protectors besides Allah, but they are not protectors in reality; Allah is the Protector, and He alone is to be taken as protector, not those who neither harm nor benefit among their protectors.

When He informed that He is the Protector, He followed it with this extraordinary act that none but Him can perform, which is giving life to the dead.

When He mentioned this attribute, He mentioned His power over every thing that His will relates to.

Al-Zamakhshari said: concerning His saying: ﴿فاللَّهُ هو الوَلِيُّ﴾, the fa' in ﴿فاللَّهُ هو الوَلِيُّ﴾ is the answer to an implied condition, as if it were said: after denying every protector other than Him, and if they meant a protector in truth, then Allah is the Protector in truth, and there is no protector other than Him. End of quotation.

There is no need to posit an omitted condition, since the speech is complete without it.

﴿وما اخْتَلَفْتُمْ فِيهِ مِن شَيْءٍ﴾ ("And whatever you differ about, its judgment is with Allah"): this is a quotation of the Messenger's words, i.e., whatever you differ about, O people, of denial or affirmation, faith or disbelief, or otherwise, its judgment and its recompense belong to Allah alone, not to me. The phrase min shay' (anything) indicates generality.

It was said: "anything" means any dispute, so they should bring it before the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and not prefer the judgment of anyone else over his judgment, as in His saying: ﴿فَإنْ تَنازَعْتُمْ في شَيْءٍ فَرُدُّوهُ إلى اللَّهِ والرَّسُولِ﴾ (An-Nisa' 59). It was said: "min shay'" means: concerning the interpretation of a verse that is unclear to you, return in its explanation to the clear verses of the Book of Allah and the apparent Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

It was said: what you differ about of the sciences that do not relate to your obligations, and for which you have no path to knowledge, then say: "Allah knows best," as with the knowledge of the spirit.

Al-Zamakhshari said: i.e., what the disbelievers, among the People of the Book and the polytheists, opposed you in, so that you and they differed regarding matters of religion; the judgment about that disputed matter is entrusted to Allah, who rewards those among the believers who are right in it and reproaches the wrongdoers. End of quotation.

(ذَلِكم) ("That is your Judge"): ﴿رَبِّي عَلَيْهِ تَوَكَّلْتُ﴾ ("My Lord, upon Him I have relied") in repelling the plots of the enemies of the religion, and to Him I return for protection from their evil. End of quotation.

The majority read (فاطِرُ) with nominative case, i.e., He is the Creator (fatir), or it is a predicate after a predicate, like His saying (ذَلِكم).

Zayd ibn 'Ali read (فاطِرِ) in the genitive, as an attribute of (إلى اللَّهِ), and the clause after it is a parenthetical clause between the attribute and the thing described.

﴿جَعَلَ لَكم مِن أنْفُسِكُمْ﴾ ("He made for you from yourselves"), i.e., from the kind of your own selves, i.e., human beings. (أزْواجًا) ("mates"): females. Or: He made, for our father Adam, from his rib, Hawwa' as a spouse for him, as creation for us. ﴿ومِنَ الأنْعامِ أزْواجًا﴾ ("and from the cattle, mates"), i.e., many kinds, males and females, or mates that are females.

﴿يَذْرَؤُكم فِيهِ﴾ ("He multiplies you through it"). Ibn 'Abbas said: i.e., He makes for you in it a livelihood by which you live. Ibn Zayd said: He provides for you in it, and this is close to the previous saying.

Mujahid said: He creates you in the wombs of females. Ibn Zayd also said: He multiplies you through what He created of the heavens and the earth. Al-Zajjaj said: He increases you by it, i.e., in it, i.e., He increases you in your creation as mates.

'Ali ibn Sulayman said: He moves you from one state to another.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the pronoun in fihi refers to the making (al-ja'l), i.e., He creates you and multiplies you in the making, as you say: "I spoke to Zayd a speech, I honored him in it." He said: the word dhara'a adds a meaning beyond the word khalaqa that is not in khalaqa, namely the succession of generations over the passage of time.

Al-Zamakhshari said: (يَذْرَؤُكم): He multiplies you. It is said dhara'a Allah the creation: He scattered them and multiplied them, and dhar', dhurū', and dharwa' are siblings in this arrangement, which is that He made for people and cattle mates, so that between their males and females there is procreation and propagation.

The pronoun in yadhra'ukum refers to the addressees, and (al-an'am) has the rational addressees given precedence over the non-rational, and this is among the rulings with two causes. End of quotation.

His saying "this is among the rulings with two causes" is a strange technical term; he means that address takes precedence over absence when they are combined, so you say: "You and Zayd will stand," and rational beings take precedence over non-rational when combined, so you say: "The animals and others glorify their Creator."

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, what is the meaning of "He multiplies you" in this arrangement? Why was it not said "He multiplies you through it"? I answer: He made this arrangement like a spring and a mine for scattering and multiplying. Do you not see that you say of animals in the creation of pairs that there is multiplication? As He, exalted, said: ﴿ولَكم في القِصاصِ حَياةٌ﴾ (Al-Baqarah 179). End of quotation.

﴿لَيْسَ كَمِثْلِهِ شَيْءٌ﴾ ("There is nothing like His likeness"): the Arabs say, "one like you does not do such-and-such," meaning the addressee, as if when they negate the attribute from the likeness of a person, that is a negation from the person himself, and this is from the category of hyperbole. Similar to the verse is the saying of Aws ibn Hajar:

"There is not like the youth Zuhayr / a character that matches him in virtues."

Another said:

"And slain men like trunks of palm trees / covered by a pouring downpour."

Another said:

"Sa'd ibn Zayd, when you look at their excellence / there is not, among people, anyone like them."

So the verse proceeds in that matter according to the manner of Arabic speech, applying the word "like" to the very self of a thing. As for what al-Tabari and others held, that mithl is redundant for emphasis, like the kaf in His saying:

"So she became like a devoured stalk,"

and in the saying:

"And lofty ones like the pots that are set up on stones,"

this is not sound, because mithl is a noun, and nouns are not made redundant, unlike the kaf, which is a particle and so is suitable for redundancy.

The parallel of attributing "likeness" to one who has no likeness is your saying: "So-and-so's hand is outstretched," meaning that he is generous, though in reality there is no hand for him, as in His saying: ﴿بَلْ يَداهُ مَبْسُوطَتانِ﴾ (Al-Ma'idah 64).

Just as you made that a metaphor for generosity regarding one who has no hand, so you made likeness a metaphor for essence regarding one who has no likeness.

It is also possible that by "likeness" is meant the attribute, and that is permissible: the word mithl is used in the sense of attribute, so the meaning becomes: no attribute among the attributes of others is like the attribute of Him, exalted. This is an easy interpretation, while the first is subtler.

Ibn Qutaybah said: The Arabs use the example to stand in place of the self, so one says: "One like me is not told this," meaning: "I am not told this." End of quotation.

Thus this has become a metaphor for the essence, and there is no difference between your saying "There is nothing like Allah" and "There is nothing like the likeness of Allah." The exegetes have agreed that the kaf and mithl are not meant in their literal sense of comparison, since that would imply affirming a likeness to Allah, exalted, which is impossible.

﴿وهُوَ السَّمِيعُ﴾ ("And He is the All-Hearing") of the speech of creatures, (البَصِيرُ) ("the All-Seeing") of their deeds. The explanation of ﴿لَهُ مَقالِيدُ السَّماواتِ والأرْضِ﴾ has been given earlier in Surah az-Zumar. It was read (ويَقْدِرُ), i.e., He straitens.

﴿إنَّهُ بِكُلِّ شَيْءٍ عَلِيمٌ﴾ ("Indeed, He is All-Knowing of everything"), i.e., He expands for whom He wills and straitens for whom He wills. Al-Zamakhshari said: When He knows that wealth is good for the servant, He enriches him, not impoverishes him. End of quotation. In this there is a trace of Mu'tazilite doctrine.

Muqatil said: the bearers of the Throne and the glorification; it was said: their saying "Subhan Allah," and it was said: they say "La ilaha illa Allah." The apparent meaning of (yastaghfirun) is seeking forgiveness, and for the people of the earth is a general statement specified by His words: ﴿and they seek forgiveness for those who believe﴾ [Ghafir: 7], as said by al-Suddi. It was also said: it is general. The meaning of seeking forgiveness is seeking guidance which leads to forgiveness, as if they were saying: "O Allah, guide the people of the earth, and forgive them."

This is indicated by His being described with forgiveness, mercy and opening.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is possible that they intend by seeking forgiveness for them: asking for forbearance and pardon, as in His words: ﴿Allah holds the heavens and the earth lest they cease; surely He is Forbearing, Forgiving﴾ [Fatir: 41], and His words: ﴿Surely your Lord is full of forgiveness for mankind despite their wrongdoing﴾ [al-Ra'd: 6], and the meaning is forbearance towards them, and that He does not hasten to punish them, so it is general. End of quotation.

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi spoke about His words ﴿the heavens are almost torn apart﴾ with statements outside the usual meanings of Arabic, drawn from the words of the philosophers and those who follow their path; this can be consulted in his book.

﴿Those who take protectors other than Him﴾: that is, idols and images; ﴿Allah is Watchful over them﴾: that is, over their deeds and the One who will recompense them for them; ﴿and you are not a guardian over them﴾: that is, not one entrusted with their affair nor one responsible for them.

What is in this of conciliation has been abrogated by the verse of the sword. (And thus) that is: like this revelation and decree, you are not a guardian over them, ﴿We have revealed to you an Arabic Qur'an﴾.

Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 42, verses 1–12 (part 2 of 2):

He used the kaf (كاف) as a noun within the speech, and this is the view of al-Akhfash (al-Akhfash, the grammarian).

﴿لِتُنْذِرَ أُمَّ القُرى﴾ ("that you may warn the Mother of Towns"): Makkah, i.e., the people of Umm al-Qura. Likewise, the first object is omitted, and the second is ﴿يَوْمَ الجَمْعِ﴾ ("the Day of Assembly"), i.e., the gathering of creatures. The thing warned of is what takes place on the Day of Assembly of recompense and the division of the gathering into two groups, or the gathering of spirits with bodies, or the people of the earth with the people of the heavens, or people with their deeds. These are four opinions.

(لِيُنْذِرَ) with the ya' of the third person, i.e., "that it may warn": the Qur'an is the subject.

﴿لا رَيْبَ فِيهِ﴾ ("there is no doubt in it"), i.e., there is no doubt about its occurrence.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿لا رَيْبَ فِيهِ﴾ is certainly a parenthetical clause (i'tiraḍ). End of quotation.

It does not appear that it is a parenthetical clause, in the technical grammatical sense, since it did not come between a speaker and what is spoken of.

The majority of readers read (فَرِيقٌ) with nominative case in both places, i.e., they are a group, or among them is a group. Zayd ibn 'Ali read both in the accusative, i.e., they separated, a group in such-and-such and a group in such-and-such; and the separation is indicated by the gathering understood from "the Day of Assembly."

﴿ولَوْ شاءَ اللَّهُ لَجَعَلَهم أُمَّةً واحِدَةً﴾ ("And if Allah had willed, He would have made them one community"): meaning, in faith or in disbelief. Al-Dahhak said this, and it is the view of the People of the Sunnah. This is consolation for the Messenger, for what he endured from his people's disbelief, and a reminder that this rests with His will; but whoever has been preceded by happiness, He admits into His mercy.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿لَجَعَلَهم أُمَّةً واحِدَةً﴾ means all of them believers by compulsion and coercion, like His saying: ﴿ولَوْ شِئْنا لَآتَيْنا كُلَّ نَفْسٍ هُداها﴾ (As-Sajdah 13), and His saying: ﴿ولَوْ شاءَ رَبُّكَ لَآمَنَ مَن في الأرْضِ كُلُّهم جَمِيعًا﴾ (Yunus 99).

The proof that the meaning is compulsion toward faith is His saying: ﴿أفَأنْتَ تُكْرِهُ النّاسَ حَتّى يَكُونُوا مُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ (Yunus 99). He mentioned what he thought was evidence for this, and it is in the manner of the Mu'tazilah.

Anas ibn Malik said: ﴿فِي رَحْمَتِهِ﴾ ("in His mercy") means: in the religion of Islam.

﴿أمِ اتَّخَذُوا مِن دُونِهِ أوْلِياءَ﴾ ("Or have they taken protectors besides Him?"): am here means "rather" (bal), for transition from one speech to another, and the hamzah is for denunciation of them for taking protectors besides Allah. It was said that am means only the hamzah, and the discussion of this kind was treated earlier where the disjunctive am appears. The meaning: they took protectors besides Allah, but they are not protectors in reality; Allah is the Protector, and He alone is to be taken as protector, not those who neither harm nor benefit among their protectors.

When He informed that He is the Protector, He followed it with this extraordinary act that none but Him can perform, which is giving life to the dead.

When He mentioned this attribute, He mentioned His power over every thing that His will relates to.

Al-Zamakhshari said: concerning His saying: ﴿فاللَّهُ هو الوَلِيُّ﴾, the fa' in ﴿فاللَّهُ هو الوَلِيُّ﴾ is the answer to an implied condition, as if it were said: after denying every protector other than Him, and if they meant a protector in truth, then Allah is the Protector in truth, and there is no protector other than Him. End of quotation.

There is no need to posit an omitted condition, since the speech is complete without it.

﴿وما اخْتَلَفْتُمْ فِيهِ مِن شَيْءٍ﴾ ("And whatever you differ about, its judgment is with Allah"): this is a quotation of the Messenger's words, i.e., whatever you differ about, O people, of denial or affirmation, faith or disbelief, or otherwise, its judgment and its recompense belong to Allah alone, not to me. The phrase min shay' (anything) indicates generality.

It was said: "anything" means any dispute, so they should bring it before the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and not prefer the judgment of anyone else over his judgment, as in His saying: ﴿فَإنْ تَنازَعْتُمْ في شَيْءٍ فَرُدُّوهُ إلى اللَّهِ والرَّسُولِ﴾ (An-Nisa' 59). It was said: "min shay'" means: concerning the interpretation of a verse that is unclear to you, return in its explanation to the clear verses of the Book of Allah and the apparent Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

It was said: what you differ about of the sciences that do not relate to your obligations, and for which you have no path to knowledge, then say: "Allah knows best," as with the knowledge of the spirit.

Al-Zamakhshari said: i.e., what the disbelievers, among the People of the Book and the polytheists, opposed you in, so that you and they differed regarding matters of religion; the judgment about that disputed matter is entrusted to Allah, who rewards those among the believers who are right in it and reproaches the wrongdoers. End of quotation.

(ذَلِكم) ("That is your Judge"): ﴿رَبِّي عَلَيْهِ تَوَكَّلْتُ﴾ ("My Lord, upon Him I have relied") in repelling the plots of the enemies of the religion, and to Him I return for protection from their evil. End of quotation.

The majority read (فاطِرُ) with nominative case, i.e., He is the Creator (fatir), or it is a predicate after a predicate, like His saying (ذَلِكم).

Zayd ibn 'Ali read (فاطِرِ) in the genitive, as an attribute of (إلى اللَّهِ), and the clause after it is a parenthetical clause between the attribute and the thing described.

﴿جَعَلَ لَكم مِن أنْفُسِكُمْ﴾ ("He made for you from yourselves"), i.e., from the kind of your own selves, i.e., human beings. (أزْواجًا) ("mates"): females. Or: He made, for our father Adam, from his rib, Hawwa' as a spouse for him, as creation for us. ﴿ومِنَ الأنْعامِ أزْواجًا﴾ ("and from the cattle, mates"), i.e., many kinds, males and females, or mates that are females.

Mujahid said: He creates you in the wombs of females. Ibn Zayd also said: He multiplies you through what He created of the heavens and the earth. Al-Zajjaj said: He increases you by it, i.e., in it, i.e., He increases you in your creation as mates.

'Ali ibn Sulayman said: He moves you from one state to another.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the pronoun in fihi refers to the making (al-ja'l), i.e., He creates you and multiplies you in the making, as you say: "I spoke to Zayd a speech, I honored him in it." He said: the word dhara'a adds a meaning beyond the word khalaqa that is not in khalaqa, namely the succession of generations over the passage of time.

Al-Zamakhshari said: (يَذْرَؤُكم): He multiplies you. It is said dhara'a Allah the creation: He scattered them and multiplied them, and dhar', dhurū', and dharwa' are siblings in this arrangement, which is that He made for people and cattle mates, so that between their males and females there is procreation and propagation.

The pronoun in yadhra'ukum refers to the addressees, and (al-an'am) has the rational addressees given precedence over the non-rational, and this is among the rulings with two causes. End of quotation.

His saying "this is among the rulings with two causes" is a strange technical term; he means that address takes precedence over absence when they are combined, so you say: "You and Zayd will stand," and rational beings take precedence over non-rational when combined, so you say: "The animals and others glorify their Creator."

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, what is the meaning of "He multiplies you" in this arrangement? Why was it not said "He multiplies you through it"? I answer: He made this arrangement like a spring and a mine for scattering and multiplying. Do you not see that you say of animals in the creation of pairs that there is multiplication? As He, exalted, said: ﴿ولَكم في القِصاصِ حَياةٌ﴾ (Al-Baqarah 179). End of quotation.

﴿لَيْسَ كَمِثْلِهِ شَيْءٌ﴾ ("There is nothing like His likeness"): the Arabs say, "one like you does not do such-and-such," meaning the addressee, as if when they negate the attribute from the likeness of a person, that is a negation from the person himself, and this is from the category of hyperbole. Similar to the verse is the saying of Aws ibn Hajar:

"There is not like the youth Zuhayr / a character that matches him in virtues."

Another said:

"And slain men like trunks of palm trees / covered by a pouring downpour."

Another said:

"Sa'd ibn Zayd, when you look at their excellence / there is not, among people, anyone like them."

So the verse proceeds in that matter according to the manner of Arabic speech, applying the word "like" to the very self of a thing. As for what al-Tabari and others held, that mithl is redundant for emphasis, like the kaf in His saying:

"So she became like a devoured stalk,"

and in the saying:

"And lofty ones like the pots that are set up on stones,"

this is not sound, because mithl is a noun, and nouns are not made redundant, unlike the kaf, which is a particle and so is suitable for redundancy.

The parallel of attributing "likeness" to one who has no likeness is your saying: "So-and-so's hand is outstretched," meaning that he is generous, though in reality there is no hand for him, as in His saying: ﴿بَلْ يَداهُ مَبْسُوطَتانِ﴾ (Al-Ma'idah 64).

Just as you made that a metaphor for generosity regarding one who has no hand, so you made likeness a metaphor for essence regarding one who has no likeness.

It is also possible that by "likeness" is meant the attribute, and that is permissible: the word mithl is used in the sense of attribute, so the meaning becomes: no attribute among the attributes of others is like the attribute of Him, exalted. This is an easy interpretation, while the first is subtler.

Ibn Qutaybah said: The Arabs use the example to stand in place of the self, so one says: "One like me is not told this," meaning: "I am not told this." End of quotation.

Thus this has become a metaphor for the essence, and there is no difference between your saying "There is nothing like Allah" and "There is nothing like the likeness of Allah." The exegetes have agreed that the kaf and mithl are not meant in their literal sense of comparison, since that would imply affirming a likeness to Allah, exalted, which is impossible.

﴿وهُوَ السَّمِيعُ﴾ ("And He is the All-Hearing") of the speech of creatures, (البَصِيرُ) ("the All-Seeing") of their deeds. The explanation of ﴿لَهُ مَقالِيدُ السَّماواتِ والأرْضِ﴾ has been given earlier in Surah az-Zumar. It was read (ويَقْدِرُ), i.e., He straitens.

﴿إنَّهُ بِكُلِّ شَيْءٍ عَلِيمٌ﴾ ("Indeed, He is All-Knowing of everything"), i.e., He expands for whom He wills and straitens for whom He wills. Al-Zamakhshari said: When He knows that wealth is good for the servant, He enriches him, not impoverishes him. End of quotation. In this there is a trace of Mu'tazilite doctrine.

Surah 42: al-Shura (Consultation), fifty-three verses, Meccan

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Ha, Mim﴾ ﴿'Ayn, Sin, Qaf﴾ ﴿Thus does He reveal to you, and to those before you, Allah, the Almighty, the All-Wise﴾ ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and He is the Most High, the Great﴾ ﴿The heavens are almost torn apart from above them, while the angels glorify their Lord with praise and seek forgiveness for those on earth. Surely Allah is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾ ﴿And those who take protectors other than Him—Allah is Watchful over them, and you are not a guardian over them﴾ ﴿Thus We have revealed to you an Arabic Qur'an that you may warn the Mother of Cities (Makkah) and those around it, and warn of the Day of Assembly, about which there is no doubt: a party will be in the Garden and a party in the Blaze﴾ ﴿Had Allah willed, He would have made them one community, but He admits whom He wills into His mercy, while the wrongdoers have neither protector nor helper﴾ ﴿Or have they taken protectors other than Him? But Allah is the Protector, and He gives life to the dead, and He is Powerful over all things﴾ ﴿Whatever you differ over, its judgment rests with Allah. That is Allah, my Lord; in Him I have placed my trust, and to Him I turn in repentance﴾ ﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth, He made for you mates from among yourselves, and of the cattle mates too, multiplying you thereby. There is nothing like Him, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing﴾ ﴿To Him belong the keys of the heavens and the earth. He extends provision to whom He wills and restricts it; surely He has full knowledge of all things﴾

These verses are Meccan according to al-Hasan, 'Ata', 'Ikrimah and Jabir. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is Meccan except for four verses from His words, ﴿Say, I do not ask you any reward for it, except love for the near kin﴾ [al-Shura: 23] to the end of the four verses, for they were revealed in Madinah. Muqatil said: among it, a Madinan part is His words, ﴿That is what Allah gives as good news to His servants﴾ [al-Shura: 23] up to (al-Sudur). The connection between the beginning of the surah and what precedes it is that He said, ﴿Say: Have you considered, if it is from Allah...﴾ [Fussilat: 52], and in that was a judgment that they were in error.

When they disbelieved in it, He said here "thus" (kadhalika), meaning: like the earlier revelation of the Qur'an which these people disbelieved in. ﴿He reveals to you﴾: that is, His revelation to you, may He be exalted, is continuous and uninterrupted, attending to you from time to time.

The exegetes mentioned regarding ﴿Ha, Mim﴾ ﴿'Ayn, Sin, Qaf﴾ conflicting opinions, none of which is sound, as is their habit with these openings; we set aside mentioning them entirely.

Al-Jumhur read (yuhi) in the active voice; Abu Haywa, al-A'sha from Abu Bakr, and Aban read (nuhi) with the plural of majesty (nun of greatness).

Mujahid, Ibn Kathir, 'Abbas, and Mahbub, both of whom are from Abu 'Amr, read (yuha) in the passive voice; and (Allah) is nominative by a hidden verb whose implied sense is "He revealed," or by the subject, the implied sense being: Allah, the Almighty, the All-Wise, the Revealer.

On the reading (nuhi) with the nun, ﴿Allah, the Almighty, the All-Wise﴾ is subject and predicate.

(Yuhi) either means "obligated," so that His words ﴿and to those before you﴾ are coherently linked, or it is read in its own sense, and an implied governing verb connected to (ila alladhina) is assumed, its sense being: "and He revealed to those before you." The discussion of ﴿The heavens are almost torn apart﴾ has already been covered in Surah Maryam, both in reading and interpretation.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Yunus related from Abu 'Amr, and it is an Arabic reading, (tatafattarna) with two taʼs and a nun, and its parallel is a rare form transmitted in the Nawadir of Ibn al-A'rabi: "the camels tatashammamna." End of quotation.

The apparent meaning is that this is a mistake by al-Zamakhshari in transmission, because Ibn Khalawayh mentioned in his collection of irregular readings that Yunus related from Abu 'Amr a reading that put (tafattarna) with a ta and a nun. Ibn Khalawayh said: this is a rare form, because the Arabs do not combine the two markers of feminine gender.

It is not said: "al-nisa' taqumna," but "yaqumna," and "al-walidat yurdi'na." Abu 'Umar al-Zahid had indeed transmitted in the Nawadir of Ibn al-A'rabi "al-ibl tatashammamna," which we rejected, but he strengthened it, because this is Ibn Khalawayh's statement. If the copies of al-Zamakhshari all agree on his saying with two taʼs and a nun, then it is a mistake; and if in some of them it is with one ta and a nun, it agrees with Ibn Khalawayh's statement, and the two-ta version would be a scribal distortion.

Likewise their writing of (tatafattarna) and (tatashammamna) with two ta's. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in (min fawqihinna) returns to (al-samawat). Ibn 'Atiyyah said: from their upper parts. Al-Zamakhshari said: they are split apart from the exalted greatness of Allah, and the Most High and His majesty, and this is indicated by its coming after ﴿the Most High, the Great﴾.

It has also been said: from their attributing a child to Him, like His words: ﴿The heavens are almost torn apart because of it﴾ [Maryam: 90]. If you ask: why did He say "from above them"? I say: because the greatest signs and the most indicative of majesty and greatness are above the heavens, namely the 'Arsh (throne), the Kursi (footstool), and the ranks of angels reverberating with glorification and sanctification around the Throne, and what none knows the reality of except Allah, of the traces of His supreme dominion. Therefore He said: ﴿they are split apart from above them﴾, that is, the splitting begins from the upper direction.

Al-Hawfi and a group said: (from above them), and the ha' and nun are a reference to the earths. End of quotation.

(From above them) is connected to (yatafattarna), and the earlier mention of the earth supports this view.

'Ali ibn Sulayman al-Akhfash said: the pronoun refers to the disbelievers, and the meaning is: from above the sects and the heretical groups, that is, because of their sayings. End of quotation.

It was said that am means only the hamzah, and the discussion of this kind was treated earlier where the disjunctive am appears. The meaning: they took protectors besides Allah, but they are not protectors in reality; Allah is the Protector, and He alone is to be taken as protector, not those who neither harm nor benefit among their protectors.

When He informed that He is the Protector, He followed it with this extraordinary act that none but Him can perform, which is giving life to the dead.

When He mentioned this attribute, He mentioned His power over every thing that His will relates to.

Al-Zamakhshari said: concerning His saying: ﴿فاللَّهُ هو الوَلِيُّ﴾, the fa' in ﴿فاللَّهُ هو الوَلِيُّ﴾ is the answer to an implied condition, as if it were said: after denying every protector other than Him, and if they meant a protector in truth, then Allah is the Protector in truth, and there is no protector other than Him. End of quotation.

There is no need to posit an omitted condition, since the speech is complete without it.

﴿وما اخْتَلَفْتُمْ فِيهِ مِن شَيْءٍ﴾ ("And whatever you differ about, its judgment is with Allah"): this is a quotation of the Messenger's words, i.e., whatever you differ about, O people, of denial or affirmation, faith or disbelief, or otherwise, its judgment and its recompense belong to Allah alone, not to me. The phrase min shay' (anything) indicates generality.

It was said: "anything" means any dispute, so they should bring it before the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and not prefer the judgment of anyone else over his judgment, as in His saying: ﴿فَإنْ تَنازَعْتُمْ في شَيْءٍ فَرُدُّوهُ إلى اللَّهِ والرَّسُولِ﴾ (An-Nisa' 59). It was said: "min shay'" means: concerning the interpretation of a verse that is unclear to you, return in its explanation to the clear verses of the Book of Allah and the apparent Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

It was said: what you differ about of the sciences that do not relate to your obligations, and for which you have no path to knowledge, then say: "Allah knows best," as with the knowledge of the spirit.

Al-Zamakhshari said: i.e., what the disbelievers, among the People of the Book and the polytheists, opposed you in, so that you and they differed regarding matters of religion; the judgment about that disputed matter is entrusted to Allah, who rewards those among the believers who are right in it and reproaches the wrongdoers. End of quotation.

(ذَلِكم) ("That is your Judge"): ﴿رَبِّي عَلَيْهِ تَوَكَّلْتُ﴾ ("My Lord, upon Him I have relied") in repelling the plots of the enemies of the religion, and to Him I return for protection from their evil. End of quotation.

The majority read (فاطِرُ) with nominative case, i.e., He is the Creator (fatir), or it is a predicate after a predicate, like His saying (ذَلِكم).

Zayd ibn 'Ali read (فاطِرِ) in the genitive, as an attribute of (إلى اللَّهِ), and the clause after it is a parenthetical clause between the attribute and the thing described.

﴿جَعَلَ لَكم مِن أنْفُسِكُمْ﴾ ("He made for you from yourselves"), i.e., from the kind of your own selves, i.e., human beings. (أزْواجًا) ("mates"): females. Or: He made, for our father Adam, from his rib, Hawwa' as a spouse for him, as creation for us. ﴿ومِنَ الأنْعامِ أزْواجًا﴾ ("and from the cattle, mates"), i.e., many kinds, males and females, or mates that are females.

﴿يَذْرَؤُكم فِيهِ﴾ ("He multiplies you through it"). Ibn 'Abbas said: i.e., He makes for you in it a livelihood by which you live. Ibn Zayd said: He provides for you in it, and this is close to the previous saying.

Mujahid said: He creates you in the wombs of females. Ibn Zayd also said: He multiplies you through what He created of the heavens and the earth. Al-Zajjaj said: He increases you by it, i.e., in it, i.e., He increases you in your creation as mates.

'Ali ibn Sulayman said: He moves you from one state to another.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the pronoun in fihi refers to the making (al-ja'l), i.e., He creates you and multiplies you in the making, as you say: "I spoke to Zayd a speech, I honored him in it." He said: the word dhara'a adds a meaning beyond the word khalaqa that is not in khalaqa, namely the succession of generations over the passage of time.

Al-Zamakhshari said: (يَذْرَؤُكم): He multiplies you. It is said dhara'a Allah the creation: He scattered them and multiplied them, and dhar', dhurū', and dharwa' are siblings in this arrangement, which is that He made for people and cattle mates, so that between their males and females there is procreation and propagation.

The pronoun in yadhra'ukum refers to the addressees, and (al-an'am) has the rational addressees given precedence over the non-rational, and this is among the rulings with two causes. End of quotation.

His saying "this is among the rulings with two causes" is a strange technical term; he means that address takes precedence over absence when they are combined, so you say: "You and Zayd will stand," and rational beings take precedence over non-rational when combined, so you say: "The animals and others glorify their Creator."

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, what is the meaning of "He multiplies you" in this arrangement? Why was it not said "He multiplies you through it"? I answer: He made this arrangement like a spring and a mine for scattering and multiplying. Do you not see that you say of animals in the creation of pairs that there is multiplication? As He, exalted, said: ﴿ولَكم في القِصاصِ حَياةٌ﴾ (Al-Baqarah 179). End of quotation.

﴿لَيْسَ كَمِثْلِهِ شَيْءٌ﴾ ("There is nothing like His likeness"): the Arabs say, "one like you does not do such-and-such," meaning the addressee, as if when they negate the attribute from the likeness of a person, that is a negation from the person himself, and this is from the category of hyperbole. Similar to the verse is the saying of Aws ibn Hajar:

"There is not like the youth Zuhayr / a character that matches him in virtues."

Another said:

"And slain men like trunks of palm trees / covered by a pouring downpour."

Another said:

"Sa'd ibn Zayd, when you look at their excellence / there is not, among people, anyone like them."

So the verse proceeds in that matter according to the manner of Arabic speech, applying the word "like" to the very self of a thing. As for what al-Tabari and others held, that mithl is redundant for emphasis, like the kaf in His saying:

"So she became like a devoured stalk,"

and in the saying:

"And lofty ones like the pots that are set up on stones,"

this is not sound, because mithl is a noun, and nouns are not made redundant, unlike the kaf, which is a particle and so is suitable for redundancy.

The parallel of attributing "likeness" to one who has no likeness is your saying: "So-and-so's hand is outstretched," meaning that he is generous, though in reality there is no hand for him, as in His saying: ﴿بَلْ يَداهُ مَبْسُوطَتانِ﴾ (Al-Ma'idah 64).

Just as you made that a metaphor for generosity regarding one who has no hand, so you made likeness a metaphor for essence regarding one who has no likeness.

It is also possible that by "likeness" is meant the attribute, and that is permissible: the word mithl is used in the sense of attribute, so the meaning becomes: no attribute among the attributes of others is like the attribute of Him, exalted. This is an easy interpretation, while the first is subtler.

Ibn Qutaybah said: The Arabs use the example to stand in place of the self, so one says: "One like me is not told this," meaning: "I am not told this." End of quotation.

Thus this has become a metaphor for the essence, and there is no difference between your saying "There is nothing like Allah" and "There is nothing like the likeness of Allah." The exegetes have agreed that the kaf and mithl are not meant in their literal sense of comparison, since that would imply affirming a likeness to Allah, exalted, which is impossible.

﴿وهُوَ السَّمِيعُ﴾ ("And He is the All-Hearing") of the speech of creatures, (البَصِيرُ) ("the All-Seeing") of their deeds. The explanation of ﴿لَهُ مَقالِيدُ السَّماواتِ والأرْضِ﴾ has been given earlier in Surah az-Zumar. It was read (ويَقْدِرُ), i.e., He straitens.

﴿إنَّهُ بِكُلِّ شَيْءٍ عَلِيمٌ﴾ ("Indeed, He is All-Knowing of everything"), i.e., He expands for whom He wills and straitens for whom He wills. Al-Zamakhshari said: When He knows that wealth is good for the servant, He enriches him, not impoverishes him. End of quotation. In this there is a trace of Mu'tazilite doctrine.

Surah 42: al-Shura (Consultation), fifty-three verses, Meccan

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Ha, Mim﴾ ﴿'Ayn, Sin, Qaf﴾ ﴿Thus does He reveal to you, and to those before you, Allah, the Almighty, the All-Wise﴾ ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and He is the Most High, the Great﴾ ﴿The heavens are almost torn apart from above them, while the angels glorify their Lord with praise and seek forgiveness for those on earth. Surely Allah is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾ ﴿And those who take protectors other than Him—Allah is Watchful over them, and you are not a guardian over them﴾ ﴿Thus We have revealed to you an Arabic Qur'an that you may warn the Mother of Cities (Makkah) and those around it, and warn of the Day of Assembly, about which there is no doubt: a party will be in the Garden and a party in the Blaze﴾ ﴿Had Allah willed, He would have made them one community, but He admits whom He wills into His mercy, while the wrongdoers have neither protector nor helper﴾ ﴿Or have they taken protectors other than Him? But Allah is the Protector, and He gives life to the dead, and He is Powerful over all things﴾ ﴿Whatever you differ over, its judgment rests with Allah. That is Allah, my Lord; in Him I have placed my trust, and to Him I turn in repentance﴾ ﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth, He made for you mates from among yourselves, and of the cattle mates too, multiplying you thereby. There is nothing like Him, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing﴾ ﴿To Him belong the keys of the heavens and the earth. He extends provision to whom He wills and restricts it; surely He has full knowledge of all things﴾

These verses are Meccan according to al-Hasan, 'Ata', 'Ikrimah and Jabir. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is Meccan except for four verses from His words, ﴿Say, I do not ask you any reward for it, except love for the near kin﴾ [al-Shura: 23] to the end of the four verses, for they were revealed in Madinah. Muqatil said: among it, a Madinan part is His words, ﴿That is what Allah gives as good news to His servants﴾ [al-Shura: 23] up to (al-Sudur). The connection between the beginning of the surah and what precedes it is that He said, ﴿Say: Have you considered, if it is from Allah...﴾ [Fussilat: 52], and in that was a judgment that they were in error.

When they disbelieved in it, He said here "thus" (kadhalika), meaning: like the earlier revelation of the Qur'an which these people disbelieved in. ﴿He reveals to you﴾: that is, His revelation to you, may He be exalted, is continuous and uninterrupted, attending to you from time to time.

The exegetes mentioned regarding ﴿Ha, Mim﴾ ﴿'Ayn, Sin, Qaf﴾ conflicting opinions, none of which is sound, as is their habit with these openings; we set aside mentioning them entirely.

Al-Jumhur read (yuhi) in the active voice; Abu Haywa, al-A'sha from Abu Bakr, and Aban read (nuhi) with the plural of majesty (nun of greatness).

Mujahid, Ibn Kathir, 'Abbas, and Mahbub, both of whom are from Abu 'Amr, read (yuha) in the passive voice; and (Allah) is nominative by a hidden verb whose implied sense is "He revealed," or by the subject, the implied sense being: Allah, the Almighty, the All-Wise, the Revealer.

On the reading (nuhi) with the nun, ﴿Allah, the Almighty, the All-Wise﴾ is subject and predicate.

(Yuhi) either means "obligated," so that His words ﴿and to those before you﴾ are coherently linked, or it is read in its own sense, and an implied governing verb connected to (ila alladhina) is assumed, its sense being: "and He revealed to those before you." The discussion of ﴿The heavens are almost torn apart﴾ has already been covered in Surah Maryam, both in reading and interpretation.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Yunus related from Abu 'Amr, and it is an Arabic reading, (tatafattarna) with two taʼs and a nun, and its parallel is a rare form transmitted in the Nawadir of Ibn al-A'rabi: "the camels tatashammamna." End of quotation.

The apparent meaning is that this is a mistake by al-Zamakhshari in transmission, because Ibn Khalawayh mentioned in his collection of irregular readings that Yunus related from Abu 'Amr a reading that put (tafattarna) with a ta and a nun. Ibn Khalawayh said: this is a rare form, because the Arabs do not combine the two markers of feminine gender.

It is not said: "al-nisa' taqumna," but "yaqumna," and "al-walidat yurdi'na." Abu 'Umar al-Zahid had indeed transmitted in the Nawadir of Ibn al-A'rabi "al-ibl tatashammamna," which we rejected, but he strengthened it, because this is Ibn Khalawayh's statement. If the copies of al-Zamakhshari all agree on his saying with two taʼs and a nun, then it is a mistake; and if in some of them it is with one ta and a nun, it agrees with Ibn Khalawayh's statement, and the two-ta version would be a scribal distortion.

Likewise their writing of (tatafattarna) and (tatashammamna) with two ta's. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in (min fawqihinna) returns to (al-samawat). Ibn 'Atiyyah said: from their upper parts. Al-Zamakhshari said: they are split apart from the exalted greatness of Allah, and the Most High and His majesty, and this is indicated by its coming after ﴿the Most High, the Great﴾.

It has also been said: from their attributing a child to Him, like His words: ﴿The heavens are almost torn apart because of it﴾ [Maryam: 90]. If you ask: why did He say "from above them"? I say: because the greatest signs and the most indicative of majesty and greatness are above the heavens, namely the 'Arsh (throne), the Kursi (footstool), and the ranks of angels reverberating with glorification and sanctification around the Throne, and what none knows the reality of except Allah, of the traces of His supreme dominion. Therefore He said: ﴿they are split apart from above them﴾, that is, the splitting begins from the upper direction.

Al-Hawfi and a group said: (from above them), and the ha' and nun are a reference to the earths. End of quotation.

(From above them) is connected to (yatafattarna), and the earlier mention of the earth supports this view.

'Ali ibn Sulayman al-Akhfash said: the pronoun refers to the disbelievers, and the meaning is: from above the sects and the heretical groups, that is, because of their sayings. End of quotation.

This verse is like the one in Surah Maryam. Makki considered this view unlikely, saying: it is not permissible for male sons of Adam, meaning the feminine pronoun, and what Makki mentioned is an inference. 'Ali ibn Sulayman said: above the sects and groups, and the apparent meaning of the angels is generality. Muqatil said: the bearers of the Throne and the glorification; it was said: their saying "Subhan Allah," and it was said: they say "La ilaha illa Allah." The apparent meaning of (yastaghfirun) is seeking forgiveness, and for the people of the earth is a general statement specified by His words: ﴿and they seek forgiveness for those who believe﴾ [Ghafir: 7], as said by al-Suddi. It was also said: it is general. The meaning of seeking forgiveness is seeking guidance which leads to forgiveness, as if they were saying: "O Allah, guide the people of the earth, and forgive them."

This is indicated by His being described with forgiveness, mercy and opening.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is possible that they intend by seeking forgiveness for them: asking for forbearance and pardon, as in His words: ﴿Allah holds the heavens and the earth lest they cease; surely He is Forbearing, Forgiving﴾ [Fatir: 41], and His words: ﴿Surely your Lord is full of forgiveness for mankind despite their wrongdoing﴾ [al-Ra'd: 6], and the meaning is forbearance towards them, and that He does not hasten to punish them, so it is general. End of quotation.

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi spoke about His words ﴿the heavens are almost torn apart﴾ with statements outside the usual meanings of Arabic, drawn from the words of the philosophers and those who follow their path; this can be consulted in his book.

﴿Those who take protectors other than Him﴾: that is, idols and images; ﴿Allah is Watchful over them﴾: that is, over their deeds and the One who will recompense them for them; ﴿and you are not a guardian over them﴾: that is, not one entrusted with their affair nor one responsible for them.

What is in this of conciliation has been abrogated by the verse of the sword. (And thus) that is: like this revelation and decree, you are not a guardian over them, ﴿We have revealed to you an Arabic Qur'an﴾.

(p-509) The apparent meaning is that (Qur'anan) is the object of (awhayna).

Al-Zamakhshari said: the kaf is the object, that is, We revealed it to you, and it is an Arabic Qur'an with no ambiguity upon you, since it came in your tongue. End of quotation.

I translate the passage as requested, with the Qur'anic quotations, technical terms, and the grammatical discussion handled according to the guidelines.

Likewise, the first object is omitted, and the second is ﴿يَوْمَ الجَمْعِ﴾ ("the Day of Assembly"), i.e., the gathering of creatures. The thing warned of is what takes place on the Day of Assembly of recompense and the division of the gathering into two groups, or the gathering of spirits with bodies, or the people of the earth with the people of the heavens, or people with their deeds. These are four opinions.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿لا رَيْبَ فِيهِ﴾ is certainly a parenthetical clause (i'tiraḍ). End of quotation.

It does not appear that it is a parenthetical clause, in the technical grammatical sense, since it did not come between a speaker and what is spoken of.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, what is the meaning of "He multiplies you" in this arrangement? Why was it not said "He multiplies you through it"? I answer: He made this arrangement like a spring and a mine for scattering and multiplying. Do you not see that you say of animals in the creation of pairs that there is multiplication? As He, exalted, said: ﴿ولَكم في القِصاصِ حَياةٌ﴾ (Al-Baqarah 179). End of quotation.

﴿لَيْسَ كَمِثْلِهِ شَيْءٌ﴾ ("There is nothing like His likeness"): the Arabs say, "one like you does not do such-and-such," meaning the addressee, as if when they negate the attribute from the likeness of a person, that is a negation from the person himself, and this is from the category of hyperbole. Similar to the verse is the saying of Aws ibn Hajar:

"There is not like the youth Zuhayr / a character that matches him in virtues."

Another said:

"And slain men like trunks of palm trees / covered by a pouring downpour."

Another said:

"Sa'd ibn Zayd, when you look at their excellence / there is not, among people, anyone like them."

So the verse proceeds in that matter according to the manner of Arabic speech, applying the word "like" to the very self of a thing. As for what al-Tabari and others held, that mithl is redundant for emphasis, like the kaf in His saying:

"So she became like a devoured stalk,"

and in the saying:

"And lofty ones like the pots that are set up on stones,"

this is not sound, because mithl is a noun, and nouns are not made redundant, unlike the kaf, which is a particle and so is suitable for redundancy.

The parallel of attributing "likeness" to one who has no likeness is your saying: "So-and-so's hand is outstretched," meaning that he is generous, though in reality there is no hand for him, as in His saying: ﴿بَلْ يَداهُ مَبْسُوطَتانِ﴾ (Al-Ma'idah 64).

Just as you made that a metaphor for generosity regarding one who has no hand, so you made likeness a metaphor for essence regarding one who has no likeness.

It is also possible that by "likeness" is meant the attribute, and that is permissible: the word mithl is used in the sense of attribute, so the meaning becomes: no attribute among the attributes of others is like the attribute of Him, exalted. This is an easy interpretation, while the first is subtler.

Ibn Qutaybah said: The Arabs use the example to stand in place of the self, so one says: "One like me is not told this," meaning: "I am not told this." End of quotation.

Thus this has become a metaphor for the essence, and there is no difference between your saying "There is nothing like Allah" and "There is nothing like the likeness of Allah." The exegetes have agreed that the kaf and mithl are not meant in their literal sense of comparison, since that would imply affirming a likeness to Allah, exalted, which is impossible.

﴿وهُوَ السَّمِيعُ﴾ ("And He is the All-Hearing") of the speech of creatures, (البَصِيرُ) ("the All-Seeing") of their deeds. The explanation of ﴿لَهُ مَقالِيدُ السَّماواتِ والأرْضِ﴾ has been given earlier in Surah az-Zumar. It was read (ويَقْدِرُ), i.e., He straitens.

﴿إنَّهُ بِكُلِّ شَيْءٍ عَلِيمٌ﴾ ("Indeed, He is All-Knowing of everything"), i.e., He expands for whom He wills and straitens for whom He wills. Al-Zamakhshari said: When He knows that wealth is good for the servant, He enriches him, not impoverishes him. End of quotation. In this there is a trace of Mu'tazilite doctrine.

Surah 42: al-Shura (Consultation), fifty-three verses, Meccan

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Ha, Mim﴾ ﴿'Ayn, Sin, Qaf﴾ ﴿Thus does He reveal to you, and to those before you, Allah, the Almighty, the All-Wise﴾ ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and He is the Most High, the Great﴾ ﴿The heavens are almost torn apart from above them, while the angels glorify their Lord with praise and seek forgiveness for those on earth. Surely Allah is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾ ﴿And those who take protectors other than Him—Allah is Watchful over them, and you are not a guardian over them﴾ ﴿Thus We have revealed to you an Arabic Qur'an that you may warn the Mother of Cities (Makkah) and those around it, and warn of the Day of Assembly, about which there is no doubt: a party will be in the Garden and a party in the Blaze﴾ ﴿Had Allah willed, He would have made them one community, but He admits whom He wills into His mercy, while the wrongdoers have neither protector nor helper﴾ ﴿Or have they taken protectors other than Him? But Allah is the Protector, and He gives life to the dead, and He is Powerful over all things﴾ ﴿Whatever you differ over, its judgment rests with Allah. That is Allah, my Lord; in Him I have placed my trust, and to Him I turn in repentance﴾ ﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth, He made for you mates from among yourselves, and of the cattle mates too, multiplying you thereby. There is nothing like Him, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing﴾ ﴿To Him belong the keys of the heavens and the earth. He extends provision to whom He wills and restricts it; surely He has full knowledge of all things﴾

These verses are Meccan according to al-Hasan, 'Ata', 'Ikrimah and Jabir. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is Meccan except for four verses from His words, ﴿Say, I do not ask you any reward for it, except love for the near kin﴾ [al-Shura: 23] to the end of the four verses, for they were revealed in Madinah. Muqatil said: among it, a Madinan part is His words, ﴿That is what Allah gives as good news to His servants﴾ [al-Shura: 23] up to (al-Sudur). The connection between the beginning of the surah and what precedes it is that He said, ﴿Say: Have you considered, if it is from Allah...﴾ [Fussilat: 52], and in that was a judgment that they were in error.

When they disbelieved in it, He said here "thus" (kadhalika), meaning: like the earlier revelation of the Qur'an which these people disbelieved in. ﴿He reveals to you﴾: that is, His revelation to you, may He be exalted, is continuous and uninterrupted, attending to you from time to time.

The exegetes mentioned regarding ﴿Ha, Mim﴾ ﴿'Ayn, Sin, Qaf﴾ conflicting opinions, none of which is sound, as is their habit with these openings; we set aside mentioning them entirely.

Al-Jumhur read (yuhi) in the active voice; Abu Haywa, al-A'sha from Abu Bakr, and Aban read (nuhi) with the plural of majesty (nun of greatness).

Mujahid, Ibn Kathir, 'Abbas, and Mahbub, both of whom are from Abu 'Amr, read (yuha) in the passive voice; and (Allah) is nominative by a hidden verb whose implied sense is "He revealed," or by the subject, the implied sense being: Allah, the Almighty, the All-Wise, the Revealer.

On the reading (nuhi) with the nun, ﴿Allah, the Almighty, the All-Wise﴾ is subject and predicate.

(Yuhi) either means "obligated," so that His words ﴿and to those before you﴾ are coherently linked, or it is read in its own sense, and an implied governing verb connected to (ila alladhina) is assumed, its sense being: "and He revealed to those before you." The discussion of ﴿The heavens are almost torn apart﴾ has already been covered in Surah Maryam, both in reading and interpretation.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Yunus related from Abu 'Amr, and it is an Arabic reading, (tatafattarna) with two taʼs and a nun, and its parallel is a rare form transmitted in the Nawadir of Ibn al-A'rabi: "the camels tatashammamna." End of quotation.

The apparent meaning is that this is a mistake by al-Zamakhshari in transmission, because Ibn Khalawayh mentioned in his collection of irregular readings that Yunus related from Abu 'Amr a reading that put (tafattarna) with a ta and a nun. Ibn Khalawayh said: this is a rare form, because the Arabs do not combine the two markers of feminine gender.

It is not said: "al-nisa' taqumna," but "yaqumna," and "al-walidat yurdi'na." Abu 'Umar al-Zahid had indeed transmitted in the Nawadir of Ibn al-A'rabi "al-ibl tatashammamna," which we rejected, but he strengthened it, because this is Ibn Khalawayh's statement. If the copies of al-Zamakhshari all agree on his saying with two taʼs and a nun, then it is a mistake; and if in some of them it is with one ta and a nun, it agrees with Ibn Khalawayh's statement, and the two-ta version would be a scribal distortion.

Likewise their writing of (tatafattarna) and (tatashammamna) with two ta's. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in (min fawqihinna) returns to (al-samawat). Ibn 'Atiyyah said: from their upper parts. Al-Zamakhshari said: they are split apart from the exalted greatness of Allah, and the Most High and His majesty, and this is indicated by its coming after ﴿the Most High, the Great﴾.

It has also been said: from their attributing a child to Him, like His words: ﴿The heavens are almost torn apart because of it﴾ [Maryam: 90]. If you ask: why did He say "from above them"? I say: because the greatest signs and the most indicative of majesty and greatness are above the heavens, namely the 'Arsh (throne), the Kursi (footstool), and the ranks of angels reverberating with glorification and sanctification around the Throne, and what none knows the reality of except Allah, of the traces of His supreme dominion. Therefore He said: ﴿they are split apart from above them﴾, that is, the splitting begins from the upper direction.

Al-Hawfi and a group said: (from above them), and the ha' and nun are a reference to the earths. End of quotation.

(From above them) is connected to (yatafattarna), and the earlier mention of the earth supports this view.

'Ali ibn Sulayman al-Akhfash said: the pronoun refers to the disbelievers, and the meaning is: from above the sects and the heretical groups, that is, because of their sayings. End of quotation.

This verse is like the one in Surah Maryam. Makki considered this view unlikely, saying: it is not permissible for male sons of Adam, meaning the feminine pronoun, and what Makki mentioned is an inference. 'Ali ibn Sulayman said: above the sects and groups, and the apparent meaning of the angels is generality. Muqatil said: the bearers of the Throne and the glorification; it was said: their saying "Subhan Allah," and it was said: they say "La ilaha illa Allah." The apparent meaning of (yastaghfirun) is seeking forgiveness, and for the people of the earth is a general statement specified by His words: ﴿and they seek forgiveness for those who believe﴾ [Ghafir: 7], as said by al-Suddi. It was also said: it is general. The meaning of seeking forgiveness is seeking guidance which leads to forgiveness, as if they were saying: "O Allah, guide the people of the earth, and forgive them."

This is indicated by His being described with forgiveness, mercy and opening.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is possible that they intend by seeking forgiveness for them: asking for forbearance and pardon, as in His words: ﴿Allah holds the heavens and the earth lest they cease; surely He is Forbearing, Forgiving﴾ [Fatir: 41], and His words: ﴿Surely your Lord is full of forgiveness for mankind despite their wrongdoing﴾ [al-Ra'd: 6], and the meaning is forbearance towards them, and that He does not hasten to punish them, so it is general. End of quotation.

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi spoke about His words ﴿the heavens are almost torn apart﴾ with statements outside the usual meanings of Arabic, drawn from the words of the philosophers and those who follow their path; this can be consulted in his book.

﴿Those who take protectors other than Him﴾: that is, idols and images; ﴿Allah is Watchful over them﴾: that is, over their deeds and the One who will recompense them for them; ﴿and you are not a guardian over them﴾: that is, not one entrusted with their affair nor one responsible for them.

What is in this of conciliation has been abrogated by the verse of the sword. (And thus) that is: like this revelation and decree, you are not a guardian over them, ﴿We have revealed to you an Arabic Qur'an﴾.

(p-509) The apparent meaning is that (Qur'anan) is the object of (awhayna).

Al-Zamakhshari said: the kaf is the object, that is, We revealed it to you, and it is an Arabic Qur'an with no ambiguity upon you, since it came in your tongue. End of quotation.

I translate the passage as requested, with the Qur'anic quotations, technical terms, and the grammatical discussion handled according to the guidelines.

Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 42, verses 1–12 (part 2 of 2):

He used the kaf (كاف) as a noun within the speech, and this is the view of al-Akhfash (al-Akhfash, the grammarian).

﴿لِتُنْذِرَ أُمَّ القُرى﴾ ("that you may warn the Mother of Towns"): Makkah, i.e., the people of Umm al-Qura. Likewise, the first object is omitted, and the second is ﴿يَوْمَ الجَمْعِ﴾ ("the Day of Assembly"), i.e., the gathering of creatures. The thing warned of is what takes place on the Day of Assembly of recompense and the division of the gathering into two groups, or the gathering of spirits with bodies, or the people of the earth with the people of the heavens, or people with their deeds. These are four opinions.

(لِيُنْذِرَ) with the ya' of the third person, i.e., "that it may warn": the Qur'an is the subject.

﴿لا رَيْبَ فِيهِ﴾ ("there is no doubt in it"), i.e., there is no doubt about its occurrence.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿لا رَيْبَ فِيهِ﴾ is certainly a parenthetical clause (i'tiraḍ). End of quotation.

It does not appear that it is a parenthetical clause, in the technical grammatical sense, since it did not come between a speaker and what is spoken of.

The majority of readers read (فَرِيقٌ) with nominative case in both places, i.e., they are a group, or among them is a group. Zayd ibn 'Ali read both in the accusative, i.e., they separated, a group in such-and-such and a group in such-and-such; and the separation is indicated by the gathering understood from "the Day of Assembly."

﴿ولَوْ شاءَ اللَّهُ لَجَعَلَهم أُمَّةً واحِدَةً﴾ ("And if Allah had willed, He would have made them one community"): meaning, in faith or in disbelief. Al-Dahhak said this, and it is the view of the People of the Sunnah. This is consolation for the Messenger, for what he endured from his people's disbelief, and a reminder that this rests with His will; but whoever has been preceded by happiness, He admits into His mercy.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿لَجَعَلَهم أُمَّةً واحِدَةً﴾ means all of them believers by compulsion and coercion, like His saying: ﴿ولَوْ شِئْنا لَآتَيْنا كُلَّ نَفْسٍ هُداها﴾ (As-Sajdah 13), and His saying: ﴿ولَوْ شاءَ رَبُّكَ لَآمَنَ مَن في الأرْضِ كُلُّهم جَمِيعًا﴾ (Yunus 99).

The proof that the meaning is compulsion toward faith is His saying: ﴿أفَأنْتَ تُكْرِهُ النّاسَ حَتّى يَكُونُوا مُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ (Yunus 99). He mentioned what he thought was evidence for this, and it is in the manner of the Mu'tazilah.

Anas ibn Malik said: ﴿فِي رَحْمَتِهِ﴾ ("in His mercy") means: in the religion of Islam.

﴿أمِ اتَّخَذُوا مِن دُونِهِ أوْلِياءَ﴾ ("Or have they taken protectors besides Him?"): am here means "rather" (bal), for transition from one speech to another, and the hamzah is for denunciation of them for taking protectors besides Allah. It was said that am means only the hamzah, and the discussion of this kind was treated earlier where the disjunctive am appears. The meaning: they took protectors besides Allah, but they are not protectors in reality; Allah is the Protector, and He alone is to be taken as protector, not those who neither harm nor benefit among their protectors.

When He informed that He is the Protector, He followed it with this extraordinary act that none but Him can perform, which is giving life to the dead.

When He mentioned this attribute, He mentioned His power over every thing that His will relates to.

Al-Zamakhshari said: concerning His saying: ﴿فاللَّهُ هو الوَلِيُّ﴾, the fa' in ﴿فاللَّهُ هو الوَلِيُّ﴾ is the answer to an implied condition, as if it were said: after denying every protector other than Him, and if they meant a protector in truth, then Allah is the Protector in truth, and there is no protector other than Him. End of quotation.

There is no need to posit an omitted condition, since the speech is complete without it.

﴿وما اخْتَلَفْتُمْ فِيهِ مِن شَيْءٍ﴾ ("And whatever you differ about, its judgment is with Allah"): this is a quotation of the Messenger's words, i.e., whatever you differ about, O people, of denial or affirmation, faith or disbelief, or otherwise, its judgment and its recompense belong to Allah alone, not to me. The phrase min shay' (anything) indicates generality.

It was said: "anything" means any dispute, so they should bring it before the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and not prefer the judgment of anyone else over his judgment, as in His saying: ﴿فَإنْ تَنازَعْتُمْ في شَيْءٍ فَرُدُّوهُ إلى اللَّهِ والرَّسُولِ﴾ (An-Nisa' 59). It was said: "min shay'" means: concerning the interpretation of a verse that is unclear to you, return in its explanation to the clear verses of the Book of Allah and the apparent Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

It was said: what you differ about of the sciences that do not relate to your obligations, and for which you have no path to knowledge, then say: "Allah knows best," as with the knowledge of the spirit.

Al-Zamakhshari said: i.e., what the disbelievers, among the People of the Book and the polytheists, opposed you in, so that you and they differed regarding matters of religion; the judgment about that disputed matter is entrusted to Allah, who rewards those among the believers who are right in it and reproaches the wrongdoers. End of quotation.

(ذَلِكم) ("That is your Judge"): ﴿رَبِّي عَلَيْهِ تَوَكَّلْتُ﴾ ("My Lord, upon Him I have relied") in repelling the plots of the enemies of the religion, and to Him I return for protection from their evil. End of quotation.

The majority read (فاطِرُ) with nominative case, i.e., He is the Creator (fatir), or it is a predicate after a predicate, like His saying (ذَلِكم).

Zayd ibn 'Ali read (فاطِرِ) in the genitive, as an attribute of (إلى اللَّهِ), and the clause after it is a parenthetical clause between the attribute and the thing described.

﴿جَعَلَ لَكم مِن أنْفُسِكُمْ﴾ ("He made for you from yourselves"), i.e., from the kind of your own selves, i.e., human beings. (أزْواجًا) ("mates"): females. Or: He made, for our father Adam, from his rib, Hawwa' as a spouse for him, as creation for us. ﴿ومِنَ الأنْعامِ أزْواجًا﴾ ("and from the cattle, mates"), i.e., many kinds, males and females, or mates that are females.

﴿يَذْرَؤُكم فِيهِ﴾ ("He multiplies you through it"). Ibn 'Abbas said: i.e., He makes for you in it a livelihood by which you live. Ibn Zayd said: He provides for you in it, and this is close to the previous saying.

Mujahid said: He creates you in the wombs of females. Ibn Zayd also said: He multiplies you through what He created of the heavens and the earth. Al-Zajjaj said: He increases you by it, i.e., in it, i.e., He increases you in your creation as mates.

'Ali ibn Sulayman said: He moves you from one state to another.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the pronoun in fihi refers to the making (al-ja'l), i.e., He creates you and multiplies you in the making, as you say: "I spoke to Zayd a speech, I honored him in it." He said: the word dhara'a adds a meaning beyond the word khalaqa that is not in khalaqa, namely the succession of generations over the passage of time.

Al-Zamakhshari said: (يَذْرَؤُكم): He multiplies you. It is said dhara'a Allah the creation: He scattered them and multiplied them, and dhar', dhurū', and dharwa' are siblings in this arrangement, which is that He made for people and cattle mates, so that between their males and females there is procreation and propagation.

The pronoun in yadhra'ukum refers to the addressees, and (al-an'am) has the rational addressees given precedence over the non-rational, and this is among the rulings with two causes. End of quotation.

His saying "this is among the rulings with two causes" is a strange technical term; he means that address takes precedence over absence when they are combined, so you say: "You and Zayd will stand," and rational beings take precedence over non-rational when combined, so you say: "The animals and others glorify their Creator."

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, what is the meaning of "He multiplies you" in this arrangement? Why was it not said "He multiplies you through it"? I answer: He made this arrangement like a spring and a mine for scattering and multiplying. Do you not see that you say of animals in the creation of pairs that there is multiplication? As He, exalted, said: ﴿ولَكم في القِصاصِ حَياةٌ﴾ (Al-Baqarah 179). End of quotation.

﴿لَيْسَ كَمِثْلِهِ شَيْءٌ﴾ ("There is nothing like His likeness"): the Arabs say, "one like you does not do such-and-such," meaning the addressee, as if when they negate the attribute from the likeness of a person, that is a negation from the person himself, and this is from the category of hyperbole. Similar to the verse is the saying of Aws ibn Hajar:

"There is not like the youth Zuhayr / a character that matches him in virtues."

Another said:

"And slain men like trunks of palm trees / covered by a pouring downpour."

Another said:

"Sa'd ibn Zayd, when you look at their excellence / there is not, among people, anyone like them."

So the verse proceeds in that matter according to the manner of Arabic speech, applying the word "like" to the very self of a thing. As for what al-Tabari and others held, that mithl is redundant for emphasis, like the kaf in His saying:

"So she became like a devoured stalk,"

and in the saying:

"And lofty ones like the pots that are set up on stones,"

this is not sound, because mithl is a noun, and nouns are not made redundant, unlike the kaf, which is a particle and so is suitable for redundancy.

The parallel of attributing "likeness" to one who has no likeness is your saying: "So-and-so's hand is outstretched," meaning that he is generous, though in reality there is no hand for him, as in His saying: ﴿بَلْ يَداهُ مَبْسُوطَتانِ﴾ (Al-Ma'idah 64).

Just as you made that a metaphor for generosity regarding one who has no hand, so you made likeness a metaphor for essence regarding one who has no likeness.

It is also possible that by "likeness" is meant the attribute, and that is permissible: the word mithl is used in the sense of attribute, so the meaning becomes: no attribute among the attributes of others is like the attribute of Him, exalted. This is an easy interpretation, while the first is subtler.

Ibn Qutaybah said: The Arabs use the example to stand in place of the self, so one says: "One like me is not told this," meaning: "I am not told this." End of quotation.

Thus this has become a metaphor for the essence, and there is no difference between your saying "There is nothing like Allah" and "There is nothing like the likeness of Allah." The exegetes have agreed that the kaf and mithl are not meant in their literal sense of comparison, since that would imply affirming a likeness to Allah, exalted, which is impossible.

﴿وهُوَ السَّمِيعُ﴾ ("And He is the All-Hearing") of the speech of creatures, (البَصِيرُ) ("the All-Seeing") of their deeds. The explanation of ﴿لَهُ مَقالِيدُ السَّماواتِ والأرْضِ﴾ has been given earlier in Surah az-Zumar. It was read (ويَقْدِرُ), i.e., He straitens.

﴿إنَّهُ بِكُلِّ شَيْءٍ عَلِيمٌ﴾ ("Indeed, He is All-Knowing of everything"), i.e., He expands for whom He wills and straitens for whom He wills. Al-Zamakhshari said: When He knows that wealth is good for the servant, He enriches him, not impoverishes him. End of quotation. In this there is a trace of Mu'tazilite doctrine.
