﴿And He is the Protector﴾: He who takes charge of His servants; (the Praiseworthy): the One praised for the blessings He has bestowed. (And what He has scattered) — the apparent reading is that it is in the genitive, conjoined to "the heavens and the earth." It is also permissible that it be in the nominative, conjoined to (خَلْقُ) with an elided genitive, i.e., and the creation of what He has scattered. Regarding both, it is permissible that (دابَّةٍ) be ascribed to the mentioned whole even though it is found in only some of it, as one says: "The Banu so-and-so did such-and-such," while only one of them did it; and from it [the sea] come forth both [sweet and salt water], while only salt comes from the salt [water]; or it may be from the angels, some of whom walk along with flying, so they are described with crawling as humans are; or He created in the heavens an animal that walks alongside human walking on the earth; or it means the animal found in the clouds. It sometimes occurs, like frogs, and the cloud falls within the name of "sky."

Mujahid said: (وما بَثَّ فِيهِما مِن دابَّةٍ) refers to humans and angels. Abu Ali said: it is with an elided genitive, i.e., and what He scattered in one of them. The majority read (فِيهِما) with the fa', and so it is in most of the codices. (ما) may be conditional, which is the more apparent, or relative. The fa' enters the predicate of a relative when it is treated like a condition, under conditions mentioned in grammar, and they are present. Nafi', Ibn Amir, Abu Ja'far in one narration, and Shayba read (بِما) without a fa', so (ما) is relative, and it cannot be conditional; the fa' was dropped because Sibawayh specifies that for poetry, while al-Akhfash and some Baghdad grammarians permitted it, and this is on the assumption of the fa'. The consequence of the calamities that befall [people] upon the earning of hands is present with the fa' and without it here. (المُصِيبَةُ): the afflictions and calamities in this world; they are a recompense for a person's sins and an expiation for his errors, and He, the Exalted, pardons much and does not requite it with a calamity. In a hadith: "No scratch of a stick, nor stumbling of a foot, nor twitch of a vein befalls the son of Adam except due to a sin, and what He pardons is greater." Imran ibn Husayn was asked about his illness and said: "The dearest of it to me is the dearest of it to Allah, and this is from what my hands have earned." A sore was seen on the palm of Shurayh, and it was said: "Because of what is this?" He said: "Because of what my hands have earned."

Al-Zamakhshari said: The verse is specific to the criminals, and there is no impossibility in Allah exacting the punishment of the criminal and pardoning some. As for one who has no crime, such as the prophets, children, and the insane, it is like when some pain or other befalls them, so it is for the full recompense and the benefit. From Ali: "This is the most hopeful verse for the believers." Al-Hasan said: (مِن مُصِيبَةٍ) means a limit from the limits of Allah; and those are calamities that descend upon a person's self and body, so they are only due to what your hands have earned.

(And He pardons) Allah (much), concealing it from the servants so that it is not punished.

(And you cannot escape) i.e., you are within the grasp of power. It is said: calamities such as illnesses, drought, drowning, and other things are not punishments for sins, because of His saying: ﴿Today every soul will be recompensed for what it earned﴾ [Ghafir: 17], and because the righteous and the wicked share in them; rather, what the righteous and pious are most tested with is more. In a hadith: "The prophets are singled out for trial, then the most excellent, then the next most excellent." Also, because this world is the abode of obligation, so if recompense occurred in it, it would be the abode of recompense, and the matter is not so. This view is contradicted by the texts of the Qur'an, such as His saying: ﴿So each one We seized for his sin; among them were those upon whom We sent a hurricane of stones﴾ [al-Ankabut: 40], and so on.

(p-507) ﴿Do they have partners who have instituted for them in religion what Allah has not permitted?﴾ This is an interrogative of affirmation (istifham taqrir) and reproach (tawbikh). When Exalted Allah mentioned that He had prescribed for mankind ﴿what He enjoined upon Noah﴾ [Ash-Shura: 13], up to the verse, He began to deny what others than Him had legislated.

Here "the partners" (al-shuraka') may mean their partners in disbelief, such as the devils and the misguiding men. The pronoun in "they instituted" (shara'u) refers to the partners, and the pronoun in "for them" (lahum) refers to the disbelievers contemporary with the Messenger. It may also mean the idols and images and everything they made a partner of Allah.

The partners are attributed to them (udifa) because they take them as partners of Allah. So they are attributed to them through this association, and at other times to Allah.

The pronoun in "they instituted" may refer to the partners, and "for them" to the disbelievers. Since the partners were the cause of their error and seduction, they were treated as legislators of the religion of disbelief, as Ibrahim (peace be upon him) said: ﴿My Lord, they have led many people astray﴾ [Ibrahim: 36].

It may also refer to the disbelievers, with "for them" referring to the partners, meaning: the disbelievers legislated for their idols and objects of worship, that is, they laid down for them misguidance and rulings in matters of belief, such as their saying that they are gods and that worshipping them brings one closer to Allah. Among the rulings are the baḥīra, the wasīla, the ḥāmī and others.

﴿Had it not been for the decisive word﴾: that is, the promise that the judgment will be in the Hereafter. Or: had it not been for the decree to that effect, the matter would have been judged between the believer and the disbeliever, or between the polytheists and their partners.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read "indeed the wrongdoers" (inna al-zalimina) with a kasra on the hamza, as a resumption (isti'naf) and an announcement of what will befall them in this world of killing, captivity and plunder, and in the Hereafter, the Fire. Al-A'raj and Muslim ibn Jundub read "and that" (wa-anna) with a fatḥa on the hamza, as a conjunction (ʿatf) upon "the decisive word", so it is in the position of a nominative. The meaning: had it not been for the decisive word and the fact that the wrongdoers have a painful punishment in the Hereafter, the matter would have been judged between them in this world. The conjunction is separated by the response of "had it not been", as in His saying: ﴿Had it not been for a word that preceded from your Lord, it would have been inevitable, and a specified term﴾ [Ta-Ha: 129].

﴿You see the wrongdoers﴾: that is, you see the disbelievers, since they are contrasted with the believers. "Fearful" (mushfiqin): afraid with intense fear. "Of what they have earned" (mimma kasabu): of the evil deeds. "And it befalls them" (wa-huwa): that is, the punishment; or it refers to "what they earned", with an omitted modifier, meaning: the calamity which they earned from evil deeds; or its recompense descends upon them.

﴿And it is about to befall them﴾: their fear is in this state, unlike the believers who in this world are fearful of the Hour. Since the gardens (rawdat) are the best and most pleasant part of the Gardens and their highest parts, He mentioned that the believers are in them.

The common reading is to pronounce the waw in "rawḍāt" with sukūn, while the dialect of Hudhayl ibn Mudrika is to pronounce it with a fatḥa, treating the weak letter like a sound one, as in "jafanāt". None of those whose dialect we know read it that way.

"ʿInda" (in the presence of) is an adverbial of place (ẓarf). Al-Ḥawfī said it is an operand (maʿmūl) of "they will wish" (yashāʾūn). Al-Zamakhsharī said it is governed by the adverb (ẓarf) "not wish", and that is correct. By "the adverb" he means the prepositional phrase, and in reality "for them" is not an operand of the governor of "for them". The meaning: what they wish of bliss and reward is established for them.

"In the presence of their Lord": this "presence" is one of rank and honour, not of mere location.

The majority read "yubashshiru" with a shadda on the shin, from bashshara. ʿAbd Allah ibn Yaʿmur, Ibn Abi Ishaq, al-Jaḥdarī, al-Aʿmash, Ṭalḥa in one narration, al-Kisāʾī and Ḥamza read "yabshuru" as a triliteral verb. Mujāhid and Ḥumayd ibn Qays read it with a ḍamma on the yāʾ and a sukūn on the shin, from abshara, which is transitive by the hamza, from the intransitive bashira with a kasra on the shin.

As for bashara with a fatḥa, it is transitive. Bashshara with a shadda is for intensification, not for transitivity, because the verb that is transitive to one object, when it is light (mukhaffaf), is not made transitive by doubling; so the doubling in it is for intensification, not for transitivity.

"That" (dhalika): a reference to the honour prepared for them. It is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is the relative clause, and the returning pronoun is omitted, meaning: Allah gives the good news of it to His servants.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: or "that" is the good news which Allah gives to His servants. That is the end of his words.

This view is not evident, since no mention of glad tidings (bushra) has preceded in this sūra, nor anything indicating it, such as giving good news or similar.

Some grammarians made "alladhī" (which) a verbal-noun particle (maṣdariyya), transmitted by Ibn Mālik from Yūnus, and this verse was interpreted accordingly, meaning: "that" is Allah's giving good news to His servants. But this is nothing, because it asserts a shared meaning among items of different definition without evidence.

The nominal status of "alladhī" is established, so one does not depart from that for anything that has no proof or even a plausible basis.

﴿Say: I do not ask you for any reward for it, except love for the near of kin﴾. It is related that the polytheists gathered in an assembly, and some of them said to others: "Do you see Muhammad asking a reward for what he is doing?" So this was revealed. It is also related that the Anṣār came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with money they had collected and said: "O Messenger of Allah, Allah guided us through you, and you are the son of our sister, and rights befall you, and you have no means, so use this to meet what befalls you." So the verse was revealed, and he refused it.

It was also said: the address is directed to the Quraysh when they gathered money for him and wanted to bribe him with it, on condition that he refrain from reviling their gods, but he did not do it, and the verse was revealed.

So the meaning: I do not ask you for money or leadership, but I ask you to respect the right of my kinship and to believe me in what I have brought you, and to refrain from harming me and those who follow me. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrima, Mujāhid, Abū Mālik, al-Shaʿbī and others.

al-Shaʿbī said: People made much of this verse against us, so we wrote to Ibn ʿAbbās asking him about it, and he wrote that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was the most central of the people among the Quraysh; there was no clan of theirs except that he was born to it. So Allah, Exalted, said: Say, I do not ask you for any reward for it, except that you love me for my kinship with you. So keep the ties between me and you, and believe me.

ʿIkrima said: The Quraysh used to maintain their kinship ties. al-Ḥasan said: the meaning is: except that you seek affection toward Allah by drawing near to Him.

ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Qāsim said: except that some of you show affection to others and maintain your kinship ties.

It is related that some young men of the Anṣār boasted over the Emigrants and raised their voices with words, so the verse was revealed in the sense: do not harm me in my kinship, and protect them for my sake. ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib (may Allah be pleased with them) said this in the same sense, and cited the verse when he was led as a captive to Syria. This is also the view of Ibn Jubayr, al-Suddī and ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb. On this interpretation, Ibn ʿAbbās said: It was said: O Messenger of Allah, who are your kin whose love we were commanded? He said: ʿAlī, Fāṭima and their two sons.

It was also said: they are the descendants of ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib. The apparent meaning is that His saying ﴿except love﴾ is a disjunctive exception (istithnā' munqaṭiʿ), since love is not a reward.

al-Zamakhsharī said: It may be a connected exception, meaning: I do not ask you for any reward for it, except this: that you love the people of my kinship. This was not truly a reward, because his kin are their kin, so maintaining ties with them was obligatory for them by manliness.

He also said: If you ask, why was it not said: "except the love of kinship" or "except love for the kin"? I answer: they made a place for love, and a settled ground for it, as when you say: "I have affection for the family of so-and-so, and I have a strong desire and love for them", meaning: I love them, and they are the place and seat of my love. It is not in the sense of a complement of love as the preposition "li-" would be if you said "except love for the kin"; rather it is connected to an omitted element, as the adverbial is connected to it in your saying: "the money is in the bag", and its estimation is: except love established in the kinship and settled in it. That is the end of his words, and it is good, though it is verbose. Zayd ibn ʿAlī read "except affection" (illā mawaddatan), while the majority read "except the love" (illā al-mawadda).

﴿And whoever earns a good deed﴾: that is, acquires it. The apparent meaning is that "good deed" is general, in the manner of a substitute (badal), so love for the kin and other things are included in it. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Suddī that it is the love for the family of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

The majority read "We will increase for him" (nazid) with a nūn; Zayd ibn ʿAlī, ʿAbd al-Wārith from Abū ʿAmr, and Aḥmad ibn Jubayr from al-Kisā'ī read "He will increase" (yazid) with a yā', meaning Allah will increase.

The majority read "goodness" (ḥusnan) with tanwīn; ʿAbd al-Wārith from Abū ʿAmr read "ḥusnā" without tanwīn, on the pattern of "rujʿā". The increase of its goodness is the multiplication of its reward.

﴿Indeed Allah is Forgiving, Grateful﴾: forgiving means He covers the faults of His servants; grateful means He rewards for the smallest act, and the deed of the doer is not lost before Him.

al-Suddī said: Forgiving of the sins of the family of Muhammad (peace be upon him), grateful for their good deeds.

﴿Or do they say: he has invented a lie against Allah?﴾: this turns from the preceding speech without annulling it, and asks in a manner of denial and reproach regarding this statement, meaning: someone like him is not attributed with lying (p-517) against Allah, given your previous acknowledgement of his truthfulness and trustworthiness.

﴿If Allah wills, He would seal your heart﴾. Mujāhid said: He would bind your heart with patience over their harm, so that their saying "you are a fabricator" does not grieve you. Qatāda and a group said: "He would seal your heart" means: He would make you forget the Qur'an. The intent is a refutation of the disbelievers' claim and an explanation of its falsity, as if He were saying: How could it be right that they be fabrications, when you are before Allah in sight and hearing, and He is capable? Had He willed to seal your heart, you would not understand, nor speak, nor would your fabrication continue. So the wording intended this meaning, and what the apparent wording indicates was omitted for brevity and conciseness. That is the end of his words.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya thus reported this interpretation from Qatāda, but its wording contains harshness that is not fitting to attribute to the prophets.

al-Zamakhsharī said, on the authority of Qatāda: He would make you forget the Qur'an and cut off revelation from you, meaning that if he had fabricated a lie against Allah, this would have been done to him. That is the end of his words.

al-Zamakhsharī also said: ﴿If Allah wills, He would make you one of those sealed upon their hearts, so that you would invent a lie against Him﴾; for He would not permit anyone to dare fabricate a lie against Allah except one who is in a state like theirs. This manner of speaking implies the improbability of fabrication from someone like him, and that it is as remote as associating partners with Allah, or entering among those whose hearts are sealed.

The example of this is that one of the trustworthy men betrays, then says: "Perhaps Allah has forsaken me, perhaps Allah has blinded my heart," while he does not intend to affirm the forsaking or the blindness of heart; he only intends to deem it far-fetched that one like him would betray, and to alert [the listener] that a grave matter has been committed by his betrayal. Then he said: "It is among Allah's customs to erase falsehood and establish truth through His revelation or His decree, due to His saying: ﴿Nay, We hurl the truth against falsehood, and it crushes it﴾ [al-Anbiya: 18]," meaning: if he were a fabricator, as they claim, Allah would have exposed his fabrication and annihilated him, and hurled the truth against falsehood so that it crushes it. End of quote.

It is said: the meaning is, if you had fabricated against Allah, He would have sealed your heart so that you could not memorize the Qur'an. It is also said: He would have sealed your heart with truthfulness and certainty, and He has indeed done that.

Al-Qushayri mentioned that the meaning is: He seals the hearts of the disbelievers and their tongues, and hastens punishment upon them. End of quote. Thus it would be a shift from the third person to the second, and from the plural to the singular, i.e., He seals the heart of you, O speaker, who claims that he fabricated a lie against Allah.

﴿And Allah erases falsehood﴾: a resumptive statement of information, i.e., He erases it either in this world or in the Hereafter, wherever it alights. The word (ويَمْحُ) is written without a waw, just as they wrote (سَنَدْعُ) without a waw, considering that it does not appear, since it is not stopped upon with a pause of choice.

When it has dropped from pronunciation, it has dropped from the script. Al-Zamakhshari said: It may also be a promise to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that He will erase the falsehood they are upon, of slander and denial, and establish the truth you are upon through the Qur'an and His decree, which cannot be turned back, of granting you victory over them. Indeed Allah is Knowing of what is in your breast and their breasts, so He carries out the matter according to that. End of quote. It is said: and He establishes Islam through His words, i.e., through what He sent down of the Qur'an. The discussion of the conditions of repentance has preceded. It is said: "I accepted it from him" meaning "I took it from him," due to His saying: ﴿And what prevented them from having their expenditures accepted from them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 54], i.e., taken; i.e., I made it the beginning and origin of my acceptance. "I accepted it from him" also means: I separated him from it and removed him from it. So the meaning of (عَنْ عِبادِهِ) is: He removes the return from sins.

﴿And He pardons evil deeds﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: He pardons evil deeds when one repents from them, and minor sins when major sins are avoided. End of quote. This follows the path of the Mu'tazila.

Major sins are not pardoned except through repentance. ﴿And He knows what you do﴾, so He rewards and punishes. The majority read (ما يَفْعَلُونَ) with the ya' of the third person; Abdullah, Alqama, the two brothers [Hamza and al-Kisa'i], and Hafs read with the ta' of the second person. The apparent reading is that (الَّذِينَ) is the subject, and (ويَسْتَجِيبُ), i.e., "and answers," means: those who believe answer their Lord, as He said: ﴿O you who believe, respond to Allah and the Messenger when he calls you to what gives you life﴾ [al-Anfal: 24]. So (يَسْتَجِيبُ) means (يُجِيبُ), or it remains in its own sense of requesting, i.e., those who believe ask their Lord for the response through righteous deeds.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: this refers to their action when He calls them. It was reported from Ibrahim ibn Adham that it was said to him: "Why do we supplicate and are not answered?" He said: "Because He called you and you did not respond to Him," then he recited: ﴿And Allah calls to the abode of peace﴾ [Yunus: 25].

﴿And He answers those who believe﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: (الَّذِينَ) is the object, and (اسْتَجابَ) and (أجابَ) have one meaning, so the meaning is: Allah answers those who believe, i.e., for them, as the poet said:
"So no one answered him at that time," i.e., did not respond to him. This meaning was narrated from Mu'adh ibn Jabal and Ibn Abbas.

﴿And He increases them from His bounty﴾, i.e., beyond the reward, out of grace. In a hadith: the acceptance of intercessions for the believers and [divine] contentment. Khabbab ibn al-Aratt said: We looked at the wealth of the Banu Qurayza, al-Nadir and Banu Qaynuqa', and we wished for it, so this was revealed: ﴿And if Allah had extended provision to His servants, they would have committed excess upon the earth﴾. Amr ibn Huraith said: a group of the People of the Suffa asked the Messenger (peace be upon him) that Allah enrich them and extend wealth and provisions to them, so this was revealed. Know that if provision came according to human demand, it would be the cause of their transgression and corruption, but He, the Exalted, knows best what is beneficial. Many a person is not set right, and his evil is not restrained, except by poverty, and another by wealth. In this meaning and division there is a hadith narrated by Anas, who said: "O Allah, I am among Your servants whom only wealth sets right, so do not make me poor."

(لَبَغَوْا) either means from arrogance and pride, i.e., they would have become haughty upon the earth, and did what follows from pride together with wealth. Do you not see the state of Qarun? In a hadith: "What I fear most for my nation is the splendor of the world." The poet said:
"They have made the spring rain grow between us and the Banu Rumman a thicket of nab' and shawhat [trees]," meaning: they loved [worldly things], so they dragged themselves into transgression and strife.

﴿But He sends down in measure what He wills﴾. It is said: qadara with a sukun and with a fatha, i.e., He determines for them what is most suitable for them. The majority read (قَنَطُوا) with a fatha on the nun; al-A'mash and Ibn Wathhab read it with a kasra. ﴿And spreads His mercy﴾: He manifests it through the effects of rain, in benefits and fertility. The apparent meaning is that spreading His mercy is more general than what is in the rain. Al-Suddi said: (رَحْمَتَهُ) is the rain, and he counted the same blessing with two expressions. It was said: the mercy here is the appearance of the sun, because when rain persists it becomes tiresome, so the sun comes after it with a great effect; this was mentioned by al-Mahdawi.

﴿And He is the Protector﴾: He who takes charge of His servants; (the Praiseworthy): the One praised for the blessings He has bestowed. (And what He has scattered) — the apparent reading is that it is in the genitive, conjoined to "the heavens and the earth." It is also permissible that it be in the nominative, conjoined to (خَلْقُ) with an elided genitive, i.e., and the creation of what He has scattered. Regarding both, it is permissible that (دابَّةٍ) be ascribed to the mentioned whole even though it is found in only some of it, as one says: "The Banu so-and-so did such-and-such," while only one of them did it; and from it [the sea] come forth both [sweet and salt water], while only salt comes from the salt [water]; or it may be from the angels, some of whom walk along with flying, so they are described with crawling as humans are; or He created in the heavens an animal that walks alongside human walking on the earth; or it means the animal found in the clouds. It sometimes occurs, like frogs, and the cloud falls within the name of "sky."

Mujahid said: (وما بَثَّ فِيهِما مِن دابَّةٍ) refers to humans and angels. Abu Ali said: it is with an elided genitive, i.e., and what He scattered in one of them. The majority read (فِيهِما) with the fa', and so it is in most of the codices. (ما) may be conditional, which is the more apparent, or relative. The fa' enters the predicate of a relative when it is treated like a condition, under conditions mentioned in grammar, and they are present. Nafi', Ibn Amir, Abu Ja'far in one narration, and Shayba read (بِما) without a fa', so (ما) is relative, and it cannot be conditional; the fa' was dropped because Sibawayh specifies that for poetry, while al-Akhfash and some Baghdad grammarians permitted it, and this is on the assumption of the fa'. The consequence of the calamities that befall [people] upon the earning of hands is present with the fa' and without it here. (المُصِيبَةُ): the afflictions and calamities in this world; they are a recompense for a person's sins and an expiation for his errors, and He, the Exalted, pardons much and does not requite it with a calamity. In a hadith: "No scratch of a stick, nor stumbling of a foot, nor twitch of a vein befalls the son of Adam except due to a sin, and what He pardons is greater." Imran ibn Husayn was asked about his illness and said: "The dearest of it to me is the dearest of it to Allah, and this is from what my hands have earned." A sore was seen on the palm of Shurayh, and it was said: "Because of what is this?" He said: "Because of what my hands have earned."

Al-Zamakhshari said: The verse is specific to the criminals, and there is no impossibility in Allah exacting the punishment of the criminal and pardoning some. As for one who has no crime, such as the prophets, children, and the insane, it is like when some pain or other befalls them, so it is for the full recompense and the benefit. From Ali: "This is the most hopeful verse for the believers." Al-Hasan said: (مِن مُصِيبَةٍ) means a limit from the limits of Allah; and those are calamities that descend upon a person's self and body, so they are only due to what your hands have earned.

(And He pardons) Allah (much), concealing it from the servants so that it is not punished.

(And you cannot escape) i.e., you are within the grasp of power. It is said: calamities such as illnesses, drought, drowning, and other things are not punishments for sins, because of His saying: ﴿Today every soul will be recompensed for what it earned﴾ [Ghafir: 17], and because the righteous and the wicked share in them; rather, what the righteous and pious are most tested with is more. In a hadith: "The prophets are singled out for trial, then the most excellent, then the next most excellent." Also, because this world is the abode of obligation, so if recompense occurred in it, it would be the abode of recompense, and the matter is not so. This view is contradicted by the texts of the Qur'an, such as His saying: ﴿So each one We seized for his sin; among them were those upon whom We sent a hurricane of stones﴾ [al-Ankabut: 40], and so on.

The pronoun in "they instituted" may refer to the partners, and "for them" to the disbelievers. Since the partners were the cause of their error and seduction, they were treated as legislators of the religion of disbelief, as Ibrahim (peace be upon him) said: ﴿My Lord, they have led many people astray﴾ [Ibrahim: 36].

It may also refer to the disbelievers, with "for them" referring to the partners, meaning: the disbelievers legislated for their idols and objects of worship, that is, they laid down for them misguidance and rulings in matters of belief, such as their saying that they are gods and that worshipping them brings one closer to Allah. Among the rulings are the baḥīra, the wasīla, the ḥāmī and others.

﴿Had it not been for the decisive word﴾: that is, the promise that the judgment will be in the Hereafter. Or: had it not been for the decree to that effect, the matter would have been judged between the believer and the disbeliever, or between the polytheists and their partners.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read "indeed the wrongdoers" (inna al-zalimina) with a kasra on the hamza, as a resumption (isti'naf) and an announcement of what will befall them in this world of killing, captivity and plunder, and in the Hereafter, the Fire. Al-A'raj and Muslim ibn Jundub read "and that" (wa-anna) with a fatḥa on the hamza, as a conjunction (ʿatf) upon "the decisive word", so it is in the position of a nominative. The meaning: had it not been for the decisive word and the fact that the wrongdoers have a painful punishment in the Hereafter, the matter would have been judged between them in this world. The conjunction is separated by the response of "had it not been", as in His saying: ﴿Had it not been for a word that preceded from your Lord, it would have been inevitable, and a specified term﴾ [Ta-Ha: 129].

﴿You see the wrongdoers﴾: that is, you see the disbelievers, since they are contrasted with the believers. "Fearful" (mushfiqin): afraid with intense fear. "Of what they have earned" (mimma kasabu): of the evil deeds. "And it befalls them" (wa-huwa): that is, the punishment; or it refers to "what they earned", with an omitted modifier, meaning: the calamity which they earned from evil deeds; or its recompense descends upon them.

﴿And it is about to befall them﴾: their fear is in this state, unlike the believers who in this world are fearful of the Hour. Since the gardens (rawdat) are the best and most pleasant part of the Gardens and their highest parts, He mentioned that the believers are in them.

The common reading is to pronounce the waw in "rawḍāt" with sukūn, while the dialect of Hudhayl ibn Mudrika is to pronounce it with a fatḥa, treating the weak letter like a sound one, as in "jafanāt". None of those whose dialect we know read it that way.

"ʿInda" (in the presence of) is an adverbial of place (ẓarf). Al-Ḥawfī said it is an operand (maʿmūl) of "they will wish" (yashāʾūn). Al-Zamakhsharī said it is governed by the adverb (ẓarf) "not wish", and that is correct. By "the adverb" he means the prepositional phrase, and in reality "for them" is not an operand of the governor of "for them". The meaning: what they wish of bliss and reward is established for them.

"In the presence of their Lord": this "presence" is one of rank and honour, not of mere location.

The majority read "yubashshiru" with a shadda on the shin, from bashshara. ʿAbd Allah ibn Yaʿmur, Ibn Abi Ishaq, al-Jaḥdarī, al-Aʿmash, Ṭalḥa in one narration, al-Kisāʾī and Ḥamza read "yabshuru" as a triliteral verb. Mujāhid and Ḥumayd ibn Qays read it with a ḍamma on the yāʾ and a sukūn on the shin, from abshara, which is transitive by the hamza, from the intransitive bashira with a kasra on the shin.

As for bashara with a fatḥa, it is transitive. Bashshara with a shadda is for intensification, not for transitivity, because the verb that is transitive to one object, when it is light (mukhaffaf), is not made transitive by doubling; so the doubling in it is for intensification, not for transitivity.

"That" (dhalika): a reference to the honour prepared for them. It is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is the relative clause, and the returning pronoun is omitted, meaning: Allah gives the good news of it to His servants.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: or "that" is the good news which Allah gives to His servants. That is the end of his words.

This view is not evident, since no mention of glad tidings (bushra) has preceded in this sūra, nor anything indicating it, such as giving good news or similar.

Some grammarians made "alladhī" (which) a verbal-noun particle (maṣdariyya), transmitted by Ibn Mālik from Yūnus, and this verse was interpreted accordingly, meaning: "that" is Allah's giving good news to His servants. But this is nothing, because it asserts a shared meaning among items of different definition without evidence.

The nominal status of "alladhī" is established, so one does not depart from that for anything that has no proof or even a plausible basis.

﴿Say: I do not ask you for any reward for it, except love for the near of kin﴾. It is related that the polytheists gathered in an assembly, and some of them said to others: "Do you see Muhammad asking a reward for what he is doing?" So this was revealed. It is also related that the Anṣār came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with money they had collected and said: "O Messenger of Allah, Allah guided us through you, and you are the son of our sister, and rights befall you, and you have no means, so use this to meet what befalls you." So the verse was revealed, and he refused it.

It was also said: the address is directed to the Quraysh when they gathered money for him and wanted to bribe him with it, on condition that he refrain from reviling their gods, but he did not do it, and the verse was revealed.

So the meaning: I do not ask you for money or leadership, but I ask you to respect the right of my kinship and to believe me in what I have brought you, and to refrain from harming me and those who follow me. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrima, Mujāhid, Abū Mālik, al-Shaʿbī and others.

al-Shaʿbī said: People made much of this verse against us, so we wrote to Ibn ʿAbbās asking him about it, and he wrote that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was the most central of the people among the Quraysh; there was no clan of theirs except that he was born to it. So Allah, Exalted, said: Say, I do not ask you for any reward for it, except that you love me for my kinship with you. So keep the ties between me and you, and believe me.

ʿIkrima said: The Quraysh used to maintain their kinship ties. al-Ḥasan said: the meaning is: except that you seek affection toward Allah by drawing near to Him.

ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Qāsim said: except that some of you show affection to others and maintain your kinship ties.

It is related that some young men of the Anṣār boasted over the Emigrants and raised their voices with words, so the verse was revealed in the sense: do not harm me in my kinship, and protect them for my sake. ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib (may Allah be pleased with them) said this in the same sense, and cited the verse when he was led as a captive to Syria. This is also the view of Ibn Jubayr, al-Suddī and ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb. On this interpretation, Ibn ʿAbbās said: It was said: O Messenger of Allah, who are your kin whose love we were commanded? He said: ʿAlī, Fāṭima and their two sons.

It was also said: they are the descendants of ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib. The apparent meaning is that His saying ﴿except love﴾ is a disjunctive exception (istithnā' munqaṭiʿ), since love is not a reward.

al-Zamakhsharī said: It may be a connected exception, meaning: I do not ask you for any reward for it, except this: that you love the people of my kinship. This was not truly a reward, because his kin are their kin, so maintaining ties with them was obligatory for them by manliness.

He also said: If you ask, why was it not said: "except the love of kinship" or "except love for the kin"? I answer: they made a place for love, and a settled ground for it, as when you say: "I have affection for the family of so-and-so, and I have a strong desire and love for them", meaning: I love them, and they are the place and seat of my love. It is not in the sense of a complement of love as the preposition "li-" would be if you said "except love for the kin"; rather it is connected to an omitted element, as the adverbial is connected to it in your saying: "the money is in the bag", and its estimation is: except love established in the kinship and settled in it. That is the end of his words, and it is good, though it is verbose. Zayd ibn ʿAlī read "except affection" (illā mawaddatan), while the majority read "except the love" (illā al-mawadda).

﴿And whoever earns a good deed﴾: that is, acquires it. The apparent meaning is that "good deed" is general, in the manner of a substitute (badal), so love for the kin and other things are included in it. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Suddī that it is the love for the family of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

The majority read "We will increase for him" (nazid) with a nūn; Zayd ibn ʿAlī, ʿAbd al-Wārith from Abū ʿAmr, and Aḥmad ibn Jubayr from al-Kisā'ī read "He will increase" (yazid) with a yā', meaning Allah will increase.

The majority read "goodness" (ḥusnan) with tanwīn; ʿAbd al-Wārith from Abū ʿAmr read "ḥusnā" without tanwīn, on the pattern of "rujʿā". The increase of its goodness is the multiplication of its reward.

﴿Indeed Allah is Forgiving, Grateful﴾: forgiving means He covers the faults of His servants; grateful means He rewards for the smallest act, and the deed of the doer is not lost before Him.

al-Suddī said: Forgiving of the sins of the family of Muhammad (peace be upon him), grateful for their good deeds.

﴿Or do they say: he has invented a lie against Allah?﴾: this turns from the preceding speech without annulling it, and asks in a manner of denial and reproach regarding this statement, meaning: someone like him is not attributed with lying (p-517) against Allah, given your previous acknowledgement of his truthfulness and trustworthiness.

﴿If Allah wills, He would seal your heart﴾. Mujāhid said: He would bind your heart with patience over their harm, so that their saying "you are a fabricator" does not grieve you. Qatāda and a group said: "He would seal your heart" means: He would make you forget the Qur'an. The intent is a refutation of the disbelievers' claim and an explanation of its falsity, as if He were saying: How could it be right that they be fabrications, when you are before Allah in sight and hearing, and He is capable? Had He willed to seal your heart, you would not understand, nor speak, nor would your fabrication continue. So the wording intended this meaning, and what the apparent wording indicates was omitted for brevity and conciseness. That is the end of his words.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya thus reported this interpretation from Qatāda, but its wording contains harshness that is not fitting to attribute to the prophets.

al-Zamakhsharī said, on the authority of Qatāda: He would make you forget the Qur'an and cut off revelation from you, meaning that if he had fabricated a lie against Allah, this would have been done to him. That is the end of his words.

al-Zamakhsharī also said: ﴿If Allah wills, He would make you one of those sealed upon their hearts, so that you would invent a lie against Him﴾; for He would not permit anyone to dare fabricate a lie against Allah except one who is in a state like theirs. This manner of speaking implies the improbability of fabrication from someone like him, and that it is as remote as associating partners with Allah, or entering among those whose hearts are sealed.

The example of this is that one of the trustworthy men betrays, then says: "Perhaps Allah has forsaken me, perhaps Allah has blinded my heart," while he does not intend to affirm the forsaking or the blindness of heart; he only intends to deem it far-fetched that one like him would betray, and to alert [the listener] that a grave matter has been committed by his betrayal. Then he said: "It is among Allah's customs to erase falsehood and establish truth through His revelation or His decree, due to His saying: ﴿Nay, We hurl the truth against falsehood, and it crushes it﴾ [al-Anbiya: 18]," meaning: if he were a fabricator, as they claim, Allah would have exposed his fabrication and annihilated him, and hurled the truth against falsehood so that it crushes it. End of quote.

It is said: the meaning is, if you had fabricated against Allah, He would have sealed your heart so that you could not memorize the Qur'an. It is also said: He would have sealed your heart with truthfulness and certainty, and He has indeed done that.

Al-Qushayri mentioned that the meaning is: He seals the hearts of the disbelievers and their tongues, and hastens punishment upon them. End of quote. Thus it would be a shift from the third person to the second, and from the plural to the singular, i.e., He seals the heart of you, O speaker, who claims that he fabricated a lie against Allah.

﴿And Allah erases falsehood﴾: a resumptive statement of information, i.e., He erases it either in this world or in the Hereafter, wherever it alights. The word (ويَمْحُ) is written without a waw, just as they wrote (سَنَدْعُ) without a waw, considering that it does not appear, since it is not stopped upon with a pause of choice.

When it has dropped from pronunciation, it has dropped from the script. Al-Zamakhshari said: It may also be a promise to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that He will erase the falsehood they are upon, of slander and denial, and establish the truth you are upon through the Qur'an and His decree, which cannot be turned back, of granting you victory over them. Indeed Allah is Knowing of what is in your breast and their breasts, so He carries out the matter according to that. End of quote. It is said: and He establishes Islam through His words, i.e., through what He sent down of the Qur'an. The discussion of the conditions of repentance has preceded. It is said: "I accepted it from him" meaning "I took it from him," due to His saying: ﴿And what prevented them from having their expenditures accepted from them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 54], i.e., taken; i.e., I made it the beginning and origin of my acceptance. "I accepted it from him" also means: I separated him from it and removed him from it. So the meaning of (عَنْ عِبادِهِ) is: He removes the return from sins.

﴿And He pardons evil deeds﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: He pardons evil deeds when one repents from them, and minor sins when major sins are avoided. End of quote. This follows the path of the Mu'tazila.

Major sins are not pardoned except through repentance. ﴿And He knows what you do﴾, so He rewards and punishes. The majority read (ما يَفْعَلُونَ) with the ya' of the third person; Abdullah, Alqama, the two brothers [Hamza and al-Kisa'i], and Hafs read with the ta' of the second person. The apparent reading is that (الَّذِينَ) is the subject, and (ويَسْتَجِيبُ), i.e., "and answers," means: those who believe answer their Lord, as He said: ﴿O you who believe, respond to Allah and the Messenger when he calls you to what gives you life﴾ [al-Anfal: 24]. So (يَسْتَجِيبُ) means (يُجِيبُ), or it remains in its own sense of requesting, i.e., those who believe ask their Lord for the response through righteous deeds.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: this refers to their action when He calls them. It was reported from Ibrahim ibn Adham that it was said to him: "Why do we supplicate and are not answered?" He said: "Because He called you and you did not respond to Him," then he recited: ﴿And Allah calls to the abode of peace﴾ [Yunus: 25].

﴿And He answers those who believe﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: (الَّذِينَ) is the object, and (اسْتَجابَ) and (أجابَ) have one meaning, so the meaning is: Allah answers those who believe, i.e., for them, as the poet said:
"So no one answered him at that time," i.e., did not respond to him. This meaning was narrated from Mu'adh ibn Jabal and Ibn Abbas.

﴿And He increases them from His bounty﴾, i.e., beyond the reward, out of grace. In a hadith: the acceptance of intercessions for the believers and [divine] contentment. Khabbab ibn al-Aratt said: We looked at the wealth of the Banu Qurayza, al-Nadir and Banu Qaynuqa', and we wished for it, so this was revealed: ﴿And if Allah had extended provision to His servants, they would have committed excess upon the earth﴾. Amr ibn Huraith said: a group of the People of the Suffa asked the Messenger (peace be upon him) that Allah enrich them and extend wealth and provisions to them, so this was revealed. Know that if provision came according to human demand, it would be the cause of their transgression and corruption, but He, the Exalted, knows best what is beneficial. Many a person is not set right, and his evil is not restrained, except by poverty, and another by wealth. In this meaning and division there is a hadith narrated by Anas, who said: "O Allah, I am among Your servants whom only wealth sets right, so do not make me poor."

(لَبَغَوْا) either means from arrogance and pride, i.e., they would have become haughty upon the earth, and did what follows from pride together with wealth. Do you not see the state of Qarun? In a hadith: "What I fear most for my nation is the splendor of the world." The poet said:
"They have made the spring rain grow between us and the Banu Rumman a thicket of nab' and shawhat [trees]," meaning: they loved [worldly things], so they dragged themselves into transgression and strife.

﴿But He sends down in measure what He wills﴾. It is said: qadara with a sukun and with a fatha, i.e., He determines for them what is most suitable for them. The majority read (قَنَطُوا) with a fatha on the nun; al-A'mash and Ibn Wathhab read it with a kasra. ﴿And spreads His mercy﴾: He manifests it through the effects of rain, in benefits and fertility. The apparent meaning is that spreading His mercy is more general than what is in the rain. Al-Suddi said: (رَحْمَتَهُ) is the rain, and he counted the same blessing with two expressions. It was said: the mercy here is the appearance of the sun, because when rain persists it becomes tiresome, so the sun comes after it with a great effect; this was mentioned by al-Mahdawi.

﴿And He is the Protector﴾: He who takes charge of His servants; (the Praiseworthy): the One praised for the blessings He has bestowed. (And what He has scattered) — the apparent reading is that it is in the genitive, conjoined to "the heavens and the earth." It is also permissible that it be in the nominative, conjoined to (خَلْقُ) with an elided genitive, i.e., and the creation of what He has scattered. Regarding both, it is permissible that (دابَّةٍ) be ascribed to the mentioned whole even though it is found in only some of it, as one says: "The Banu so-and-so did such-and-such," while only one of them did it; and from it [the sea] come forth both [sweet and salt water], while only salt comes from the salt [water]; or it may be from the angels, some of whom walk along with flying, so they are described with crawling as humans are; or He created in the heavens an animal that walks alongside human walking on the earth; or it means the animal found in the clouds. It sometimes occurs, like frogs, and the cloud falls within the name of "sky."

Mujahid said: (وما بَثَّ فِيهِما مِن دابَّةٍ) refers to humans and angels. Abu Ali said: it is with an elided genitive, i.e., and what He scattered in one of them. The majority read (فِيهِما) with the fa', and so it is in most of the codices. (ما) may be conditional, which is the more apparent, or relative. The fa' enters the predicate of a relative when it is treated like a condition, under conditions mentioned in grammar, and they are present. Nafi', Ibn Amir, Abu Ja'far in one narration, and Shayba read (بِما) without a fa', so (ما) is relative, and it cannot be conditional; the fa' was dropped because Sibawayh specifies that for poetry, while al-Akhfash and some Baghdad grammarians permitted it, and this is on the assumption of the fa'. The consequence of the calamities that befall [people] upon the earning of hands is present with the fa' and without it here. (المُصِيبَةُ): the afflictions and calamities in this world; they are a recompense for a person's sins and an expiation for his errors, and He, the Exalted, pardons much and does not requite it with a calamity. In a hadith: "No scratch of a stick, nor stumbling of a foot, nor twitch of a vein befalls the son of Adam except due to a sin, and what He pardons is greater." Imran ibn Husayn was asked about his illness and said: "The dearest of it to me is the dearest of it to Allah, and this is from what my hands have earned." A sore was seen on the palm of Shurayh, and it was said: "Because of what is this?" He said: "Because of what my hands have earned."

Al-Zamakhshari said: The verse is specific to the criminals, and there is no impossibility in Allah exacting the punishment of the criminal and pardoning some. As for one who has no crime, such as the prophets, children, and the insane, it is like when some pain or other befalls them, so it is for the full recompense and the benefit. From Ali: "This is the most hopeful verse for the believers." Al-Hasan said: (مِن مُصِيبَةٍ) means a limit from the limits of Allah; and those are calamities that descend upon a person's self and body, so they are only due to what your hands have earned.

(And He pardons) Allah (much), concealing it from the servants so that it is not punished.

(And you cannot escape) i.e., you are within the grasp of power. It is said: calamities such as illnesses, drought, drowning, and other things are not punishments for sins, because of His saying: ﴿Today every soul will be recompensed for what it earned﴾ [Ghafir: 17], and because the righteous and the wicked share in them; rather, what the righteous and pious are most tested with is more. In a hadith: "The prophets are singled out for trial, then the most excellent, then the next most excellent." Also, because this world is the abode of obligation, so if recompense occurred in it, it would be the abode of recompense, and the matter is not so. This view is contradicted by the texts of the Qur'an, such as His saying: ﴿So each one We seized for his sin; among them were those upon whom We sent a hurricane of stones﴾ [al-Ankabut: 40], and so on.

(p-507) ﴿Do they have partners who have instituted for them in religion what Allah has not permitted?﴾ This is an interrogative of affirmation (istifham taqrir) and reproach (tawbikh). When Exalted Allah mentioned that He had prescribed for mankind ﴿what He enjoined upon Noah﴾ [Ash-Shura: 13], up to the verse, He began to deny what others than Him had legislated.

Here "the partners" (al-shuraka') may mean their partners in disbelief, such as the devils and the misguiding men. The pronoun in "they instituted" (shara'u) refers to the partners, and the pronoun in "for them" (lahum) refers to the disbelievers contemporary with the Messenger. It may also mean the idols and images and everything they made a partner of Allah.

The partners are attributed to them (udifa) because they take them as partners of Allah. So they are attributed to them through this association, and at other times to Allah.

But this is nothing, because it asserts a shared meaning among items of different definition without evidence.

The nominal status of "alladhī" is established, so one does not depart from that for anything that has no proof or even a plausible basis.

﴿Say: I do not ask you for any reward for it, except love for the near of kin﴾. It is related that the polytheists gathered in an assembly, and some of them said to others: "Do you see Muhammad asking a reward for what he is doing?" So this was revealed. It is also related that the Anṣār came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with money they had collected and said: "O Messenger of Allah, Allah guided us through you, and you are the son of our sister, and rights befall you, and you have no means, so use this to meet what befalls you." So the verse was revealed, and he refused it.

It was also said: the address is directed to the Quraysh when they gathered money for him and wanted to bribe him with it, on condition that he refrain from reviling their gods, but he did not do it, and the verse was revealed.

So the meaning: I do not ask you for money or leadership, but I ask you to respect the right of my kinship and to believe me in what I have brought you, and to refrain from harming me and those who follow me. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrima, Mujāhid, Abū Mālik, al-Shaʿbī and others.

al-Shaʿbī said: People made much of this verse against us, so we wrote to Ibn ʿAbbās asking him about it, and he wrote that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was the most central of the people among the Quraysh; there was no clan of theirs except that he was born to it. So Allah, Exalted, said: Say, I do not ask you for any reward for it, except that you love me for my kinship with you. So keep the ties between me and you, and believe me.

ʿIkrima said: The Quraysh used to maintain their kinship ties. al-Ḥasan said: the meaning is: except that you seek affection toward Allah by drawing near to Him.

ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Qāsim said: except that some of you show affection to others and maintain your kinship ties.

It is related that some young men of the Anṣār boasted over the Emigrants and raised their voices with words, so the verse was revealed in the sense: do not harm me in my kinship, and protect them for my sake. ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib (may Allah be pleased with them) said this in the same sense, and cited the verse when he was led as a captive to Syria. This is also the view of Ibn Jubayr, al-Suddī and ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb. On this interpretation, Ibn ʿAbbās said: It was said: O Messenger of Allah, who are your kin whose love we were commanded? He said: ʿAlī, Fāṭima and their two sons.

It was also said: they are the descendants of ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib. The apparent meaning is that His saying ﴿except love﴾ is a disjunctive exception (istithnā' munqaṭiʿ), since love is not a reward.

al-Zamakhsharī said: It may be a connected exception, meaning: I do not ask you for any reward for it, except this: that you love the people of my kinship. This was not truly a reward, because his kin are their kin, so maintaining ties with them was obligatory for them by manliness.

He also said: If you ask, why was it not said: "except the love of kinship" or "except love for the kin"? I answer: they made a place for love, and a settled ground for it, as when you say: "I have affection for the family of so-and-so, and I have a strong desire and love for them", meaning: I love them, and they are the place and seat of my love. It is not in the sense of a complement of love as the preposition "li-" would be if you said "except love for the kin"; rather it is connected to an omitted element, as the adverbial is connected to it in your saying: "the money is in the bag", and its estimation is: except love established in the kinship and settled in it. That is the end of his words, and it is good, though it is verbose. Zayd ibn ʿAlī read "except affection" (illā mawaddatan), while the majority read "except the love" (illā al-mawadda).

﴿And whoever earns a good deed﴾: that is, acquires it. The apparent meaning is that "good deed" is general, in the manner of a substitute (badal), so love for the kin and other things are included in it. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Suddī that it is the love for the family of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

The majority read "We will increase for him" (nazid) with a nūn; Zayd ibn ʿAlī, ʿAbd al-Wārith from Abū ʿAmr, and Aḥmad ibn Jubayr from al-Kisā'ī read "He will increase" (yazid) with a yā', meaning Allah will increase.

The majority read "goodness" (ḥusnan) with tanwīn; ʿAbd al-Wārith from Abū ʿAmr read "ḥusnā" without tanwīn, on the pattern of "rujʿā". The increase of its goodness is the multiplication of its reward.

﴿Indeed Allah is Forgiving, Grateful﴾: forgiving means He covers the faults of His servants; grateful means He rewards for the smallest act, and the deed of the doer is not lost before Him.

al-Suddī said: Forgiving of the sins of the family of Muhammad (peace be upon him), grateful for their good deeds.

﴿Or do they say: he has invented a lie against Allah?﴾: this turns from the preceding speech without annulling it, and asks in a manner of denial and reproach regarding this statement, meaning: someone like him is not attributed with lying (p-517) against Allah, given your previous acknowledgement of his truthfulness and trustworthiness.

﴿If Allah wills, He would seal your heart﴾. Mujāhid said: He would bind your heart with patience over their harm, so that their saying "you are a fabricator" does not grieve you. Qatāda and a group said: "He would seal your heart" means: He would make you forget the Qur'an. The intent is a refutation of the disbelievers' claim and an explanation of its falsity, as if He were saying: How could it be right that they be fabrications, when you are before Allah in sight and hearing, and He is capable? Had He willed to seal your heart, you would not understand, nor speak, nor would your fabrication continue. So the wording intended this meaning, and what the apparent wording indicates was omitted for brevity and conciseness. That is the end of his words.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya thus reported this interpretation from Qatāda, but its wording contains harshness that is not fitting to attribute to the prophets.

al-Zamakhsharī said, on the authority of Qatāda: He would make you forget the Qur'an and cut off revelation from you, meaning that if he had fabricated a lie against Allah, this would have been done to him. That is the end of his words.

al-Zamakhsharī also said: ﴿If Allah wills, He would make you one of those sealed upon their hearts, so that you would invent a lie against Him﴾; for He would not permit anyone to dare fabricate a lie against Allah except one who is in a state like theirs. This manner of speaking implies the improbability of fabrication from someone like him, and that it is as remote as associating partners with Allah, or entering among those whose hearts are sealed.

The example of this is that one of the trustworthy men betrays, then says: "Perhaps Allah has forsaken me, perhaps Allah has blinded my heart," while he does not intend to affirm the forsaking or the blindness of heart; he only intends to deem it far-fetched that one like him would betray, and to alert [the listener] that a grave matter has been committed by his betrayal. Then he said: "It is among Allah's customs to erase falsehood and establish truth through His revelation or His decree, due to His saying: ﴿Nay, We hurl the truth against falsehood, and it crushes it﴾ [al-Anbiya: 18]," meaning: if he were a fabricator, as they claim, Allah would have exposed his fabrication and annihilated him, and hurled the truth against falsehood so that it crushes it. End of quote.

It is said: the meaning is, if you had fabricated against Allah, He would have sealed your heart so that you could not memorize the Qur'an. It is also said: He would have sealed your heart with truthfulness and certainty, and He has indeed done that.

Al-Qushayri mentioned that the meaning is: He seals the hearts of the disbelievers and their tongues, and hastens punishment upon them. End of quote. Thus it would be a shift from the third person to the second, and from the plural to the singular, i.e., He seals the heart of you, O speaker, who claims that he fabricated a lie against Allah.

﴿And Allah erases falsehood﴾: a resumptive statement of information, i.e., He erases it either in this world or in the Hereafter, wherever it alights. The word (ويَمْحُ) is written without a waw, just as they wrote (سَنَدْعُ) without a waw, considering that it does not appear, since it is not stopped upon with a pause of choice.

When it has dropped from pronunciation, it has dropped from the script. Al-Zamakhshari said: It may also be a promise to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that He will erase the falsehood they are upon, of slander and denial, and establish the truth you are upon through the Qur'an and His decree, which cannot be turned back, of granting you victory over them. Indeed Allah is Knowing of what is in your breast and their breasts, so He carries out the matter according to that. End of quote. It is said: and He establishes Islam through His words, i.e., through what He sent down of the Qur'an. The discussion of the conditions of repentance has preceded. It is said: "I accepted it from him" meaning "I took it from him," due to His saying: ﴿And what prevented them from having their expenditures accepted from them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 54], i.e., taken; i.e., I made it the beginning and origin of my acceptance. "I accepted it from him" also means: I separated him from it and removed him from it. So the meaning of (عَنْ عِبادِهِ) is: He removes the return from sins.

﴿And He pardons evil deeds﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: He pardons evil deeds when one repents from them, and minor sins when major sins are avoided. End of quote. This follows the path of the Mu'tazila.

Major sins are not pardoned except through repentance. ﴿And He knows what you do﴾, so He rewards and punishes. The majority read (ما يَفْعَلُونَ) with the ya' of the third person; Abdullah, Alqama, the two brothers [Hamza and al-Kisa'i], and Hafs read with the ta' of the second person. The apparent reading is that (الَّذِينَ) is the subject, and (ويَسْتَجِيبُ), i.e., "and answers," means: those who believe answer their Lord, as He said: ﴿O you who believe, respond to Allah and the Messenger when he calls you to what gives you life﴾ [al-Anfal: 24]. So (يَسْتَجِيبُ) means (يُجِيبُ), or it remains in its own sense of requesting, i.e., those who believe ask their Lord for the response through righteous deeds.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: this refers to their action when He calls them. It was reported from Ibrahim ibn Adham that it was said to him: "Why do we supplicate and are not answered?" He said: "Because He called you and you did not respond to Him," then he recited: ﴿And Allah calls to the abode of peace﴾ [Yunus: 25].

﴿And He answers those who believe﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: (الَّذِينَ) is the object, and (اسْتَجابَ) and (أجابَ) have one meaning, so the meaning is: Allah answers those who believe, i.e., for them, as the poet said:
"So no one answered him at that time," i.e., did not respond to him. This meaning was narrated from Mu'adh ibn Jabal and Ibn Abbas.

﴿And He increases them from His bounty﴾, i.e., beyond the reward, out of grace. In a hadith: the acceptance of intercessions for the believers and [divine] contentment. Khabbab ibn al-Aratt said: We looked at the wealth of the Banu Qurayza, al-Nadir and Banu Qaynuqa', and we wished for it, so this was revealed: ﴿And if Allah had extended provision to His servants, they would have committed excess upon the earth﴾. Amr ibn Huraith said: a group of the People of the Suffa asked the Messenger (peace be upon him) that Allah enrich them and extend wealth and provisions to them, so this was revealed. Know that if provision came according to human demand, it would be the cause of their transgression and corruption, but He, the Exalted, knows best what is beneficial. Many a person is not set right, and his evil is not restrained, except by poverty, and another by wealth. In this meaning and division there is a hadith narrated by Anas, who said: "O Allah, I am among Your servants whom only wealth sets right, so do not make me poor."

(لَبَغَوْا) either means from arrogance and pride, i.e., they would have become haughty upon the earth, and did what follows from pride together with wealth. Do you not see the state of Qarun? In a hadith: "What I fear most for my nation is the splendor of the world." The poet said:
"They have made the spring rain grow between us and the Banu Rumman a thicket of nab' and shawhat [trees]," meaning: they loved [worldly things], so they dragged themselves into transgression and strife.

﴿But He sends down in measure what He wills﴾. It is said: qadara with a sukun and with a fatha, i.e., He determines for them what is most suitable for them. The majority read (قَنَطُوا) with a fatha on the nun; al-A'mash and Ibn Wathhab read it with a kasra. ﴿And spreads His mercy﴾: He manifests it through the effects of rain, in benefits and fertility. The apparent meaning is that spreading His mercy is more general than what is in the rain. Al-Suddi said: (رَحْمَتَهُ) is the rain, and he counted the same blessing with two expressions. It was said: the mercy here is the appearance of the sun, because when rain persists it becomes tiresome, so the sun comes after it with a great effect; this was mentioned by al-Mahdawi.

﴿And He is the Protector﴾: He who takes charge of His servants; (the Praiseworthy): the One praised for the blessings He has bestowed. (And what He has scattered) — the apparent reading is that it is in the genitive, conjoined to "the heavens and the earth." It is also permissible that it be in the nominative, conjoined to (خَلْقُ) with an elided genitive, i.e., and the creation of what He has scattered. Regarding both, it is permissible that (دابَّةٍ) be ascribed to the mentioned whole even though it is found in only some of it, as one says: "The Banu so-and-so did such-and-such," while only one of them did it; and from it [the sea] come forth both [sweet and salt water], while only salt comes from the salt [water]; or it may be from the angels, some of whom walk along with flying, so they are described with crawling as humans are; or He created in the heavens an animal that walks alongside human walking on the earth; or it means the animal found in the clouds. It sometimes occurs, like frogs, and the cloud falls within the name of "sky."

Mujahid said: (وما بَثَّ فِيهِما مِن دابَّةٍ) refers to humans and angels. Abu Ali said: it is with an elided genitive, i.e., and what He scattered in one of them. The majority read (فِيهِما) with the fa', and so it is in most of the codices. (ما) may be conditional, which is the more apparent, or relative. The fa' enters the predicate of a relative when it is treated like a condition, under conditions mentioned in grammar, and they are present. Nafi', Ibn Amir, Abu Ja'far in one narration, and Shayba read (بِما) without a fa', so (ما) is relative, and it cannot be conditional; the fa' was dropped because Sibawayh specifies that for poetry, while al-Akhfash and some Baghdad grammarians permitted it, and this is on the assumption of the fa'. The consequence of the calamities that befall [people] upon the earning of hands is present with the fa' and without it here. (المُصِيبَةُ): the afflictions and calamities in this world; they are a recompense for a person's sins and an expiation for his errors, and He, the Exalted, pardons much and does not requite it with a calamity. In a hadith: "No scratch of a stick, nor stumbling of a foot, nor twitch of a vein befalls the son of Adam except due to a sin, and what He pardons is greater." Imran ibn Husayn was asked about his illness and said: "The dearest of it to me is the dearest of it to Allah, and this is from what my hands have earned." A sore was seen on the palm of Shurayh, and it was said: "Because of what is this?" He said: "Because of what my hands have earned."

Al-Zamakhshari said: The verse is specific to the criminals, and there is no impossibility in Allah exacting the punishment of the criminal and pardoning some. As for one who has no crime, such as the prophets, children, and the insane, it is like when some pain or other befalls them, so it is for the full recompense and the benefit. From Ali: "This is the most hopeful verse for the believers." Al-Hasan said: (مِن مُصِيبَةٍ) means a limit from the limits of Allah; and those are calamities that descend upon a person's self and body, so they are only due to what your hands have earned.

(And He pardons) Allah (much), concealing it from the servants so that it is not punished.

(And you cannot escape) i.e., you are within the grasp of power. It is said: calamities such as illnesses, drought, drowning, and other things are not punishments for sins, because of His saying: ﴿Today every soul will be recompensed for what it earned﴾ [Ghafir: 17], and because the righteous and the wicked share in them; rather, what the righteous and pious are most tested with is more. In a hadith: "The prophets are singled out for trial, then the most excellent, then the next most excellent." Also, because this world is the abode of obligation, so if recompense occurred in it, it would be the abode of recompense, and the matter is not so. This view is contradicted by the texts of the Qur'an, such as His saying: ﴿So each one We seized for his sin; among them were those upon whom We sent a hurricane of stones﴾ [al-Ankabut: 40], and so on.

(p-507) ﴿Do they have partners who have instituted for them in religion what Allah has not permitted?﴾ This is an interrogative of affirmation (istifham taqrir) and reproach (tawbikh). When Exalted Allah mentioned that He had prescribed for mankind ﴿what He enjoined upon Noah﴾ [Ash-Shura: 13], up to the verse, He began to deny what others than Him had legislated.

Here "the partners" (al-shuraka') may mean their partners in disbelief, such as the devils and the misguiding men. The pronoun in "they instituted" (shara'u) refers to the partners, and the pronoun in "for them" (lahum) refers to the disbelievers contemporary with the Messenger. It may also mean the idols and images and everything they made a partner of Allah.

The partners are attributed to them (udifa) because they take them as partners of Allah. So they are attributed to them through this association, and at other times to Allah.

The pronoun in "they instituted" may refer to the partners, and "for them" to the disbelievers. Since the partners were the cause of their error and seduction, they were treated as legislators of the religion of disbelief, as Ibrahim (peace be upon him) said: ﴿My Lord, they have led many people astray﴾ [Ibrahim: 36].

It may also refer to the disbelievers, with "for them" referring to the partners, meaning: the disbelievers legislated for their idols and objects of worship, that is, they laid down for them misguidance and rulings in matters of belief, such as their saying that they are gods and that worshipping them brings one closer to Allah. Among the rulings are the baḥīra, the wasīla, the ḥāmī and others.

﴿Had it not been for the decisive word﴾: that is, the promise that the judgment will be in the Hereafter. Or: had it not been for the decree to that effect, the matter would have been judged between the believer and the disbeliever, or between the polytheists and their partners.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read "indeed the wrongdoers" (inna al-zalimina) with a kasra on the hamza, as a resumption (isti'naf) and an announcement of what will befall them in this world of killing, captivity and plunder, and in the Hereafter, the Fire. Al-A'raj and Muslim ibn Jundub read "and that" (wa-anna) with a fatḥa on the hamza, as a conjunction (ʿatf) upon "the decisive word", so it is in the position of a nominative. The meaning: had it not been for the decisive word and the fact that the wrongdoers have a painful punishment in the Hereafter, the matter would have been judged between them in this world. The conjunction is separated by the response of "had it not been", as in His saying: ﴿Had it not been for a word that preceded from your Lord, it would have been inevitable, and a specified term﴾ [Ta-Ha: 129].

﴿You see the wrongdoers﴾: that is, you see the disbelievers, since they are contrasted with the believers. "Fearful" (mushfiqin): afraid with intense fear. "Of what they have earned" (mimma kasabu): of the evil deeds. "And it befalls them" (wa-huwa): that is, the punishment; or it refers to "what they earned", with an omitted modifier, meaning: the calamity which they earned from evil deeds; or its recompense descends upon them.

﴿And it is about to befall them﴾: their fear is in this state, unlike the believers who in this world are fearful of the Hour. Since the gardens (rawdat) are the best and most pleasant part of the Gardens and their highest parts, He mentioned that the believers are in them.

The common reading is to pronounce the waw in "rawḍāt" with sukūn, while the dialect of Hudhayl ibn Mudrika is to pronounce it with a fatḥa, treating the weak letter like a sound one, as in "jafanāt". None of those whose dialect we know read it that way.

"ʿInda" (in the presence of) is an adverbial of place (ẓarf). Al-Ḥawfī said it is an operand (maʿmūl) of "they will wish" (yashāʾūn). Al-Zamakhsharī said it is governed by the adverb (ẓarf) "not wish", and that is correct. By "the adverb" he means the prepositional phrase, and in reality "for them" is not an operand of the governor of "for them". The meaning: what they wish of bliss and reward is established for them.

"In the presence of their Lord": this "presence" is one of rank and honour, not of mere location.

The majority read "yubashshiru" with a shadda on the shin, from bashshara. ʿAbd Allah ibn Yaʿmur, Ibn Abi Ishaq, al-Jaḥdarī, al-Aʿmash, Ṭalḥa in one narration, al-Kisāʾī and Ḥamza read "yabshuru" as a triliteral verb. Mujāhid and Ḥumayd ibn Qays read it with a ḍamma on the yāʾ and a sukūn on the shin, from abshara, which is transitive by the hamza, from the intransitive bashira with a kasra on the shin.

As for bashara with a fatḥa, it is transitive. Bashshara with a shadda is for intensification, not for transitivity, because the verb that is transitive to one object, when it is light (mukhaffaf), is not made transitive by doubling; so the doubling in it is for intensification, not for transitivity.

"That" (dhalika): a reference to the honour prepared for them. It is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is the relative clause, and the returning pronoun is omitted, meaning: Allah gives the good news of it to His servants.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: or "that" is the good news which Allah gives to His servants. That is the end of his words.

This view is not evident, since no mention of glad tidings (bushra) has preceded in this sūra, nor anything indicating it, such as giving good news or similar.

Some grammarians made "alladhī" (which) a verbal-noun particle (maṣdariyya), transmitted by Ibn Mālik from Yūnus, and this verse was interpreted accordingly, meaning: "that" is Allah's giving good news to His servants. But this is nothing, because it asserts a shared meaning among items of different definition without evidence.

The nominal status of "alladhī" is established, so one does not depart from that for anything that has no proof or even a plausible basis.

﴿Say: I do not ask you for any reward for it, except love for the near of kin﴾. It is related that the polytheists gathered in an assembly, and some of them said to others: "Do you see Muhammad asking a reward for what he is doing?" So this was revealed. It is also related that the Anṣār came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with money they had collected and said: "O Messenger of Allah, Allah guided us through you, and you are the son of our sister, and rights befall you, and you have no means, so use this to meet what befalls you." So the verse was revealed, and he refused it.

It was also said: the address is directed to the Quraysh when they gathered money for him and wanted to bribe him with it, on condition that he refrain from reviling their gods, but he did not do it, and the verse was revealed.

So the meaning: I do not ask you for money or leadership, but I ask you to respect the right of my kinship and to believe me in what I have brought you, and to refrain from harming me and those who follow me. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrima, Mujāhid, Abū Mālik, al-Shaʿbī and others.

al-Shaʿbī said: People made much of this verse against us, so we wrote to Ibn ʿAbbās asking him about it, and he wrote that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was the most central of the people among the Quraysh; there was no clan of theirs except that he was born to it. So Allah, Exalted, said: Say, I do not ask you for any reward for it, except that you love me for my kinship with you. So keep the ties between me and you, and believe me.

ʿIkrima said: The Quraysh used to maintain their kinship ties. al-Ḥasan said: the meaning is: except that you seek affection toward Allah by drawing near to Him.

ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Qāsim said: except that some of you show affection to others and maintain your kinship ties.

It is related that some young men of the Anṣār boasted over the Emigrants and raised their voices with words, so the verse was revealed in the sense: do not harm me in my kinship, and protect them for my sake. ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib (may Allah be pleased with them) said this in the same sense, and cited the verse when he was led as a captive to Syria. This is also the view of Ibn Jubayr, al-Suddī and ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb. On this interpretation, Ibn ʿAbbās said: It was said: O Messenger of Allah, who are your kin whose love we were commanded? He said: ʿAlī, Fāṭima and their two sons.

It was also said: they are the descendants of ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib. The apparent meaning is that His saying ﴿except love﴾ is a disjunctive exception (istithnā' munqaṭiʿ), since love is not a reward.

al-Zamakhsharī said: It may be a connected exception, meaning: I do not ask you for any reward for it, except this: that you love the people of my kinship. This was not truly a reward, because his kin are their kin, so maintaining ties with them was obligatory for them by manliness.

He also said: If you ask, why was it not said: "except the love of kinship" or "except love for the kin"? I answer: they made a place for love, and a settled ground for it, as when you say: "I have affection for the family of so-and-so, and I have a strong desire and love for them", meaning: I love them, and they are the place and seat of my love. It is not in the sense of a complement of love as the preposition "li-" would be if you said "except love for the kin"; rather it is connected to an omitted element, as the adverbial is connected to it in your saying: "the money is in the bag", and its estimation is: except love established in the kinship and settled in it. That is the end of his words, and it is good, though it is verbose. Zayd ibn ʿAlī read "except affection" (illā mawaddatan), while the majority read "except the love" (illā al-mawadda).

﴿And whoever earns a good deed﴾: that is, acquires it. The apparent meaning is that "good deed" is general, in the manner of a substitute (badal), so love for the kin and other things are included in it. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Suddī that it is the love for the family of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

The majority read "We will increase for him" (nazid) with a nūn; Zayd ibn ʿAlī, ʿAbd al-Wārith from Abū ʿAmr, and Aḥmad ibn Jubayr from al-Kisā'ī read "He will increase" (yazid) with a yā', meaning Allah will increase.

The majority read "goodness" (ḥusnan) with tanwīn; ʿAbd al-Wārith from Abū ʿAmr read "ḥusnā" without tanwīn, on the pattern of "rujʿā". The increase of its goodness is the multiplication of its reward.

﴿Indeed Allah is Forgiving, Grateful﴾: forgiving means He covers the faults of His servants; grateful means He rewards for the smallest act, and the deed of the doer is not lost before Him.

al-Suddī said: Forgiving of the sins of the family of Muhammad (peace be upon him), grateful for their good deeds.

﴿Or do they say: he has invented a lie against Allah?﴾: this turns from the preceding speech without annulling it, and asks in a manner of denial and reproach regarding this statement, meaning: someone like him is not attributed with lying (p-517) against Allah, given your previous acknowledgement of his truthfulness and trustworthiness.

﴿If Allah wills, He would seal your heart﴾. Mujāhid said: He would bind your heart with patience over their harm, so that their saying "you are a fabricator" does not grieve you.
