Rather, the meaning is an informing about the unseen events under the condition of His will; so it is coordinated with the jussive in wording, not in meaning. And a group read *wa-ya'fu* in the *raf'*, which is good in meaning. He finished. What he said is not good, for he did not grasp the signified meaning of the structure. The meaning is: if He wills, He destroys some people and saves others by way of pardoning them.

Al-Zamakhshari said: (if you ask) on what is *yubiqhunna* coordinated? (I answer): on *yuskin*, because the meaning is: if He wills, He stills the wind so they remain still, or He drives it so they drown by its driving. He finished.

It is not required that the estimate be "or He drives it so they drown," because the destruction of ships is not necessarily by the driving of the wind; He may destroy them by a cause other than the wind, such as the sinking of their deck due to excessive weight, or the breaking of a plank becoming the cause of their destruction, or an enemy attacking their people. Al-A'raj, Abu Ja'far, Shayba, Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Zayd ibn 'Ali read *wa-ya'lama* with the *raf'* (nominative) on the basis of a new sentence (*qat'*). The majority read *wa-ya'lama* with the *nasb* (accusative). Abu 'Ali said: the *nasb* is good when there is a condition and an apodosis before it, and each of them is not obligatory. Al-Zajjaj said: it is by implicit *an*, because before it there is an apodosis. You say: "Whatever you do, I do the like of it, and I honour you," and if you wish: "and I honour you" meaning "and I (am) honouring you," and if you wish: "and honour you" in the jussive.

Al-Zamakhshari said: there is a problem with this, for what Sibawayh set down in his book. He said: know that the *nasb* after the *fa'* and the *waw* in his saying "If you come to me I will come to you and give you" is weak, and it is of the kind of the poet's saying:

> And I join [the road to] the Hijaz, so that I may rest.

This is not permissible; it is neither the limit of speech nor its way, except that in the apodosis it has become somewhat stronger, because it is not obligatory that he will do it unless there is an action from the first part. When it resembles what is not obligatory, like the interrogative and the like, they allowed it in this case despite its weakness. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is not permissible to bear the widely transmitted reading on a weak form that is neither the limit of speech nor its way; and if it were of this type, Sibawayh would not have left it out of his book, and he mentioned its parallels from the ambiguous verses. He finished.

Al-Zamakhshari interpreted the *nasb* as coordinated with an omitted causal clause. He said: its estimate is: "in order that He may take vengeance upon them and that He may know those who dispute." This is disliked in coordination with an omitted causal clause, and it is not rare in the Qur'an, such as His saying: "And that We may make you a sign for the people" (Al-Baqara: 259), and His saying: "Allah created the heavens and the earth in truth" (Al-'Ankabut: 44), and "that every soul may be recompensed for what it earned" (Al-Jathiya: 22). He finished.

But his estimate "to take vengeance upon them" is distant, because the destruction of a people is what is consequent upon the condition, so "that He may take vengeance upon them" is not appropriate. As for the two verses, the *lam* can be connected to an omitted verb, meaning: "And that We may make him a sign for the people" (Maryam: 21), "and that every soul may be recompensed for what it earned" (Al-Jathiya: 22); We did that. It is often estimated that this verb is omitted before the *lam* of cause when there is no apparent verb to be connected to.

Al-Zamakhshari mentioned that His saying "wa-ya'lama" was read with the *jazm*. (If you ask): how is the meaning correct on the jussive of "wa-ya'lama"? (I answer): as if He said: "or if He wills, He gathers three matters: the destruction of a people, the salvation of a people, and the warning of others," because His saying "and those who dispute concerning Our signs will know" includes warning them of Allah's punishment; and "they have no place of escape" is in the position of the accusative, because "ya'lamu" is suspended (*mu'allaqa*), like your saying: "I knew what Zayd is standing." Ibn 'Atiyya said, regarding the *nasb* reading: this *waw* and others like it, which the Kufans call *waw al-sarf* (the "diverting" *waw*), since the real sense of *waw al-sarf* as they intend it is the coordination of a verb on a supposed noun; so *an* is supposed to be with the verb with the sense of a verbal noun, so its coordination on the noun is good. He finished.

This is not his statement as an explanation of their saying "*waw al-sarf*"; it is rather an exposition of the position of the Basrans. As for the Kufans, *waw al-sarf* is itself an operator in the accusative, not by the implicit *an* after it.

Abu 'Ubayd said: "on the *sarf*" like the one in Al 'Imran: "And that Allah may know those of you who strove and may know the steadfast" (Al 'Imran: 142). The meaning of *sarf* is that it was in one direction and then turned to another, so the case-marking changed because of the turning. Coordination does not necessarily determine simultaneity in existence, as in coordination in nouns, like: "Zayd came and 'Amr." If "'Amr" were in the accusative it would require simultaneity; and likewise *waw al-sarf*, to express the sense of simultaneity and specify the meaning of togetherness. For this reason there is consensus on the accusative in His saying "and may know the steadfast" (Al 'Imran: 142), meaning: "and may know the strivers and the steadfast together."

On the authority of 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him): Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) acquired property, and he gave all of it in charity in the way of Allah and for good. The Muslims blamed him, and the disbelievers considered him in error; so there was revealed: "And whatever you have been given of a thing..." The apparent sense is that it is addressed to people.

It was said: it is addressed to the polytheists. *Ma* here is conditional; it is the second object of *utitum* (you were given), and *min shay'* (of a thing) is an explanation of *ma*. The meaning: of a thing of the finery and wealth of the world and the abundance in it. The *fa'* is the apodosis of the condition, meaning: then it is enjoyment, i.e. it is enjoyed in the life.

*Wa-ma 'inda Allah* means what is with Allah, i.e. of His reward and what He prepared for His friends, "is better and more lasting" than what you were given, because it has no cessation.

The discussion of the major sins (*al-kaba'ir*) occurred before in His saying: "If you avoid the major sins of what you are forbidden" (Al-Nisa': 31), in the chapter of Women. The majority read *kaba'ir* in the plural here and in al-Najm, while Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it in the singular.

*Wa-alladhina yajtanibuna* (and those who avoid) is coordinated on *alladhina amanu* (those who believed), and likewise what follows. Abu al-Baqa' fell into an error in recitation: he believed that it is *alladhina yajtanibuna* without a *waw*, so he built the i'rab on that and said: *alladhina yajtanibuna* (An-Najm: 32) is in the position of the genitive as a substitute (*badal*) for *alladhina amanu*, and it may be in the accusative position by an implicit verb, namely "I mean," and in the nominative position with the estimate "they are." He finished.

The governing element of *idha* (when) is *yaghfiruna* (they forgive), and it is a clause of subject and predicate coordinated on *yajtanibuna*. It is permissible that *hum* be an emphasis for the subject in *ghadibu* (they became angry).

Abu al-Baqa' said: *hum* is a subject, *yaghfiruna* is the predicate, and the clause is the apodosis of *idha*. He finished. This is not permissible, because if the clause were the apodosis of *idha* it would have to have the *fa'*; you say: "When Zayd comes, then 'Amr is departing," and it is not permissible to drop the *fa'* except if it occurs in poetry.

It was said: *hum* is in the nominative by an omitted verb which *yaghfiruna* explains; and when the verb was omitted, the pronoun was separated. This statement needs consideration, namely that the apodosis of *idha* is explained as the verb of the condition after it is explained, as in "When the heaven splits asunder" (Al-Inshiqaq: 1). And it is not far that this is permissible according to Sibawayh's view, since it occurs with the jussive conditional particle, like: "If Zayd departs, he departs," where Zayd is by Sibawayh the subject of an omitted verb explained by the apodosis, meaning: "Zayd departs." Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' prevented this.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "*hum yaghfiruna*" means: they are the ones specially for forgiveness, in the state of anger; anger does not confuse their forbearance, as it confuses people's intellects. The coming of them and its occurrence is a subject, and the attribution of "*yaghfiruna*" to it is for this benefit. He finished. In this there is an exhortation to restrain anger.

And in the hadith: "Advise me." He said: "Do not become angry." He said: "Advise me further." He said: "Do not become angry." He said: "Advise me further." He said: "Do not become angry."

﴿And those who respond to their Lord﴾. It was said: it was revealed concerning the Ansar. Allah called them to faith in Him and obedience to Him, and they responded. Before Islam, and before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to Medina, whenever a matter befell them they would consult one another, so Allah praised them for this. They would not act alone in a matter until they agreed upon it.

From al-Hasan: "No people consulted together except that they were guided to the most right course of their affair." End of quote.

Consultation (shura) brings about unity of word, mutual affection, and cooperation in good. The Messenger (ﷺ), peace be upon him, consulted in matters concerning the interests of war, and the Companions after him did likewise, such as Umar's consultation with al-Hurmuz. And in legal rulings, such as fighting the people of apostasy (ridda), the inheritance of a harbi (non-Muslim combatant), the number of lashes for drinkers of wine, and other matters.

Shura is a verbal noun like futya, meaning consultation, with an omitted modifier, i.e. "and their affair is by consultation among them." The phrase ﴿they defend themselves﴾ (hum yantasiruna) is a relative clause for alladhina (those who). Idha (when) is governed by yantasiruna. It is not permissible for ﴿they defend themselves﴾ to be the response (jawab) of idha, because the conditional clause and its response would then be a relative clause, given what we mentioned about the requirement of the fa' (the particle "then"). Here it is permissible for hum to be the subject of an omitted verb, according to the opinion stated concerning ﴿they forgive﴾ (hum yaghfiruna). Al-Hawfi said: "If you wish, you may make hum a corroborative of the ha' and mim, meaning in (asabahum), which is a nominative pronoun." There is scrutiny in this, since it involves separating the corroborated from the corroborator by a verb, which is apparently not prohibited. Intisar (defending oneself) means confining oneself to what Allah has set as its limit and not transgressing.

Al-Nakha'i said: "They used to dislike humiliating themselves, lest the wicked become emboldened against them. Whoever defends himself without transgressing is obedient and praiseworthy." Muqatil and Hisham, from Urwa, said: the verse refers to the one wronged who takes his right from the wrongdoer through retaliation (qisas). Ibn Abbas said: the polytheists transgressed against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his Companions and expelled them from Mecca, so Allah permitted them to go out into the earth, and He gave them victory over those who oppressed them.

Al-Kiya al-Tabari said: the apparent meaning is that defending oneself in this context is better. Do you not see that He linked it to responding to Allah and His Messenger and establishing the prayer? This accords with what al-Nakha'i mentioned. This applies to one who transgresses and persists, whereas the command to pardon applies when the offender is remorseful and has given up (his wrongdoing). He stated, after this verse, ﴿And whoever defends himself after being wronged﴾, the verse, which implies permission for defending oneself. He followed it with His saying: ﴿And whoever is patient and forgives﴾, and this is to be understood, according to the Qur'an, as applying to one who is not persistent. As for the one who persists in transgression, defending oneself against him is better, by the evidence of the verse before it. Ibn Bahr said: the meaning is that they support one another against him, removing him from them.

Abu Bakr ibn al-Arabi said something similar to what al-Kiya said.

The majority said: if a believer transgresses against a believer, it is not permissible for the latter to take redress by himself, but rather he refers the matter to the imam (ruler) or his deputy. A group said: he may do so.

﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾: this is an explanation of defending oneself, meaning one must not exceed the limit in what he repays the one who transgressed against him.

Ibn Abi Najih and al-Suddi said: if he is insulted, he may return the like of what he was insulted with, without exceeding. Retaliation was called an "evil" by way of correspondence, or because it grieves the one against whom it is applied, just as menstruation (al-hayd) is called a harm. The apparent meaning of His saying "like it" is equivalence absolutely in all circumstances, not in what the evidence has specified. The jurists introduced specification in many cases on the basis of analogy (qiyas).

Mujahid and al-Suddi said: if he says to him, "May Allah disgrace you," he may say, "May Allah disgrace you." And if he slanders him in a way that requires the prescribed punishment (hadd), then the hadd is what Allah has commanded.

﴿Whoever pardons and makes reconciliation﴾, meaning between himself and his adversary through pardon, ﴿his reward is with Allah﴾: a vague promise whose greatness cannot be measured, since it is with Allah.

﴿Indeed, He does not love the wrongdoers﴾, meaning the treacherous. If He does not love such a person, while he has been urged to pardon him, then the pardon that Allah loves is more worthy of being pardoned. Or, He does not love the wrongdoers, meaning those who go beyond the limit and transgress against those who were wronged when they defend themselves, especially in the state of war and the heat of zeal, for he may then do wrong without realizing it.

In the hadith: "When the Day of Resurrection comes, a caller will call out: whoever has a reward with Allah, let him stand. He said: So a multitude will stand, and it will be said to them: What is your reward with Allah? They will say: We pardoned those who wronged us. It will be said to them: Enter Paradise by the permission of Allah."

The lam in ﴿And whoever defends himself﴾ is a lam of emphasis. Al-Hawfi said: in it is the meaning of an oath. Ibn Atiyya said: it is the lam of the meeting of an oath (lam al-taqaqi al-qasam), meaning that it is the lam with which an oath is introduced, so the oath is omitted before it. Man is conditional. ﴿Defends himself after his being wronged﴾ is construed according to the wording of man, and ﴿then those﴾ is construed according to the meaning of man. The fa' is the response of the condition. Zulmihi (his being wronged) is a verbal noun annexed to its object.

Al-Zamakhshari said: the reading of one who reads "after he was wronged" (ba'da ma zulima) explains it.

﴿There is no way against them﴾: it was said, meaning no path to blame; and it was said: no path against the one who punishes, nor against the one who reproaches or is reproached. This is an exaggeration in permitting defending oneself.

﴿The way is only﴾, meaning the way of sin and blame, ﴿against those who wrong﴾, meaning those who debase themselves through wrongdoing, ﴿and who transgress in the earth﴾, meaning they act arrogantly in it, rise above others, and cause corruption. It was said: (and who wrong people), meaning they put things in other than their proper places through killing, seizing property, and harm with hand and tongue.

Transgression (baghy) is without right, and it is a kind of wrongdoing. He singled it out for mention to draw attention to its severity and the bad state of its perpetrator. End of quote.

﴿And whoever is patient﴾, meaning in the face of wrongdoing and harm, (and forgives), and does not defend himself. The lam in (wa-man) may be the introductory lam (al-lam al-muwatti'a) for the omitted oath, with man as conditional, and the response of the oath is His saying (inna dhalika, "indeed that"), and the response of the condition is omitted because the response of the oath indicates it.

It is also permissible that the lam be the lam of the inception (lam al-ibtida'), and man a relative pronoun serving as subject, with the clause emphasized by inna in the position of the predicate.

Al-Hawfi said: man is in the nominative by inception, and the predicate is omitted, and the response of the condition is inna and what is connected to it, with the fa' omitted, as the poet said:

"Whoever does good deeds, Allah will reward them."

meaning: then Allah will reward them. End of quote. This is not sound, because omitting the fa' is specific to poetry according to Sibawayh. The demonstrative dhalika refers to what is understood from the verbal noun of sabara and ghafara, and the returning pronoun in the predicate linked to the subject is omitted, meaning: indeed that is from him, by the meaning's indication: ﴿truly, it is among the steadfast resolves of affairs﴾. If dhalika refers to the verbal noun understood from His saying ﴿and whoever is patient and forgives﴾, then there is no omission in ﴿steadfast resolves of affairs﴾. If dhalika refers to the subject, then it is the linking element, and it needs no estimation from it, and ﴿steadfast resolves of affairs﴾ would mean: indeed he is among those possessing steadfast resolves of affairs.

[p. 524] A man insulted another man in the assembly of al-Hasan. The one insulted kept silent, perspiring and wiping the sweat. Then he stood up and recited the verse. Al-Hasan said: "By Allah, he understood it and grasped it. Why do the ignorant neglect it?"

The clause ﴿the way is only﴾ is a parenthetical insertion between His saying ﴿and whoever defends himself﴾ and His saying ﴿and whoever is patient﴾.

﴿And whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no protector after Him﴾, meaning no helper who would take charge of him, (after Him), meaning after his being led astray. This is a belittling of the state of the disbelievers.

﴿And you see the wrongdoers﴾: the address is to the Messenger, and the meaning is: you see their condition and the bewilderment they are in, ﴿when they see the punishment﴾, they say: ﴿Is there any way to return?﴾, meaning: is there a path to return to the world? That is because of the horrible things they have witnessed and the evil that befalls them.

﴿And you see them presented before it﴾ [al-Shura: 45], meaning before the Fire; the mention of the punishment indicates it. (Humbled), meaning shrinking and abased because of what overtakes them, (from humiliation).

Talha read (min al-dhilli) with a kasra on the dhal, while the majority read it with a damma. Khushu' means submissiveness, and it is praiseworthy. It was its being joined with punishment that turned it into dispraise. It was said: (min al-dhull) is related to ﴿they look with a furtive glance﴾ [al-Shura: 45].

Ibn Abbas said: "Humiliated." End of quote.

It was said: it is described as furtive because their glance is weak and their gaze is at its limit. The poet said:

"So lower your gaze, for you are of Numayr."

It was said: they will be raised blind. Since their looking is with the eyes of their hearts, He made it a furtive glance, meaning their looking does not show. This interpretation involves strain.

Al-Suddi and Qatada said: the meaning is that they steal glances because of the grief and bad state they are in; they cannot look with the whole eye, but look with only part of it. On this interpretation, the word tarf (glance) may be a verbal noun, meaning a furtive glance. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿from a furtive glance﴾ [al-Shura: 45] means that their looking begins with a weak, hidden movement of the eyelids, by stealth, just as you see the one who examines a sword looking at it, and so is the glance of one who looks at hateful things: he cannot open his eyelids upon them and fill his eye with them, as he does when looking at those who love one another.

(p-520) [Qur'an 42:32] And among His signs are the ships running in the sea like mountains. [42:33] If He wills, He stills the wind, and they remain motionless on its surface. Indeed, in that are signs for every steadfast, grateful one. [42:34] Or He destroys them for what they have earned, and pardons much. [42:35] And those who dispute concerning Our signs will know that they have no place of escape. [42:36] So whatever you have been given is but the enjoyment of the worldly life; and what is with Allah is better and more lasting for those who believe and rely upon their Lord. [42:37] And those who avoid the major sins and immoralities and, when they are angry, forgive. [42:38] And those who have responded to their Lord, established prayer, whose affair is by consultation among themselves, and who spend from what We have provided them. [42:39] And those who, when oppression afflicts them, defend themselves. [42:40] And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it, but whoever pardons and makes reconciliation, his reward is with Allah. Indeed, He does not love the wrongdoers. [42:41] And whoever defends himself after being wronged, those have no blame upon them. [42:42] The blame is only upon those who wrong people and oppress throughout the earth without right; those will have a painful punishment. [42:43] And whoever is patient and forgives, indeed that is of the matters requiring determination. [42:44] And whom Allah leaves astray, for him there is no protector after Him. And you will see the wrongdoers, when they see the punishment, saying, "Is there any way of return?" [42:45] And you will see them exposed to it, humbled by humiliation, glancing with a furtive look. [al-Shura: 45]

When He mentioned among the proofs of His oneness several kinds, He then mentioned the greater world, which is the heavens and the earth; then the lesser world, which is the animal kingdom. Then, having followed this with the mention of the Return, He followed it with the mention of the ships running in the sea, because in them there is great evidence of power: water is a subtle, transparent body in which a heavy thing sinks, while ships are carried by heavy, dense bodies. Despite this, Allah made for the water a strength by which it bears them and prevents them from sinking. Then He made the winds the cause of their movement; so when He wills that they come to rest, He stills the wind, and they do not move from their place.

*al-Jawari* is the plural of *jariya*, and its original form is *al-sufun al-jawari* (the running ships). The qualified noun was omitted and its adjective took its place. What made this acceptable is His saying *fi al-bahr* (in the sea), which shows that the adjective refers to the ships; otherwise the adjective is not specific, and by analogy (*qiyas*) the qualified noun should not have been omitted and replaced by its adjective. It may be said that it is a predominant adjective (*sifa ghaliba*), like *al-abtah*, so it may stand in place of the governed noun without mention of the qualified noun. *Al-jawari* has also been read with and without the *ya'*, and it has been heard from the Arabs with i'rab (grammatical case-marking, i.e. inflection) on the *ra'*. *Fi al-bahr* is attached to *al-jawari*, and *ka-al-a'lam* is in the position of a circumstantial accusative (*hal*). *Al-a'lam* means mountains, and from this is the saying of al-Khansa', sister of Sakhr and Mu'awiya:

> Indeed, Sakhr, the guided ones take guidance by him,
> as if he were a banner with fire upon its head.

And from it:

> When they crossed a landmark, a landmark appeared.

The majority of the Seven read *al-riha* (the wind) in the singular, while Nafi' read it in the plural. The majority read *fa-yazlalna* with a *fatha* on the *lam*, while Qatada read it with a *kasra*; the analogical form is the *fatha*, because the perfect of this verb has a *kasra* on the 'ayn, so the *kasra* in the imperfect is anomalous (*shadh*). Al-Zamakhshari said: it comes from *zalla yazallu* and *yazillu*, like *dalla yadallu* and *yadillu*. He finished.

This is not as he mentioned, because *yadallu* with a *fatha* on the 'ayn comes from *daliltu* with a *kasra* in the perfect, and *yadillu* with a *kasra* comes from *dalaltu* with a *fatha* in the perfect; both are analogical.

*Li-kulli sabbar* (for every steadfast one) in affliction, *shakur* (grateful) for His blessings.

*Aw yubiqhunna* means He destroys them, i.e. the ships. It is coordinated with *yuskin* (He stills). The pronoun in *kasabu* refers to the passengers of the ships, meaning: because of their sins. Al-A'mash read *wa-ya'fu* with a *waw*, and it is reported from the people of Madina that they read the *waw* with a *fatha*, while the majority read *wa-ya'fu* in the jussive (*majzum*), coordinated with *yubiqhunna*. As for the reading of al-A'mash, it informs that He pardons much, i.e. He does not punish for everything a person has earned. As for the *fatha* reading, it is by implicit *an* after the *waw*, like the *fatha* after the *fa'* in the reading of the one who read *yuhasibkum bihi Allah fa-yaghfiru* (Al-Baqara: 284), and after the *waw* in the verse of the poet:

> If Abu Qabus perishes, there will perish
> the spring of the people and the sacred month.

> And after him we take up the tail of a life,
> its back bare of hump, having no hump.

It is narrated with *wa-na'khudhu* in the *fatha*, the *raf'* (nominative) and the *jazm* (jussive).

In this reading the coordination is with a supposed verbal noun (*masdar mutawahham*), i.e. there occurs a destruction and a pardoning of much. As for the jussive, it falls under the judgment of the apodosis of the condition (*jawab al-shart*), since it is coordinated with it; in meaning it returns to the *fatha* reading, but this is coordination of a verb on a verb, whereas in the *fatha* it is coordination of a supposed verbal noun on a verb.

Al-Qushayri said: it was read *wa-ya'fu* in the jussive, and there is a problem in it, because the meaning is: if He wills, He stills the wind so the ships remain motionless, or He destroys them for the sins of their people. So *wa-ya'fu* cannot be coordinated with these; the meaning would become "if He wills, He pardons," which is not the meaning. Rather, the meaning is an informing about the unseen events under the condition of His will; so it is coordinated with the jussive in wording, not in meaning. And a group read *wa-ya'fu* in the *raf'*, which is good in meaning. He finished. What he said is not good, for he did not grasp the signified meaning of the structure. The meaning is: if He wills, He destroys some people and saves others by way of pardoning them.

Al-Zamakhshari said: (if you ask) on what is *yubiqhunna* coordinated? (I answer): on *yuskin*, because the meaning is: if He wills, He stills the wind so they remain still, or He drives it so they drown by its driving. He finished.

It is not required that the estimate be "or He drives it so they drown," because the destruction of ships is not necessarily by the driving of the wind; He may destroy them by a cause other than the wind, such as the sinking of their deck due to excessive weight, or the breaking of a plank becoming the cause of their destruction, or an enemy attacking their people. Al-A'raj, Abu Ja'far, Shayba, Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Zayd ibn 'Ali read *wa-ya'lama* with the *raf'* (nominative) on the basis of a new sentence (*qat'*). The majority read *wa-ya'lama* with the *nasb* (accusative). Abu 'Ali said: the *nasb* is good when there is a condition and an apodosis before it, and each of them is not obligatory. Al-Zajjaj said: it is by implicit *an*, because before it there is an apodosis. You say: "Whatever you do, I do the like of it, and I honour you," and if you wish: "and I honour you" meaning "and I (am) honouring you," and if you wish: "and honour you" in the jussive.

Al-Zamakhshari said: there is a problem with this, for what Sibawayh set down in his book. He said: know that the *nasb* after the *fa'* and the *waw* in his saying "If you come to me I will come to you and give you" is weak, and it is of the kind of the poet's saying:

> And I join [the road to] the Hijaz, so that I may rest.

This is not permissible; it is neither the limit of speech nor its way, except that in the apodosis it has become somewhat stronger, because it is not obligatory that he will do it unless there is an action from the first part. When it resembles what is not obligatory, like the interrogative and the like, they allowed it in this case despite its weakness. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is not permissible to bear the widely transmitted reading on a weak form that is neither the limit of speech nor its way; and if it were of this type, Sibawayh would not have left it out of his book, and he mentioned its parallels from the ambiguous verses. He finished.

Al-Zamakhshari interpreted the *nasb* as coordinated with an omitted causal clause. He said: its estimate is: "in order that He may take vengeance upon them and that He may know those who dispute." This is disliked in coordination with an omitted causal clause, and it is not rare in the Qur'an, such as His saying: "And that We may make you a sign for the people" (Al-Baqara: 259), and His saying: "Allah created the heavens and the earth in truth" (Al-'Ankabut: 44), and "that every soul may be recompensed for what it earned" (Al-Jathiya: 22). He finished.

But his estimate "to take vengeance upon them" is distant, because the destruction of a people is what is consequent upon the condition, so "that He may take vengeance upon them" is not appropriate. As for the two verses, the *lam* can be connected to an omitted verb, meaning: "And that We may make him a sign for the people" (Maryam: 21), "and that every soul may be recompensed for what it earned" (Al-Jathiya: 22); We did that. It is often estimated that this verb is omitted before the *lam* of cause when there is no apparent verb to be connected to.

Al-Zamakhshari mentioned that His saying "wa-ya'lama" was read with the *jazm*. (If you ask): how is the meaning correct on the jussive of "wa-ya'lama"? (I answer): as if He said: "or if He wills, He gathers three matters: the destruction of a people, the salvation of a people, and the warning of others," because His saying "and those who dispute concerning Our signs will know" includes warning them of Allah's punishment; and "they have no place of escape" is in the position of the accusative, because "ya'lamu" is suspended (*mu'allaqa*), like your saying: "I knew what Zayd is standing." Ibn 'Atiyya said, regarding the *nasb* reading: this *waw* and others like it, which the Kufans call *waw al-sarf* (the "diverting" *waw*), since the real sense of *waw al-sarf* as they intend it is the coordination of a verb on a supposed noun; so *an* is supposed to be with the verb with the sense of a verbal noun, so its coordination on the noun is good. He finished.

This is not his statement as an explanation of their saying "*waw al-sarf*"; it is rather an exposition of the position of the Basrans. As for the Kufans, *waw al-sarf* is itself an operator in the accusative, not by the implicit *an* after it.

Abu 'Ubayd said: "on the *sarf*" like the one in Al 'Imran: "And that Allah may know those of you who strove and may know the steadfast" (Al 'Imran: 142). The meaning of *sarf* is that it was in one direction and then turned to another, so the case-marking changed because of the turning. Coordination does not necessarily determine simultaneity in existence, as in coordination in nouns, like: "Zayd came and 'Amr." If "'Amr" were in the accusative it would require simultaneity; and likewise *waw al-sarf*, to express the sense of simultaneity and specify the meaning of togetherness. For this reason there is consensus on the accusative in His saying "and may know the steadfast" (Al 'Imran: 142), meaning: "and may know the strivers and the steadfast together."

On the authority of 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him): Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) acquired property, and he gave all of it in charity in the way of Allah and for good. The Muslims blamed him, and the disbelievers considered him in error; so there was revealed: "And whatever you have been given of a thing..." The apparent sense is that it is addressed to people.

It was said: it is addressed to the polytheists. *Ma* here is conditional; it is the second object of *utitum* (you were given), and *min shay'* (of a thing) is an explanation of *ma*. The meaning: of a thing of the finery and wealth of the world and the abundance in it. The *fa'* is the apodosis of the condition, meaning: then it is enjoyment, i.e. it is enjoyed in the life.

*Wa-ma 'inda Allah* means what is with Allah, i.e. of His reward and what He prepared for His friends, "is better and more lasting" than what you were given, because it has no cessation.

The discussion of the major sins (*al-kaba'ir*) occurred before in His saying: "If you avoid the major sins of what you are forbidden" (Al-Nisa': 31), in the chapter of Women. The majority read *kaba'ir* in the plural here and in al-Najm, while Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it in the singular.

*Wa-alladhina yajtanibuna* (and those who avoid) is coordinated on *alladhina amanu* (those who believed), and likewise what follows. Abu al-Baqa' fell into an error in recitation: he believed that it is *alladhina yajtanibuna* without a *waw*, so he built the i'rab on that and said: *alladhina yajtanibuna* (An-Najm: 32) is in the position of the genitive as a substitute (*badal*) for *alladhina amanu*, and it may be in the accusative position by an implicit verb, namely "I mean," and in the nominative position with the estimate "they are." He finished.

The governing element of *idha* (when) is *yaghfiruna* (they forgive), and it is a clause of subject and predicate coordinated on *yajtanibuna*. It is permissible that *hum* be an emphasis for the subject in *ghadibu* (they became angry).

Abu al-Baqa' said: *hum* is a subject, *yaghfiruna* is the predicate, and the clause is the apodosis of *idha*. He finished. This is not permissible, because if the clause were the apodosis of *idha* it would have to have the *fa'*; you say: "When Zayd comes, then 'Amr is departing," and it is not permissible to drop the *fa'* except if it occurs in poetry.

It was said: *hum* is in the nominative by an omitted verb which *yaghfiruna* explains; and when the verb was omitted, the pronoun was separated. This statement needs consideration, namely that the apodosis of *idha* is explained as the verb of the condition after it is explained, as in "When the heaven splits asunder" (Al-Inshiqaq: 1). And it is not far that this is permissible according to Sibawayh's view, since it occurs with the jussive conditional particle, like: "If Zayd departs, he departs," where Zayd is by Sibawayh the subject of an omitted verb explained by the apodosis, meaning: "Zayd departs." Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' prevented this.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "*hum yaghfiruna*" means: they are the ones specially for forgiveness, in the state of anger; anger does not confuse their forbearance, as it confuses people's intellects. The coming of them and its occurrence is a subject, and the attribution of "*yaghfiruna*" to it is for this benefit. He finished. In this there is an exhortation to restrain anger.

And in the hadith: "Advise me." He said: "Do not become angry." He said: "Advise me further." He said: "Do not become angry." He said: "Advise me further." He said: "Do not become angry."

﴿And those who respond to their Lord﴾. It was said: it was revealed concerning the Ansar. Allah called them to faith in Him and obedience to Him, and they responded. Before Islam, and before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to Medina, whenever a matter befell them they would consult one another, so Allah praised them for this. They would not act alone in a matter until they agreed upon it.

From al-Hasan: "No people consulted together except that they were guided to the most right course of their affair." End of quote.

Consultation (shura) brings about unity of word, mutual affection, and cooperation in good. The Messenger (ﷺ), peace be upon him, consulted in matters concerning the interests of war, and the Companions after him did likewise, such as Umar's consultation with al-Hurmuz. And in legal rulings, such as fighting the people of apostasy (ridda), the inheritance of a harbi (non-Muslim combatant), the number of lashes for drinkers of wine, and other matters.

Shura is a verbal noun like futya, meaning consultation, with an omitted modifier, i.e. "and their affair is by consultation among them." The phrase ﴿they defend themselves﴾ (hum yantasiruna) is a relative clause for alladhina (those who). Idha (when) is governed by yantasiruna. It is not permissible for ﴿they defend themselves﴾ to be the response (jawab) of idha, because the conditional clause and its response would then be a relative clause, given what we mentioned about the requirement of the fa' (the particle "then"). Here it is permissible for hum to be the subject of an omitted verb, according to the opinion stated concerning ﴿they forgive﴾ (hum yaghfiruna). Al-Hawfi said: "If you wish, you may make hum a corroborative of the ha' and mim, meaning in (asabahum), which is a nominative pronoun." There is scrutiny in this, since it involves separating the corroborated from the corroborator by a verb, which is apparently not prohibited. Intisar (defending oneself) means confining oneself to what Allah has set as its limit and not transgressing.

Al-Nakha'i said: "They used to dislike humiliating themselves, lest the wicked become emboldened against them. Whoever defends himself without transgressing is obedient and praiseworthy." Muqatil and Hisham, from Urwa, said: the verse refers to the one wronged who takes his right from the wrongdoer through retaliation (qisas). Ibn Abbas said: the polytheists transgressed against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his Companions and expelled them from Mecca, so Allah permitted them to go out into the earth, and He gave them victory over those who oppressed them.

Al-Kiya al-Tabari said: the apparent meaning is that defending oneself in this context is better. Do you not see that He linked it to responding to Allah and His Messenger and establishing the prayer? This accords with what al-Nakha'i mentioned. This applies to one who transgresses and persists, whereas the command to pardon applies when the offender is remorseful and has given up (his wrongdoing). He stated, after this verse, ﴿And whoever defends himself after being wronged﴾, the verse, which implies permission for defending oneself. He followed it with His saying: ﴿And whoever is patient and forgives﴾, and this is to be understood, according to the Qur'an, as applying to one who is not persistent. As for the one who persists in transgression, defending oneself against him is better, by the evidence of the verse before it. Ibn Bahr said: the meaning is that they support one another against him, removing him from them.

Abu Bakr ibn al-Arabi said something similar to what al-Kiya said.

The majority said: if a believer transgresses against a believer, it is not permissible for the latter to take redress by himself, but rather he refers the matter to the imam (ruler) or his deputy. A group said: he may do so.

﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾: this is an explanation of defending oneself, meaning one must not exceed the limit in what he repays the one who transgressed against him.

Ibn Abi Najih and al-Suddi said: if he is insulted, he may return the like of what he was insulted with, without exceeding. Retaliation was called an "evil" by way of correspondence, or because it grieves the one against whom it is applied, just as menstruation (al-hayd) is called a harm. The apparent meaning of His saying "like it" is equivalence absolutely in all circumstances, not in what the evidence has specified. The jurists introduced specification in many cases on the basis of analogy (qiyas).

Mujahid and al-Suddi said: if he says to him, "May Allah disgrace you," he may say, "May Allah disgrace you." And if he slanders him in a way that requires the prescribed punishment (hadd), then the hadd is what Allah has commanded.

﴿Whoever pardons and makes reconciliation﴾, meaning between himself and his adversary through pardon, ﴿his reward is with Allah﴾: a vague promise whose greatness cannot be measured, since it is with Allah.

﴿Indeed, He does not love the wrongdoers﴾, meaning the treacherous. If He does not love such a person, while he has been urged to pardon him, then the pardon that Allah loves is more worthy of being pardoned. Or, He does not love the wrongdoers, meaning those who go beyond the limit and transgress against those who were wronged when they defend themselves, especially in the state of war and the heat of zeal, for he may then do wrong without realizing it.

In the hadith: "When the Day of Resurrection comes, a caller will call out: whoever has a reward with Allah, let him stand. He said: So a multitude will stand, and it will be said to them: What is your reward with Allah? They will say: We pardoned those who wronged us. It will be said to them: Enter Paradise by the permission of Allah."

The lam in ﴿And whoever defends himself﴾ is a lam of emphasis. Al-Hawfi said: in it is the meaning of an oath. Ibn Atiyya said: it is the lam of the meeting of an oath (lam al-taqaqi al-qasam), meaning that it is the lam with which an oath is introduced, so the oath is omitted before it. Man is conditional. ﴿Defends himself after his being wronged﴾ is construed according to the wording of man, and ﴿then those﴾ is construed according to the meaning of man. The fa' is the response of the condition. Zulmihi (his being wronged) is a verbal noun annexed to its object.

Al-Zamakhshari said: the reading of one who reads "after he was wronged" (ba'da ma zulima) explains it.

﴿There is no way against them﴾: it was said, meaning no path to blame; and it was said: no path against the one who punishes, nor against the one who reproaches or is reproached. This is an exaggeration in permitting defending oneself.

﴿The way is only﴾, meaning the way of sin and blame, ﴿against those who wrong﴾, meaning those who debase themselves through wrongdoing, ﴿and who transgress in the earth﴾, meaning they act arrogantly in it, rise above others, and cause corruption. It was said: (and who wrong people), meaning they put things in other than their proper places through killing, seizing property, and harm with hand and tongue.

Transgression (baghy) is without right, and it is a kind of wrongdoing. He singled it out for mention to draw attention to its severity and the bad state of its perpetrator. End of quote.

﴿And whoever is patient﴾, meaning in the face of wrongdoing and harm, (and forgives), and does not defend himself. The lam in (wa-man) may be the introductory lam (al-lam al-muwatti'a) for the omitted oath, with man as conditional, and the response of the oath is His saying (inna dhalika, "indeed that"), and the response of the condition is omitted because the response of the oath indicates it.

It is also permissible that the lam be the lam of the inception (lam al-ibtida'), and man a relative pronoun serving as subject, with the clause emphasized by inna in the position of the predicate.

Al-Hawfi said: man is in the nominative by inception, and the predicate is omitted, and the response of the condition is inna and what is connected to it, with the fa' omitted, as the poet said:

"Whoever does good deeds, Allah will reward them."

meaning: then Allah will reward them. End of quote. This is not sound, because omitting the fa' is specific to poetry according to Sibawayh. The demonstrative dhalika refers to what is understood from the verbal noun of sabara and ghafara, and the returning pronoun in the predicate linked to the subject is omitted, meaning: indeed that is from him, by the meaning's indication: ﴿truly, it is among the steadfast resolves of affairs﴾. If dhalika refers to the verbal noun understood from His saying ﴿and whoever is patient and forgives﴾, then there is no omission in ﴿steadfast resolves of affairs﴾. If dhalika refers to the subject, then it is the linking element, and it needs no estimation from it, and ﴿steadfast resolves of affairs﴾ would mean: indeed he is among those possessing steadfast resolves of affairs.

[p. 524] A man insulted another man in the assembly of al-Hasan. The one insulted kept silent, perspiring and wiping the sweat. Then he stood up and recited the verse. Al-Hasan said: "By Allah, he understood it and grasped it. Why do the ignorant neglect it?"

The clause ﴿the way is only﴾ is a parenthetical insertion between His saying ﴿and whoever defends himself﴾ and His saying ﴿and whoever is patient﴾.

﴿And whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no protector after Him﴾, meaning no helper who would take charge of him, (after Him), meaning after his being led astray. This is a belittling of the state of the disbelievers.

﴿And you see the wrongdoers﴾: the address is to the Messenger, and the meaning is: you see their condition and the bewilderment they are in, ﴿when they see the punishment﴾, they say: ﴿Is there any way to return?﴾, meaning: is there a path to return to the world? That is because of the horrible things they have witnessed and the evil that befalls them.

﴿And you see them presented before it﴾ [al-Shura: 45], meaning before the Fire; the mention of the punishment indicates it. (Humbled), meaning shrinking and abased because of what overtakes them, (from humiliation).

Talha read (min al-dhilli) with a kasra on the dhal, while the majority read it with a damma. Khushu' means submissiveness, and it is praiseworthy. It was its being joined with punishment that turned it into dispraise. It was said: (min al-dhull) is related to ﴿they look with a furtive glance﴾ [al-Shura: 45].

Ibn Abbas said: "Humiliated." End of quote.

It was said: it is described as furtive because their glance is weak and their gaze is at its limit. The poet said:

"So lower your gaze, for you are of Numayr."

It was said: they will be raised blind. Since their looking is with the eyes of their hearts, He made it a furtive glance, meaning their looking does not show. This interpretation involves strain.

Al-Suddi and Qatada said: the meaning is that they steal glances because of the grief and bad state they are in; they cannot look with the whole eye, but look with only part of it. On this interpretation, the word tarf (glance) may be a verbal noun, meaning a furtive glance. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿from a furtive glance﴾ [al-Shura: 45] means that their looking begins with a weak, hidden movement of the eyelids, by stealth, just as you see the one who examines a sword looking at it, and so is the glance of one who looks at hateful things: he cannot open his eyelids upon them and fill his eye with them, as he does when looking at those who love one another.

(p-520) [Qur'an 42:32] And among His signs are the ships running in the sea like mountains. [42:33] If He wills, He stills the wind, and they remain motionless on its surface. Indeed, in that are signs for every steadfast, grateful one. [42:34] Or He destroys them for what they have earned, and pardons much. [42:35] And those who dispute concerning Our signs will know that they have no place of escape. [42:36] So whatever you have been given is but the enjoyment of the worldly life; and what is with Allah is better and more lasting for those who believe and rely upon their Lord. [42:37] And those who avoid the major sins and immoralities and, when they are angry, forgive. [42:38] And those who have responded to their Lord, established prayer, whose affair is by consultation among themselves, and who spend from what We have provided them. [42:39] And those who, when oppression afflicts them, defend themselves. [42:40] And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it, but whoever pardons and makes reconciliation, his reward is with Allah. Indeed, He does not love the wrongdoers. [42:41] And whoever defends himself after being wronged, those have no blame upon them. [42:42] The blame is only upon those who wrong people and oppress throughout the earth without right; those will have a painful punishment. [42:43] And whoever is patient and forgives, indeed that is of the matters requiring determination. [42:44] And whom Allah leaves astray, for him there is no protector after Him. And you will see the wrongdoers, when they see the punishment, saying, "Is there any way of return?" [42:45] And you will see them exposed to it, humbled by humiliation, glancing with a furtive look. [al-Shura: 45]

When He mentioned among the proofs of His oneness several kinds, He then mentioned the greater world, which is the heavens and the earth; then the lesser world, which is the animal kingdom. Then, having followed this with the mention of the Return, He followed it with the mention of the ships running in the sea, because in them there is great evidence of power: water is a subtle, transparent body in which a heavy thing sinks, while ships are carried by heavy, dense bodies. Despite this, Allah made for the water a strength by which it bears them and prevents them from sinking. Then He made the winds the cause of their movement; so when He wills that they come to rest, He stills the wind, and they do not move from their place.

*al-Jawari* is the plural of *jariya*, and its original form is *al-sufun al-jawari* (the running ships). The qualified noun was omitted and its adjective took its place. What made this acceptable is His saying *fi al-bahr* (in the sea), which shows that the adjective refers to the ships; otherwise the adjective is not specific, and by analogy (*qiyas*) the qualified noun should not have been omitted and replaced by its adjective. It may be said that it is a predominant adjective (*sifa ghaliba*), like *al-abtah*, so it may stand in place of the governed noun without mention of the qualified noun. *Al-jawari* has also been read with and without the *ya'*, and it has been heard from the Arabs with i'rab (grammatical case-marking, i.e. inflection) on the *ra'*. *Fi al-bahr* is attached to *al-jawari*, and *ka-al-a'lam* is in the position of a circumstantial accusative (*hal*). *Al-a'lam* means mountains, and from this is the saying of al-Khansa', sister of Sakhr and Mu'awiya:

> Indeed, Sakhr, the guided ones take guidance by him,
> as if he were a banner with fire upon its head.

And from it:

> When they crossed a landmark, a landmark appeared.

The majority of the Seven read *al-riha* (the wind) in the singular, while Nafi' read it in the plural. The majority read *fa-yazlalna* with a *fatha* on the *lam*, while Qatada read it with a *kasra*; the analogical form is the *fatha*, because the perfect of this verb has a *kasra* on the 'ayn, so the *kasra* in the imperfect is anomalous (*shadh*). Al-Zamakhshari said: it comes from *zalla yazallu* and *yazillu*, like *dalla yadallu* and *yadillu*. He finished.

This is not as he mentioned, because *yadallu* with a *fatha* on the 'ayn comes from *daliltu* with a *kasra* in the perfect, and *yadillu* with a *kasra* comes from *dalaltu* with a *fatha* in the perfect; both are analogical.

*Li-kulli sabbar* (for every steadfast one) in affliction, *shakur* (grateful) for His blessings.

*Aw yubiqhunna* means He destroys them, i.e. the ships. It is coordinated with *yuskin* (He stills). The pronoun in *kasabu* refers to the passengers of the ships, meaning: because of their sins. Al-A'mash read *wa-ya'fu* with a *waw*, and it is reported from the people of Madina that they read the *waw* with a *fatha*, while the majority read *wa-ya'fu* in the jussive (*majzum*), coordinated with *yubiqhunna*. As for the reading of al-A'mash, it informs that He pardons much, i.e. He does not punish for everything a person has earned. As for the *fatha* reading, it is by implicit *an* after the *waw*, like the *fatha* after the *fa'* in the reading of the one who read *yuhasibkum bihi Allah fa-yaghfiru* (Al-Baqara: 284), and after the *waw* in the verse of the poet:

> If Abu Qabus perishes, there will perish
> the spring of the people and the sacred month.

> And after him we take up the tail of a life,
> its back bare of hump, having no hump.

It is narrated with *wa-na'khudhu* in the *fatha*, the *raf'* (nominative) and the *jazm* (jussive).

In this reading the coordination is with a supposed verbal noun (*masdar mutawahham*), i.e. there occurs a destruction and a pardoning of much. As for the jussive, it falls under the judgment of the apodosis of the condition (*jawab al-shart*), since it is coordinated with it; in meaning it returns to the *fatha* reading, but this is coordination of a verb on a verb, whereas in the *fatha* it is coordination of a supposed verbal noun on a verb.

Al-Qushayri said: it was read *wa-ya'fu* in the jussive, and there is a problem in it, because the meaning is: if He wills, He stills the wind so the ships remain motionless, or He destroys them for the sins of their people. So *wa-ya'fu* cannot be coordinated with these; the meaning would become "if He wills, He pardons," which is not the meaning. Rather, the meaning is an informing about the unseen events under the condition of His will; so it is coordinated with the jussive in wording, not in meaning. And a group read *wa-ya'fu* in the *raf'*, which is good in meaning. He finished. What he said is not good, for he did not grasp the signified meaning of the structure. The meaning is: if He wills, He destroys some people and saves others by way of pardoning them.

Al-Zamakhshari said: (if you ask) on what is *yubiqhunna* coordinated? (I answer): on *yuskin*, because the meaning is: if He wills, He stills the wind so they remain still, or He drives it so they drown by its driving. He finished.

It is not required that the estimate be "or He drives it so they drown," because the destruction of ships is not necessarily by the driving of the wind; He may destroy them by a cause other than the wind, such as the sinking of their deck due to excessive weight, or the breaking of a plank becoming the cause of their destruction, or an enemy attacking their people. Al-A'raj, Abu Ja'far, Shayba, Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Zayd ibn 'Ali read *wa-ya'lama* with the *raf'* (nominative) on the basis of a new sentence (*qat'*). The majority read *wa-ya'lama* with the *nasb* (accusative). Abu 'Ali said: the *nasb* is good when there is a condition and an apodosis before it, and each of them is not obligatory. Al-Zajjaj said: it is by implicit *an*, because before it there is an apodosis. You say: "Whatever you do, I do the like of it, and I honour you," and if you wish: "and I honour you" meaning "and I (am) honouring you," and if you wish: "and honour you" in the jussive.

Al-Zamakhshari said: there is a problem with this, for what Sibawayh set down in his book. He said: know that the *nasb* after the *fa'* and the *waw* in his saying "If you come to me I will come to you and give you" is weak, and it is of the kind of the poet's saying:

> And I join [the road to] the Hijaz, so that I may rest.

This is not permissible; it is neither the limit of speech nor its way, except that in the apodosis it has become somewhat stronger, because it is not obligatory that he will do it unless there is an action from the first part. When it resembles what is not obligatory, like the interrogative and the like, they allowed it in this case despite its weakness. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is not permissible to bear the widely transmitted reading on a weak form that is neither the limit of speech nor its way; and if it were of this type, Sibawayh would not have left it out of his book, and he mentioned its parallels from the ambiguous verses. He finished.

Al-Zamakhshari interpreted the *nasb* as coordinated with an omitted causal clause. He said: its estimate is: "in order that He may take vengeance upon them and that He may know those who dispute." This is disliked in coordination with an omitted causal clause, and it is not rare in the Qur'an, such as His saying: "And that We may make you a sign for the people" (Al-Baqara: 259), and His saying: "Allah created the heavens and the earth in truth" (Al-'Ankabut: 44), and "that every soul may be recompensed for what it earned" (Al-Jathiya: 22). He finished.

But his estimate "to take vengeance upon them" is distant, because the destruction of a people is what is consequent upon the condition, so "that He may take vengeance upon them" is not appropriate. As for the two verses, the *lam* can be connected to an omitted verb, meaning: "And that We may make him a sign for the people" (Maryam: 21), "and that every soul may be recompensed for what it earned" (Al-Jathiya: 22); We did that. It is often estimated that this verb is omitted before the *lam* of cause when there is no apparent verb to be connected to.

Al-Zamakhshari mentioned that His saying "wa-ya'lama" was read with the *jazm*. (If you ask): how is the meaning correct on the jussive of "wa-ya'lama"? (I answer): as if He said: "or if He wills, He gathers three matters: the destruction of a people, the salvation of a people, and the warning of others," because His saying "and those who dispute concerning Our signs will know" includes warning them of Allah's punishment; and "they have no place of escape" is in the position of the accusative, because "ya'lamu" is suspended (*mu'allaqa*), like your saying: "I knew what Zayd is standing." Ibn 'Atiyya said, regarding the *nasb* reading: this *waw* and others like it, which the Kufans call *waw al-sarf* (the "diverting" *waw*), since the real sense of *waw al-sarf* as they intend it is the coordination of a verb on a supposed noun; so *an* is supposed to be with the verb with the sense of a verbal noun, so its coordination on the noun is good. He finished.

This is not his statement as an explanation of their saying "*waw al-sarf*"; it is rather an exposition of the position of the Basrans. As for the Kufans, *waw al-sarf* is itself an operator in the accusative, not by the implicit *an* after it.

Abu 'Ubayd said: "on the *sarf*" like the one in Al 'Imran: "And that Allah may know those of you who strove and may know the steadfast" (Al 'Imran: 142). The meaning of *sarf* is that it was in one direction and then turned to another, so the case-marking changed because of the turning. Coordination does not necessarily determine simultaneity in existence, as in coordination in nouns, like: "Zayd came and 'Amr." If "'Amr" were in the accusative it would require simultaneity; and likewise *waw al-sarf*, to express the sense of simultaneity and specify the meaning of togetherness. For this reason there is consensus on the accusative in His saying "and may know the steadfast" (Al 'Imran: 142), meaning: "and may know the strivers and the steadfast together."

On the authority of 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him): Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) acquired property, and he gave all of it in charity in the way of Allah and for good. The Muslims blamed him, and the disbelievers considered him in error; so there was revealed: "And whatever you have been given of a thing..." The apparent sense is that it is addressed to people.

It was said: it is addressed to the polytheists. *Ma* here is conditional; it is the second object of *utitum* (you were given), and *min shay'* (of a thing) is an explanation of *ma*. The meaning: of a thing of the finery and wealth of the world and the abundance in it. The *fa'* is the apodosis of the condition, meaning: then it is enjoyment, i.e. it is enjoyed in the life.

*Wa-ma 'inda Allah* means what is with Allah, i.e. of His reward and what He prepared for His friends, "is better and more lasting" than what you were given, because it has no cessation.

The discussion of the major sins (*al-kaba'ir*) occurred before in His saying: "If you avoid the major sins of what you are forbidden" (Al-Nisa': 31), in the chapter of Women. The majority read *kaba'ir* in the plural here and in al-Najm, while Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it in the singular.

*Wa-alladhina yajtanibuna* (and those who avoid) is coordinated on *alladhina amanu* (those who believed), and likewise what follows. Abu al-Baqa' fell into an error in recitation: he believed that it is *alladhina yajtanibuna* without a *waw*, so he built the i'rab on that and said: *alladhina yajtanibuna* (An-Najm: 32) is in the position of the genitive as a substitute (*badal*) for *alladhina amanu*, and it may be in the accusative position by an implicit verb, namely "I mean," and in the nominative position with the estimate "they are." He finished.

The governing element of *idha* (when) is *yaghfiruna* (they forgive), and it is a clause of subject and predicate coordinated on *yajtanibuna*. It is permissible that *hum* be an emphasis for the subject in *ghadibu* (they became angry).

Abu al-Baqa' said: *hum* is a subject, *yaghfiruna* is the predicate, and the clause is the apodosis of *idha*. He finished. This is not permissible, because if the clause were the apodosis of *idha* it would have to have the *fa'*; you say: "When Zayd comes, then 'Amr is departing," and it is not permissible to drop the *fa'* except if it occurs in poetry.

It was said: *hum* is in the nominative by an omitted verb which *yaghfiruna* explains; and when the verb was omitted, the pronoun was separated. This statement needs consideration, namely that the apodosis of *idha* is explained as the verb of the condition after it is explained, as in "When the heaven splits asunder" (Al-Inshiqaq: 1). And it is not far that this is permissible according to Sibawayh's view, since it occurs with the jussive conditional particle, like: "If Zayd departs, he departs," where Zayd is by Sibawayh the subject of an omitted verb explained by the apodosis, meaning: "Zayd departs." Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' prevented this.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "*hum yaghfiruna*" means: they are the ones specially for forgiveness, in the state of anger; anger does not confuse their forbearance, as it confuses people's intellects. The coming of them and its occurrence is a subject, and the attribution of "*yaghfiruna*" to it is for this benefit. He finished. In this there is an exhortation to restrain anger.

And in the hadith: "Advise me." He said: "Do not become angry." He said: "Advise me further." He said: "Do not become angry." He said: "Advise me further." He said: "Do not become angry."

﴿And those who respond to their Lord﴾. It was said: it was revealed concerning the Ansar. Allah called them to faith in Him and obedience to Him, and they responded. Before Islam, and before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to Medina, whenever a matter befell them they would consult one another, so Allah praised them for this. They would not act alone in a matter until they agreed upon it.

From al-Hasan: "No people consulted together except that they were guided to the most right course of their affair." End of quote.

Consultation (shura) brings about unity of word, mutual affection, and cooperation in good. The Messenger (ﷺ), peace be upon him, consulted in matters concerning the interests of war, and the Companions after him did likewise, such as Umar's consultation with al-Hurmuz. And in legal rulings, such as fighting the people of apostasy (ridda), the inheritance of a harbi (non-Muslim combatant), the number of lashes for drinkers of wine, and other matters.

Shura is a verbal noun like futya, meaning consultation, with an omitted modifier, i.e. "and their affair is by consultation among them." The phrase ﴿they defend themselves﴾ (hum yantasiruna) is a relative clause for alladhina (those who). Idha (when) is governed by yantasiruna. It is not permissible for ﴿they defend themselves﴾ to be the response (jawab) of idha, because the conditional clause and its response would then be a relative clause, given what we mentioned about the requirement of the fa' (the particle "then"). Here it is permissible for hum to be the subject of an omitted verb, according to the opinion stated concerning ﴿they forgive﴾ (hum yaghfiruna). Al-Hawfi said: "If you wish, you may make hum a corroborative of the ha' and mim, meaning in (asabahum), which is a nominative pronoun." There is scrutiny in this, since it involves separating the corroborated from the corroborator by a verb, which is apparently not prohibited. Intisar (defending oneself) means confining oneself to what Allah has set as its limit and not transgressing.

Al-Nakha'i said: "They used to dislike humiliating themselves, lest the wicked become emboldened against them. Whoever defends himself without transgressing is obedient and praiseworthy." Muqatil and Hisham, from Urwa, said: the verse refers to the one wronged who takes his right from the wrongdoer through retaliation (qisas). Ibn Abbas said: the polytheists transgressed against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his Companions and expelled them from Mecca, so Allah permitted them to go out into the earth, and He gave them victory over those who oppressed them.

Al-Kiya al-Tabari said: the apparent meaning is that defending oneself in this context is better. Do you not see that He linked it to responding to Allah and His Messenger and establishing the prayer? This accords with what al-Nakha'i mentioned. This applies to one who transgresses and persists, whereas the command to pardon applies when the offender is remorseful and has given up (his wrongdoing). He stated, after this verse, ﴿And whoever defends himself after being wronged﴾, the verse, which implies permission for defending oneself. He followed it with His saying: ﴿And whoever is patient and forgives﴾, and this is to be understood, according to the Qur'an, as applying to one who is not persistent. As for the one who persists in transgression, defending oneself against him is better, by the evidence of the verse before it. Ibn Bahr said: the meaning is that they support one another against him, removing him from them.

Abu Bakr ibn al-Arabi said something similar to what al-Kiya said.

The majority said: if a believer transgresses against a believer, it is not permissible for the latter to take redress by himself, but rather he refers the matter to the imam (ruler) or his deputy. A group said: he may do so.

﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾: this is an explanation of defending oneself, meaning one must not exceed the limit in what he repays the one who transgressed against him.

Ibn Abi Najih and al-Suddi said: if he is insulted, he may return the like of what he was insulted with, without exceeding. Retaliation was called an "evil" by way of correspondence, or because it grieves the one against whom it is applied, just as menstruation (al-hayd) is called a harm. The apparent meaning of His saying "like it" is equivalence absolutely in all circumstances, not in what the evidence has specified. The jurists introduced specification in many cases on the basis of analogy (qiyas).

Mujahid and al-Suddi said: if he says to him, "May Allah disgrace you," he may say, "May Allah disgrace you." And if he slanders him in a way that requires the prescribed punishment (hadd), then the hadd is what Allah has commanded.

﴿Whoever pardons and makes reconciliation﴾, meaning between himself and his adversary through pardon, ﴿his reward is with Allah﴾: a vague promise whose greatness cannot be measured, since it is with Allah.

﴿Indeed, He does not love the wrongdoers﴾, meaning the treacherous. If He does not love such a person, while he has been urged to pardon him, then the pardon that Allah loves is more worthy of being pardoned. Or, He does not love the wrongdoers, meaning those who go beyond the limit and transgress against those who were wronged when they defend themselves, especially in the state of war and the heat of zeal, for he may then do wrong without realizing it.

In the hadith: "When the Day of Resurrection comes, a caller will call out: whoever has a reward with Allah, let him stand. He said: So a multitude will stand, and it will be said to them: What is your reward with Allah? They will say: We pardoned those who wronged us. It will be said to them: Enter Paradise by the permission of Allah."

The lam in ﴿And whoever defends himself﴾ is a lam of emphasis. Al-Hawfi said: in it is the meaning of an oath. Ibn Atiyya said: it is the lam of the meeting of an oath (lam al-taqaqi al-qasam), meaning that it is the lam with which an oath is introduced, so the oath is omitted before it. Man is conditional. ﴿Defends himself after his being wronged﴾ is construed according to the wording of man, and ﴿then those﴾ is construed according to the meaning of man. The fa' is the response of the condition. Zulmihi (his being wronged) is a verbal noun annexed to its object.

Al-Zamakhshari said: the reading of one who reads "after he was wronged" (ba'da ma zulima) explains it.

﴿There is no way against them﴾: it was said, meaning no path to blame; and it was said: no path against the one who punishes, nor against the one who reproaches or is reproached. This is an exaggeration in permitting defending oneself.

﴿The way is only﴾, meaning the way of sin and blame, ﴿against those who wrong﴾, meaning those who debase themselves through wrongdoing, ﴿and who transgress in the earth﴾, meaning they act arrogantly in it, rise above others, and cause corruption. It was said: (and who wrong people), meaning they put things in other than their proper places through killing, seizing property, and harm with hand and tongue.

Transgression (baghy) is without right, and it is a kind of wrongdoing. He singled it out for mention to draw attention to its severity and the bad state of its perpetrator. End of quote.

﴿And whoever is patient﴾, meaning in the face of wrongdoing and harm, (and forgives), and does not defend himself. The lam in (wa-man) may be the introductory lam (al-lam al-muwatti'a) for the omitted oath, with man as conditional, and the response of the oath is His saying (inna dhalika, "indeed that"), and the response of the condition is omitted because the response of the oath indicates it.

It is also permissible that the lam be the lam of the inception (lam al-ibtida'), and man a relative pronoun serving as subject, with the clause emphasized by inna in the position of the predicate.

Al-Hawfi said: man is in the nominative by inception, and the predicate is omitted, and the response of the condition is inna and what is connected to it, with the fa' omitted, as the poet said:

"Whoever does good deeds, Allah will reward them."

meaning: then Allah will reward them. End of quote. This is not sound, because omitting the fa' is specific to poetry according to Sibawayh. The demonstrative dhalika refers to what is understood from the verbal noun of sabara and ghafara, and the returning pronoun in the predicate linked to the subject is omitted, meaning: indeed that is from him, by the meaning's indication: ﴿truly, it is among the steadfast resolves of affairs﴾. If dhalika refers to the verbal noun understood from His saying ﴿and whoever is patient and forgives﴾, then there is no omission in ﴿steadfast resolves of affairs﴾. If dhalika refers to the subject, then it is the linking element, and it needs no estimation from it, and ﴿steadfast resolves of affairs﴾ would mean: indeed he is among those possessing steadfast resolves of affairs.

[p. 524] A man insulted another man in the assembly of al-Hasan. The one insulted kept silent, perspiring and wiping the sweat. Then he stood up and recited the verse. Al-Hasan said: "By Allah, he understood it and grasped it. Why do the ignorant neglect it?"

The clause ﴿the way is only﴾ is a parenthetical insertion between His saying ﴿and whoever defends himself﴾ and His saying ﴿and whoever is patient﴾.

﴿And whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no protector after Him﴾, meaning no helper who would take charge of him, (after Him), meaning after his being led astray. This is a belittling of the state of the disbelievers.

﴿And you see the wrongdoers﴾: the address is to the Messenger, and the meaning is: you see their condition and the bewilderment they are in, ﴿when they see the punishment﴾, they say: ﴿Is there any way to return?﴾, meaning: is there a path to return to the world? That is because of the horrible things they have witnessed and the evil that befalls them.

﴿And you see them presented before it﴾ [al-Shura: 45], meaning before the Fire; the mention of the punishment indicates it. (Humbled), meaning shrinking and abased because of what overtakes them, (from humiliation).

Talha read (min al-dhilli) with a kasra on the dhal, while the majority read it with a damma. Khushu' means submissiveness, and it is praiseworthy. It was its being joined with punishment that turned it into dispraise. It was said: (min al-dhull) is related to ﴿they look with a furtive glance﴾ [al-Shura: 45].

Ibn Abbas said: "Humiliated." End of quote.

It was said: it is described as furtive because their glance is weak and their gaze is at its limit. The poet said:

"So lower your gaze, for you are of Numayr."

It was said: they will be raised blind. Since their looking is with the eyes of their hearts, He made it a furtive glance, meaning their looking does not show. This interpretation involves strain.

Al-Suddi and Qatada said: the meaning is that they steal glances because of the grief and bad state they are in; they cannot look with the whole eye, but look with only part of it. On this interpretation, the word tarf (glance) may be a verbal noun, meaning a furtive glance. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿from a furtive glance﴾ [al-Shura: 45] means that their looking begins with a weak, hidden movement of the eyelids, by stealth, just as you see the one who examines a sword looking at it, and so is the glance of one who looks at hateful things: he cannot open his eyelids upon them and fill his eye with them, as he does when looking at those who love one another.

(p-520) [Qur'an 42:32] And among His signs are the ships running in the sea like mountains. [42:33] If He wills, He stills the wind, and they remain motionless on its surface. Indeed, in that are signs for every steadfast, grateful one. [42:34] Or He destroys them for what they have earned, and pardons much. [42:35] And those who dispute concerning Our signs will know that they have no place of escape. [42:36] So whatever you have been given is but the enjoyment of the worldly life; and what is with Allah is better and more lasting for those who believe and rely upon their Lord. [42:37] And those who avoid the major sins and immoralities and, when they are angry, forgive. [42:38] And those who have responded to their Lord, established prayer, whose affair is by consultation among themselves, and who spend from what We have provided them. [42:39] And those who, when oppression afflicts them, defend themselves. [42:40] And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it, but whoever pardons and makes reconciliation, his reward is with Allah. Indeed, He does not love the wrongdoers. [42:41] And whoever defends himself after being wronged, those have no blame upon them. [42:42] The blame is only upon those who wrong people and oppress throughout the earth without right; those will have a painful punishment. [42:43] And whoever is patient and forgives, indeed that is of the matters requiring determination. [42:44] And whom Allah leaves astray, for him there is no protector after Him. And you will see the wrongdoers, when they see the punishment, saying, "Is there any way of return?" [42:45] And you will see them exposed to it, humbled by humiliation, glancing with a furtive look. [al-Shura: 45]

When He mentioned among the proofs of His oneness several kinds, He then mentioned the greater world, which is the heavens and the earth; then the lesser world, which is the animal kingdom. Then, having followed this with the mention of the Return, He followed it with the mention of the ships running in the sea, because in them there is great evidence of power: water is a subtle, transparent body in which a heavy thing sinks, while ships are carried by heavy, dense bodies. Despite this, Allah made for the water a strength by which it bears them and prevents them from sinking. Then He made the winds the cause of their movement; so when He wills that they come to rest, He stills the wind, and they do not move from their place.

*al-Jawari* is the plural of *jariya*, and its original form is *al-sufun al-jawari* (the running ships). The qualified noun was omitted and its adjective took its place. What made this acceptable is His saying *fi al-bahr* (in the sea), which shows that the adjective refers to the ships; otherwise the adjective is not specific, and by analogy (*qiyas*) the qualified noun should not have been omitted and replaced by its adjective. It may be said that it is a predominant adjective (*sifa ghaliba*), like *al-abtah*, so it may stand in place of the governed noun without mention of the qualified noun. *Al-jawari* has also been read with and without the *ya'*, and it has been heard from the Arabs with i'rab (grammatical case-marking, i.e. inflection) on the *ra'*. *Fi al-bahr* is attached to *al-jawari*, and *ka-al-a'lam* is in the position of a circumstantial accusative (*hal*). *Al-a'lam* means mountains, and from this is the saying of al-Khansa', sister of Sakhr and Mu'awiya:

> Indeed, Sakhr, the guided ones take guidance by him,
> as if he were a banner with fire upon its head.

And from it:

> When they crossed a landmark, a landmark appeared.

The majority of the Seven read *al-riha* (the wind) in the singular, while Nafi' read it in the plural. The majority read *fa-yazlalna* with a *fatha* on the *lam*, while Qatada read it with a *kasra*; the analogical form is the *fatha*, because the perfect of this verb has a *kasra* on the 'ayn, so the *kasra* in the imperfect is anomalous (*shadh*). Al-Zamakhshari said: it comes from *zalla yazallu* and *yazillu*, like *dalla yadallu* and *yadillu*. He finished.

This is not as he mentioned, because *yadallu* with a *fatha* on the 'ayn comes from *daliltu* with a *kasra* in the perfect, and *yadillu* with a *kasra* comes from *dalaltu* with a *fatha* in the perfect; both are analogical.

*Li-kulli sabbar* (for every steadfast one) in affliction, *shakur* (grateful) for His blessings.

*Aw yubiqhunna* means He destroys them, i.e. the ships. It is coordinated with *yuskin* (He stills). The pronoun in *kasabu* refers to the passengers of the ships, meaning: because of their sins.
