Al-A'mash read *wa-ya'fu* with a *waw*, and it is reported from the people of Madina that they read the *waw* with a *fatha*, while the majority read *wa-ya'fu* in the jussive (*majzum*), coordinated with *yubiqhunna*. As for the reading of al-A'mash, it informs that He pardons much, i.e. He does not punish for everything a person has earned. As for the *fatha* reading, it is by implicit *an* after the *waw*, like the *fatha* after the *fa'* in the reading of the one who read *yuhasibkum bihi Allah fa-yaghfiru* (Al-Baqara: 284), and after the *waw* in the verse of the poet:

> If Abu Qabus perishes, there will perish
> the spring of the people and the sacred month.

> And after him we take up the tail of a life,
> its back bare of hump, having no hump.

It is narrated with *wa-na'khudhu* in the *fatha*, the *raf'* (nominative) and the *jazm* (jussive).

In this reading the coordination is with a supposed verbal noun (*masdar mutawahham*), i.e. there occurs a destruction and a pardoning of much. As for the jussive, it falls under the judgment of the apodosis of the condition (*jawab al-shart*), since it is coordinated with it; in meaning it returns to the *fatha* reading, but this is coordination of a verb on a verb, whereas in the *fatha* it is coordination of a supposed verbal noun on a verb.

Al-Qushayri said: it was read *wa-ya'fu* in the jussive, and there is a problem in it, because the meaning is: if He wills, He stills the wind so the ships remain motionless, or He destroys them for the sins of their people. So *wa-ya'fu* cannot be coordinated with these; the meaning would become "if He wills, He pardons," which is not the meaning. Rather, the meaning is an informing about the unseen events under the condition of His will; so it is coordinated with the jussive in wording, not in meaning. And a group read *wa-ya'fu* in the *raf'*, which is good in meaning. He finished. What he said is not good, for he did not grasp the signified meaning of the structure. The meaning is: if He wills, He destroys some people and saves others by way of pardoning them.

Al-Zamakhshari said: (if you ask) on what is *yubiqhunna* coordinated? (I answer): on *yuskin*, because the meaning is: if He wills, He stills the wind so they remain still, or He drives it so they drown by its driving. He finished.

It is not required that the estimate be "or He drives it so they drown," because the destruction of ships is not necessarily by the driving of the wind; He may destroy them by a cause other than the wind, such as the sinking of their deck due to excessive weight, or the breaking of a plank becoming the cause of their destruction, or an enemy attacking their people. Al-A'raj, Abu Ja'far, Shayba, Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Zayd ibn 'Ali read *wa-ya'lama* with the *raf'* (nominative) on the basis of a new sentence (*qat'*). The majority read *wa-ya'lama* with the *nasb* (accusative). Abu 'Ali said: the *nasb* is good when there is a condition and an apodosis before it, and each of them is not obligatory. Al-Zajjaj said: it is by implicit *an*, because before it there is an apodosis. You say: "Whatever you do, I do the like of it, and I honour you," and if you wish: "and I honour you" meaning "and I (am) honouring you," and if you wish: "and honour you" in the jussive.

Al-Zamakhshari said: there is a problem with this, for what Sibawayh set down in his book. He said: know that the *nasb* after the *fa'* and the *waw* in his saying "If you come to me I will come to you and give you" is weak, and it is of the kind of the poet's saying:

> And I join [the road to] the Hijaz, so that I may rest.

This is not permissible; it is neither the limit of speech nor its way, except that in the apodosis it has become somewhat stronger, because it is not obligatory that he will do it unless there is an action from the first part. When it resembles what is not obligatory, like the interrogative and the like, they allowed it in this case despite its weakness. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is not permissible to bear the widely transmitted reading on a weak form that is neither the limit of speech nor its way; and if it were of this type, Sibawayh would not have left it out of his book, and he mentioned its parallels from the ambiguous verses. He finished.

Al-Zamakhshari interpreted the *nasb* as coordinated with an omitted causal clause. He said: its estimate is: "in order that He may take vengeance upon them and that He may know those who dispute." This is disliked in coordination with an omitted causal clause, and it is not rare in the Qur'an, such as His saying: "And that We may make you a sign for the people" (Al-Baqara: 259), and His saying: "Allah created the heavens and the earth in truth" (Al-'Ankabut: 44), and "that every soul may be recompensed for what it earned" (Al-Jathiya: 22). He finished.

But his estimate "to take vengeance upon them" is distant, because the destruction of a people is what is consequent upon the condition, so "that He may take vengeance upon them" is not appropriate. As for the two verses, the *lam* can be connected to an omitted verb, meaning: "And that We may make him a sign for the people" (Maryam: 21), "and that every soul may be recompensed for what it earned" (Al-Jathiya: 22); We did that. It is often estimated that this verb is omitted before the *lam* of cause when there is no apparent verb to be connected to.

Al-Zamakhshari mentioned that His saying "wa-ya'lama" was read with the *jazm*. (If you ask): how is the meaning correct on the jussive of "wa-ya'lama"? (I answer): as if He said: "or if He wills, He gathers three matters: the destruction of a people, the salvation of a people, and the warning of others," because His saying "and those who dispute concerning Our signs will know" includes warning them of Allah's punishment; and "they have no place of escape" is in the position of the accusative, because "ya'lamu" is suspended (*mu'allaqa*), like your saying: "I knew what Zayd is standing." Ibn 'Atiyya said, regarding the *nasb* reading: this *waw* and others like it, which the Kufans call *waw al-sarf* (the "diverting" *waw*), since the real sense of *waw al-sarf* as they intend it is the coordination of a verb on a supposed noun; so *an* is supposed to be with the verb with the sense of a verbal noun, so its coordination on the noun is good. He finished.

This is not his statement as an explanation of their saying "*waw al-sarf*"; it is rather an exposition of the position of the Basrans. As for the Kufans, *waw al-sarf* is itself an operator in the accusative, not by the implicit *an* after it.

Abu 'Ubayd said: "on the *sarf*" like the one in Al 'Imran: "And that Allah may know those of you who strove and may know the steadfast" (Al 'Imran: 142). The meaning of *sarf* is that it was in one direction and then turned to another, so the case-marking changed because of the turning. Coordination does not necessarily determine simultaneity in existence, as in coordination in nouns, like: "Zayd came and 'Amr." If "'Amr" were in the accusative it would require simultaneity; and likewise *waw al-sarf*, to express the sense of simultaneity and specify the meaning of togetherness. For this reason there is consensus on the accusative in His saying "and may know the steadfast" (Al 'Imran: 142), meaning: "and may know the strivers and the steadfast together."

On the authority of 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him): Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) acquired property, and he gave all of it in charity in the way of Allah and for good. The Muslims blamed him, and the disbelievers considered him in error; so there was revealed: "And whatever you have been given of a thing..." The apparent sense is that it is addressed to people.

It was said: it is addressed to the polytheists. *Ma* here is conditional; it is the second object of *utitum* (you were given), and *min shay'* (of a thing) is an explanation of *ma*. The meaning: of a thing of the finery and wealth of the world and the abundance in it. The *fa'* is the apodosis of the condition, meaning: then it is enjoyment, i.e. it is enjoyed in the life.

*Wa-ma 'inda Allah* means what is with Allah, i.e. of His reward and what He prepared for His friends, "is better and more lasting" than what you were given, because it has no cessation.

The discussion of the major sins (*al-kaba'ir*) occurred before in His saying: "If you avoid the major sins of what you are forbidden" (Al-Nisa': 31), in the chapter of Women. The majority read *kaba'ir* in the plural here and in al-Najm, while Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it in the singular.

*Wa-alladhina yajtanibuna* (and those who avoid) is coordinated on *alladhina amanu* (those who believed), and likewise what follows. Abu al-Baqa' fell into an error in recitation: he believed that it is *alladhina yajtanibuna* without a *waw*, so he built the i'rab on that and said: *alladhina yajtanibuna* (An-Najm: 32) is in the position of the genitive as a substitute (*badal*) for *alladhina amanu*, and it may be in the accusative position by an implicit verb, namely "I mean," and in the nominative position with the estimate "they are." He finished.

The governing element of *idha* (when) is *yaghfiruna* (they forgive), and it is a clause of subject and predicate coordinated on *yajtanibuna*. It is permissible that *hum* be an emphasis for the subject in *ghadibu* (they became angry).

Abu al-Baqa' said: *hum* is a subject, *yaghfiruna* is the predicate, and the clause is the apodosis of *idha*. He finished. This is not permissible, because if the clause were the apodosis of *idha* it would have to have the *fa'*; you say: "When Zayd comes, then 'Amr is departing," and it is not permissible to drop the *fa'* except if it occurs in poetry.

It was said: *hum* is in the nominative by an omitted verb which *yaghfiruna* explains; and when the verb was omitted, the pronoun was separated. This statement needs consideration, namely that the apodosis of *idha* is explained as the verb of the condition after it is explained, as in "When the heaven splits asunder" (Al-Inshiqaq: 1). And it is not far that this is permissible according to Sibawayh's view, since it occurs with the jussive conditional particle, like: "If Zayd departs, he departs," where Zayd is by Sibawayh the subject of an omitted verb explained by the apodosis, meaning: "Zayd departs." Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' prevented this.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "*hum yaghfiruna*" means: they are the ones specially for forgiveness, in the state of anger; anger does not confuse their forbearance, as it confuses people's intellects. The coming of them and its occurrence is a subject, and the attribution of "*yaghfiruna*" to it is for this benefit. He finished. In this there is an exhortation to restrain anger.

And in the hadith: "Advise me." He said: "Do not become angry." He said: "Advise me further." He said: "Do not become angry." He said: "Advise me further." He said: "Do not become angry."

﴿And those who respond to their Lord﴾. It was said: it was revealed concerning the Ansar. Allah called them to faith in Him and obedience to Him, and they responded. Before Islam, and before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to Medina, whenever a matter befell them they would consult one another, so Allah praised them for this. They would not act alone in a matter until they agreed upon it.

From al-Hasan: "No people consulted together except that they were guided to the most right course of their affair." End of quote.

Consultation (shura) brings about unity of word, mutual affection, and cooperation in good. The Messenger (ﷺ), peace be upon him, consulted in matters concerning the interests of war, and the Companions after him did likewise, such as Umar's consultation with al-Hurmuz. And in legal rulings, such as fighting the people of apostasy (ridda), the inheritance of a harbi (non-Muslim combatant), the number of lashes for drinkers of wine, and other matters.

Shura is a verbal noun like futya, meaning consultation, with an omitted modifier, i.e. "and their affair is by consultation among them." The phrase ﴿they defend themselves﴾ (hum yantasiruna) is a relative clause for alladhina (those who). Idha (when) is governed by yantasiruna. It is not permissible for ﴿they defend themselves﴾ to be the response (jawab) of idha, because the conditional clause and its response would then be a relative clause, given what we mentioned about the requirement of the fa' (the particle "then"). Here it is permissible for hum to be the subject of an omitted verb, according to the opinion stated concerning ﴿they forgive﴾ (hum yaghfiruna). Al-Hawfi said: "If you wish, you may make hum a corroborative of the ha' and mim, meaning in (asabahum), which is a nominative pronoun." There is scrutiny in this, since it involves separating the corroborated from the corroborator by a verb, which is apparently not prohibited. Intisar (defending oneself) means confining oneself to what Allah has set as its limit and not transgressing.

Al-Nakha'i said: "They used to dislike humiliating themselves, lest the wicked become emboldened against them. Whoever defends himself without transgressing is obedient and praiseworthy." Muqatil and Hisham, from Urwa, said: the verse refers to the one wronged who takes his right from the wrongdoer through retaliation (qisas). Ibn Abbas said: the polytheists transgressed against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his Companions and expelled them from Mecca, so Allah permitted them to go out into the earth, and He gave them victory over those who oppressed them.

Al-Kiya al-Tabari said: the apparent meaning is that defending oneself in this context is better. Do you not see that He linked it to responding to Allah and His Messenger and establishing the prayer? This accords with what al-Nakha'i mentioned. This applies to one who transgresses and persists, whereas the command to pardon applies when the offender is remorseful and has given up (his wrongdoing). He stated, after this verse, ﴿And whoever defends himself after being wronged﴾, the verse, which implies permission for defending oneself. He followed it with His saying: ﴿And whoever is patient and forgives﴾, and this is to be understood, according to the Qur'an, as applying to one who is not persistent. As for the one who persists in transgression, defending oneself against him is better, by the evidence of the verse before it. Ibn Bahr said: the meaning is that they support one another against him, removing him from them.

Abu Bakr ibn al-Arabi said something similar to what al-Kiya said.

The majority said: if a believer transgresses against a believer, it is not permissible for the latter to take redress by himself, but rather he refers the matter to the imam (ruler) or his deputy. A group said: he may do so.

﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾: this is an explanation of defending oneself, meaning one must not exceed the limit in what he repays the one who transgressed against him.

Ibn Abi Najih and al-Suddi said: if he is insulted, he may return the like of what he was insulted with, without exceeding. Retaliation was called an "evil" by way of correspondence, or because it grieves the one against whom it is applied, just as menstruation (al-hayd) is called a harm. The apparent meaning of His saying "like it" is equivalence absolutely in all circumstances, not in what the evidence has specified. The jurists introduced specification in many cases on the basis of analogy (qiyas).

Mujahid and al-Suddi said: if he says to him, "May Allah disgrace you," he may say, "May Allah disgrace you." And if he slanders him in a way that requires the prescribed punishment (hadd), then the hadd is what Allah has commanded.

﴿Whoever pardons and makes reconciliation﴾, meaning between himself and his adversary through pardon, ﴿his reward is with Allah﴾: a vague promise whose greatness cannot be measured, since it is with Allah.

﴿Indeed, He does not love the wrongdoers﴾, meaning the treacherous. If He does not love such a person, while he has been urged to pardon him, then the pardon that Allah loves is more worthy of being pardoned. Or, He does not love the wrongdoers, meaning those who go beyond the limit and transgress against those who were wronged when they defend themselves, especially in the state of war and the heat of zeal, for he may then do wrong without realizing it.

In the hadith: "When the Day of Resurrection comes, a caller will call out: whoever has a reward with Allah, let him stand. He said: So a multitude will stand, and it will be said to them: What is your reward with Allah? They will say: We pardoned those who wronged us. It will be said to them: Enter Paradise by the permission of Allah."

The lam in ﴿And whoever defends himself﴾ is a lam of emphasis. Al-Hawfi said: in it is the meaning of an oath. Ibn Atiyya said: it is the lam of the meeting of an oath (lam al-taqaqi al-qasam), meaning that it is the lam with which an oath is introduced, so the oath is omitted before it. Man is conditional. ﴿Defends himself after his being wronged﴾ is construed according to the wording of man, and ﴿then those﴾ is construed according to the meaning of man. The fa' is the response of the condition. Zulmihi (his being wronged) is a verbal noun annexed to its object.

Al-Zamakhshari said: the reading of one who reads "after he was wronged" (ba'da ma zulima) explains it.

﴿There is no way against them﴾: it was said, meaning no path to blame; and it was said: no path against the one who punishes, nor against the one who reproaches or is reproached. This is an exaggeration in permitting defending oneself.

﴿The way is only﴾, meaning the way of sin and blame, ﴿against those who wrong﴾, meaning those who debase themselves through wrongdoing, ﴿and who transgress in the earth﴾, meaning they act arrogantly in it, rise above others, and cause corruption. It was said: (and who wrong people), meaning they put things in other than their proper places through killing, seizing property, and harm with hand and tongue.

Transgression (baghy) is without right, and it is a kind of wrongdoing. He singled it out for mention to draw attention to its severity and the bad state of its perpetrator. End of quote.

﴿And whoever is patient﴾, meaning in the face of wrongdoing and harm, (and forgives), and does not defend himself. The lam in (wa-man) may be the introductory lam (al-lam al-muwatti'a) for the omitted oath, with man as conditional, and the response of the oath is His saying (inna dhalika, "indeed that"), and the response of the condition is omitted because the response of the oath indicates it.

It is also permissible that the lam be the lam of the inception (lam al-ibtida'), and man a relative pronoun serving as subject, with the clause emphasized by inna in the position of the predicate.

Al-Hawfi said: man is in the nominative by inception, and the predicate is omitted, and the response of the condition is inna and what is connected to it, with the fa' omitted, as the poet said:

"Whoever does good deeds, Allah will reward them."

meaning: then Allah will reward them. End of quote. This is not sound, because omitting the fa' is specific to poetry according to Sibawayh. The demonstrative dhalika refers to what is understood from the verbal noun of sabara and ghafara, and the returning pronoun in the predicate linked to the subject is omitted, meaning: indeed that is from him, by the meaning's indication: ﴿truly, it is among the steadfast resolves of affairs﴾. If dhalika refers to the verbal noun understood from His saying ﴿and whoever is patient and forgives﴾, then there is no omission in ﴿steadfast resolves of affairs﴾. If dhalika refers to the subject, then it is the linking element, and it needs no estimation from it, and ﴿steadfast resolves of affairs﴾ would mean: indeed he is among those possessing steadfast resolves of affairs.

[p. 524] A man insulted another man in the assembly of al-Hasan. The one insulted kept silent, perspiring and wiping the sweat. Then he stood up and recited the verse. Al-Hasan said: "By Allah, he understood it and grasped it. Why do the ignorant neglect it?"

The clause ﴿the way is only﴾ is a parenthetical insertion between His saying ﴿and whoever defends himself﴾ and His saying ﴿and whoever is patient﴾.

﴿And whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no protector after Him﴾, meaning no helper who would take charge of him, (after Him), meaning after his being led astray. This is a belittling of the state of the disbelievers.

﴿And you see the wrongdoers﴾: the address is to the Messenger, and the meaning is: you see their condition and the bewilderment they are in, ﴿when they see the punishment﴾, they say: ﴿Is there any way to return?﴾, meaning: is there a path to return to the world? That is because of the horrible things they have witnessed and the evil that befalls them.

﴿And you see them presented before it﴾ [al-Shura: 45], meaning before the Fire; the mention of the punishment indicates it. (Humbled), meaning shrinking and abased because of what overtakes them, (from humiliation).

Talha read (min al-dhilli) with a kasra on the dhal, while the majority read it with a damma. Khushu' means submissiveness, and it is praiseworthy. It was its being joined with punishment that turned it into dispraise. It was said: (min al-dhull) is related to ﴿they look with a furtive glance﴾ [al-Shura: 45].

Ibn Abbas said: "Humiliated." End of quote.

It was said: it is described as furtive because their glance is weak and their gaze is at its limit. The poet said:

"So lower your gaze, for you are of Numayr."

It was said: they will be raised blind. Since their looking is with the eyes of their hearts, He made it a furtive glance, meaning their looking does not show. This interpretation involves strain.

Al-Suddi and Qatada said: the meaning is that they steal glances because of the grief and bad state they are in; they cannot look with the whole eye, but look with only part of it. On this interpretation, the word tarf (glance) may be a verbal noun, meaning a furtive glance. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿from a furtive glance﴾ [al-Shura: 45] means that their looking begins with a weak, hidden movement of the eyelids, by stealth, just as you see the one who examines a sword looking at it, and so is the glance of one who looks at hateful things: he cannot open his eyelids upon them and fill his eye with them, as he does when looking at those who love one another.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 42, verse 45–53 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And those who believe will say: "Indeed, the losers are those who have lost themselves and their families on the Day of Resurrection. Unquestionably, the wrongdoers are in lasting torment."﴾ ﴿They will have no allies to help them against Allah. And whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no way.﴾ ﴿Respond to your Lord before there comes a Day from Allah that cannot be turned back. You will have no refuge that Day, nor will you have any denial.﴾ ﴿But if they turn away, We did not send you as a guardian over them; your duty is only to convey. Indeed, when We let man taste mercy from Us, he rejoices in it; but if an evil befalls them because of what their hands have sent forth, then indeed man is ungrateful.﴾ ﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. He creates what He wills. He bestows females upon whom He wills and bestows males upon whom He wills.﴾ ﴿Or He pairs them, males and females, and He makes whom He wills barren. Indeed, He is All-Knowing, All-Powerful.﴾ ﴿It is not for any human that Allah should speak to him except by inspiration, or from behind a veil, or by sending a messenger who inspires by His permission what He wills. Indeed, He is Most High, All-Wise.﴾ ﴿And thus We have revealed to you an inspired Spirit by Our command. You did not know what the Book was, nor what faith was; but We made it a light by which We guide whom We will of Our servants. And indeed, you guide to a straight path,﴾ ﴿the path of Allah, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. Unquestionably, to Allah all matters are returned.﴾.

(p-٥٢٥) The apparent meaning is that "qāla" (said) is past both in wording and in meaning, i.e., "And those who believed said" in the life of this world, and "yawm al-qiyāmah" (the Day of Resurrection) is an object (ma'mūl) of "khasirū" (lost). It is also possible that the meaning of "qāla" is "yaqūlu" (says), and "yawm al-qiyāmah" is the object of "law yaqūlū" (if they said), i.e., they will say on that Day when they witness what has befallen the disbelievers and their families.

The apparent meaning is that "ahlīhim" refers to those who were their families in the world. If they are with them in the Fire, then they have lost them, meaning they gain nothing from them; and if they are in Paradise because they were believers, like the wife of Pharaoh (Āsiyah), then they likewise gain nothing from them. It was also said: their "ahl" (families) are the houses of the ḥūr (companions) that had been prepared for them had they believed. The apparent meaning is that His saying: ﴿Indeed, the wrongdoers are in lasting torment﴾ is from the words of the believers; and it was said: it is a new statement (isti'nāf) of information from Allah, exalted is He.

﴿Before there comes a Day﴾: it was said: it is the day of the arrival of death; and the apparent meaning is that it is the Day of Resurrection. "Min Allāh" (from Allah) is connected to a deleted element indicated by what has preceded, i.e., that Day will not come back with anything that Allah has decreed concerning it. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "min Allāh" is a complement of "lā maradd" (no turning back). End.

This is not the better view, for if it were its complement, it would be a governed noun and would be declined with tanwīn. It was also said: "min Allāh" is connected to "ya'tiya" (comes): before there comes from Allah a Day that no one can turn back.

(What you have, no refuge) you may take refuge in, by which you escape the punishment; and (nor have you any denial) of any of your deeds that bring you into the Fire. "Nakīr" is the verbal noun of "ankara" (to deny) by non-analogical form.

It was said: it may be an active participle of intensive form, but this is distant, because "nakara" does not have this meaning of distinguishing.

(But if they turn away) the verse: it is consolation for the Messenger and reassurance for him, and removal of his concern for them. "Al-insān" (man) is intended as a genus, and therefore ﴿if an evil befalls them﴾ came. The answer of the conditional came as ﴿indeed man﴾ and did not come as "fa-innahu" nor "fa-innahum," to indicate that this kind is marked by ingratitude for blessings, as He said: ﴿Indeed, man is greatly unjust, ungrateful﴾ [Ibrahim: 34], ﴿Indeed, man is to his Lord ungrateful﴾ [al-'Adiyat: 6].

When He mentioned that he disbelieves the blessings, He followed that with the fact that to Him belongs the dominion of the higher and lower worlds, that He does what He wills, and alerted to His great power, and that all existing things arise from His will. So He mentioned that He grants some females, and to some males, and to some both, and makes some barren so that they bear no child.

Ishaq ibn Bishr said: this verse was revealed concerning the prophets, then it became general. Lot was a father of daughters, to whom no males were born; Abraham was the opposite; Muhammad ﷺ and [Ibrahim]... both were born to both kinds; Yahya was barren. End.

Shu'ayb was also mentioned along with Lot, and 'Isa along with Yahya. Allah, exalted is He, placed the granting of daughters first, to comfort them and honor them, so that their protection and kindness to them would be given attention.

In a hadith: "Whoever is tested with any of these daughters and treats them well, they will be a shield for him from the Fire."

Wathilah ibn al-Asqa' said: among the blessings of a woman is that she is early with a female before a male, because Allah, exalted is He, began with females.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: (If you ask): Why did He place females before males, though males precede them, and then return and place males first? And why did He define the males after indefinitely mentioning the females? (I answer): Because He mentioned the trial at the end of the first verse. And the ingratitude of man is his forgetting the previous mercy he had received.

Then He reminded him by mentioning His dominion and His will, and the mention of the division of children, so He placed females first, because the context of speech is that He does what He wills, not what man wills; so the mention of females, who are among what man does not will, was more important, and importance necessitates precedence.

The trial: the genus that the Arabs used to count as a trial; He mentioned the trial and delayed the males. When He delayed them for this reason, He compensated for their delay, and they are more deserving of precedence by their definiteness; for definiteness is distinction and renown, as if He said: He grants to whom He wills both groups, the known ones mentioned who are not hidden from you. Then after that He gave each of the two kinds its share of precedence and delay; and the definiteness of placing them first was not due to their precedence, but to another requirement, so He said: ﴿males and females﴾, as He said: ﴿Indeed, We created you from a male and a female﴾ [al-Hujurat: 13], ﴿and made of him the pair, the male and the female﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 39]. End.

It was also said: He began with females, then followed with males, to move him from grief to joy. It was also said: so that he would know that there is no objection to Allah, so that he would be content. (p-٥٢٦) When He grants him a male, he knows that it is an increase and grace from Allah and a kindness to him.

It was also said: He placed them first as an indication that when weakness and need are theirs, Allah's care is greater.

Mujahid said: it is that a woman gives birth to a boy, then gives birth to a girl. Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah said: that she gives birth to twins, a boy and a girl. Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi said: "aw yuzawwijuhum dhukrānan wa-inātha" (or He pairs them, males and females). Our scholars said: he means Adam; Hawwa' used to bear him twins in every birth, a male and a female; he would marry the male of one birth to the female of the other birth. End.

When He mentioned the granting regarding females and the granting regarding males, He dispensed with mentioning it in His saying: ﴿or He pairs them, males and females﴾. Since barrenness is not praiseworthy, He said: ﴿and makes whom He wills barren﴾, and it is the counterpart of the one to whom a child is born. Since the hermaphrodite is among those whose existence causes grief, Allah, exalted is He, did not mention it. They said: the creation was constant, male and female, until in the first Jahiliyyah the hermaphrodite occurred. 'Amir ibn al-Zarib, the oldest and most experienced of the Arabs, was asked about its inheritance, and he did not know what to say and deferred them.

When night fell on him, he began to turn over, and his thoughts carried him away. His servant noticed his state and asked him, and he said: "I am bewildered by a matter about which I do not know what to say." She said to him: "What is it?" He said: "A person who has a penis and a vulva; what is its state in inheritance?" The slave-woman said to him: "Give it inheritance from where it urinates." He understood her and in the morning presented it to them, and they agreed to it.

Islam came in accordance with that, and 'Ali, may Allah honor his face, judged by it. Indeed, He is All-Knowing of the interests of the servants, All-Powerful over the bringing into being of whatever He wills.

There was among the disbelievers a dispute about the meaning of Allah's speaking to Musa, so Quraysh and the Jews went to anthropomorphism regarding it, and this verse was revealed. It was also said: Quraysh used to say: "Will you not speak to Allah and look at Him, if you are a truthful prophet, as Musa spoke to Him and looked at Him?" The Messenger, peace be upon him, said to them: "Musa did not look at Allah," and then this verse was revealed: ﴿It is not for any human that Allah should speak to him﴾, clarifying the form of Allah's speaking to His servants, i.e., it is not fitting and not possible for a human that anything be revealed to him except one of the modes of revelation, including inspiration.

Mujahid said: or the breathing into the heart. Al-Naqqash said: or a revelation in a dream. Al-Nakha'i said: among the prophets there was one to whom it was written on the ground, or by making him hear His speech without the speaker's direction or place being known to him, as with Musa, peace be upon him. This is the meaning of ﴿from behind a veil﴾, i.e., from concealment from the speaker; He is not limited, nor is He imagined in the mind as being in a place, and it is not like a veil in what is seen. Or by sending to him an angel who speaks to him with revelation from Allah, exalted is He. This was stated by Ibn 'Atiyyah.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: It is not valid for any human that Allah should speak to him except in three ways:

Either by way of revelation, which is inspiration and casting into the heart and in a dream, as He revealed to the mother of Musa and to Ibrahim, peace be upon him, regarding the slaughter of his son.

From Mujahid: Allah revealed the Psalms to Dawud, peace be upon him, in his chest. 'Abid ibn al-Abras said:
"And Allah inspired me that they have ordered
Ibn Abi Awfa, so I rose against a man."
That is: He inspired me and cast it into my heart.

Or by making him hear His speech, which He creates in some bodies, without the hearer seeing who is speaking to him, since He in His essence is not seen.

His saying: ﴿from behind a veil﴾ is a parable: just as a king who is veiled speaks to some of his intimates, and he is behind a veil, so he hears his voice and does not see his person; and this is like how Allah spoke to Musa and speaks to the angels. Or by sending to him a messenger from the angels, who conveys revelation to him, as He spoke to the prophets other than Musa. End.

This follows the way of the Mu'tazilah in the impossibility of seeing Allah and the negation of true speech from Allah.

All three of these categories are truly called revelation, but the first was specially named "revelation" here, because what falls into the heart by way of inspiration falls all at once, so it is better to specify the term "revelation" for it.

It was said: "wahyan" (by inspiration) is as He revealed to the messengers through angels. ﴿Or He sends a messenger﴾, i.e., a prophet, as He spoke to the nations of the prophets through their tongues; this was related by al-Zamakhsharī, who omitted the explanation of ﴿or from behind a veil﴾, and its meaning in this view is: as He spoke to Muhammad and Musa, peace be upon them.

(p-٥٢٧) The majority read "ḥijāb" in the singular; Ibn Abi 'Abalah read "ḥujub" in the plural. The majority read both verbs in the accusative, coordinating "aw yursila" with the implied element to which "min warā' ḥijāb" is connected; its estimate: "aw yukallimahu min warā' ḥijāb," and this implied element is coordinated with "waḥyan." The meaning: except by inspiration, or by hearing from behind a veil, or by sending a messenger, who then inspires to the prophet to whom he is sent, by Allah's permission, what He wills. It is not permissible to coordinate "aw yursila" with "an yukallimahu Allāh," because the meaning would be corrupted.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: "Waḥyan" and "an yursila" are two verbal nouns functioning as adverbial accusatives of circumstance (ḥāl), because "an yursila" means "irsālan"; and "min warā' ḥijāb" is a adverbial phrase also functioning as a circumstance, like His saying: ﴿and upon their sides﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 191]. The estimate: "It is not valid that He speaks to anyone except inspiring, or making him hear from behind a veil, or sending." End.

As for the maṣdar (verbal noun) occupying the position of a ḥāl (circumstantial clause), this is not a general rule. The Arabs only used it in certain fixed expressions. Likewise, it is not permissible to say جاءَ زَيْدٌ بُكاءً (Zayd came weeping), meaning باكِيًا (weeping). al-Mubarrad allowed it by analogy where the maṣdar denotes a type of the verb, as in جاءَ زَيْدٌ مَشْيًا أوْ سُرْعَةً (Zayd came walking or hurrying). Sibawayh prohibited the construction of أنْ with the verb, which is interpreted as a maṣdar, occupying the position of a ḥāl. So it is not permissible to say جاءَ زَيْدٌ أنْ يَضْحَكَ, meaning ضَحِكًا in place of ضاحِكًا (laughing). Accordingly, treating وَحْيًا (revelation) as a maṣdar in the position of a ḥāl is among the things that are not analogically valid. And أنْ يُرْسِلَ, meaning إرْسالًا in place of مُرْسِلًا (sending), is forbidden by the explicit statement of Sibawayh.

Nafi' and the people of Medina recited ﴿أوْ يُرْسِلَ رَسُولًا فَيُوحِيَ﴾ with raising (rafʿ) in both places. This is explained either as an implied subject, "he sends," or as governed by what precedes it, مِن وراءِ (from behind), since the implied sense is: "or he speaks from behind a veil." وَحْيًا is a maṣdar in the position of a ḥāl, and the implied element is conjoined to it, أوْ يُرْسِلَ (or sends). The meaning is: "except by revealing, or speaking from behind a veil, or sending."

Attributing speech to God through His sending a messenger is a metaphor (majāz), as when you say: "The king proclaimed to the people such-and-such," while in fact the proclaimer was the town crier circulating in the markets. The act performed through an intermediary is treated as if it were performed directly.

Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: In this verse there is evidence that a message (risālah) is a kind of speech, and that a person who swears not to speak to someone, and then sends a messenger to him, while not intending direct address at the time of his oath, has not broken his oath. End of quotation.

﴿إنَّهُ عَلِيٌّ﴾, meaning He is Exalted above the attributes of created beings, ﴿حَكِيمٌ﴾: His actions proceed according to what wisdom requires. He speaks through an intermediary and without one.

﴿وكَذَلِكَ أوْحَيْنا﴾, meaning: Just as that decisive revelation, We revealed to you. For the Prophet (ﷺ) had gathered all three modes: the inspiration cast into the heart and the dream; God's direct speaking to him in reality on the night of the Ascension (al-Isrāʾ); and the sending of a messenger to him, who was Jibril (Gabriel). It is also said: just as We revealed to the prophets before you. ﴿أوْحَيْنا إلَيْكَ رُوحًا مِن أمْرِنا﴾ (We revealed to you a spirit by Our command). Ibn ʿAbbas said: prophethood. al-Suddi said: revelation. Qatadah said: mercy. al-Kalbi said: a book. al-Rabiʿ said: Jibril. It is also said: the Qur'an. He called what was revealed to him "spirit" because life comes through it from ignorance.

Malik ibn Dinar said: O people of the Qur'an, what has the Qur'an sown in your hearts? For the Qur'an is the spring of the hearts, just as grass is the spring of the earth.

﴿ما كُنْتَ تَدْرِي ما الكِتابُ ولا الإيمانُ﴾ (You did not know what the Book was, nor faith): this is a statement affirming the magnitude of the favor, and he (ﷺ) knew better than anyone its value. He coordinated ﴿ولا الإيمانُ﴾ (nor faith) with ﴿ما الكِتابُ﴾ (what the Book was). Its meaning is: the faith that is perceived through hearing, because there are aspects of faith that are known only through revelation.

As for the oneness of God, His freedom from deficiencies, and knowledge of His exalted attributes, all the prophets, upon them be blessings and peace, knew these things, and they are protected from making any error concerning them. Knowledge of these things preceded their receiving revelation. The word "faith" (īmān) is applied to prayer in His saying: ﴿وما كانَ اللَّهُ لِيُضِيعَ إيمانَكُمْ﴾ (God would never waste your faith) [al-Baqarah: 143], since prayer is part of what faith includes.

Whoever studies the biographies of the prophets from (p-528) their upbringing to their mission will be certain that they were protected from every defect, and that they were monotheists devoted to God from the time they grew up.

God the Exalted said concerning Yahya (John), peace be upon him: ﴿وآتَيْناهُ الحُكْمَ صَبِيًّا﴾ (And We gave him wisdom while still a child) [Maryam: 12]. Maʿmar said: he was two or three years old.

From Abu al-ʿAliyah: "You did not know before the revelation that you would recite the Qur'an, nor how you would call people to faith."

al-Qadi said: "Faith" (al-īmān) here means the obligations and rulings. He said: He was a believer in the oneness of God before that, then the obligations were revealed, which he had not known before, so he increased in faith through being charged with them.

al-Qushayri said: it is permissible to apply the term "faith" to the details of the Sharia. al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: it is elliptical, with an omitted noun, meaning: nor the people of faith, from among those who believed, such as Abu Talib, al-ʿAbbas, or others. ʿAli ibn ʿIsa said: that was when you were in the cradle.

It is also said: "What the Book was" means: were it not for Our favor upon you, and "nor faith" means: were it not for Our guidance to you. It is also said: meaning, you were among an unlettered people who did not know faith or the Book, so you took what you brought to them from someone among them who knew these things.

﴿ما الكِتابُ﴾ is an interrogative clause, a subject and predicate, and it occupies the position of an object governed by تَدْرِي (you knew), and it is suspended (muʿallaqah) in that position.

﴿ولَكِنْ جَعَلْناهُ نُورًا﴾ (But We made it a light): the pronoun may refer to "spirit" (rūḥan) mentioned earlier, to "the Book," or to "faith," and the nearest mention is the most likely. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: it refers to the Book. End of quotation.

It is also said that it refers to both the Book and faith together, since their purpose is one, and this is like His saying: ﴿واللَّهُ ورَسُولُهُ أحَقُّ أنْ يُرْضُوهُ﴾ (God and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him) [al-Tawbah: 62].

The majority recited لَتَهْدِي (you guide), the imperfect of هَدى in the active voice. Hawshab recited it in the passive voice, responding to the Prophet's (ﷺ) request: ﴿اهْدِنا الصِّراطَ المُسْتَقِيمَ﴾ (Guide us to the straight path) [al-Fatihah: 6]. Ibn al-Sumayqaʿ recited لَتُهْدِي with a ḍammah on the tāʾ and a kasrah on the dāl. It is reported from al-Jahdari that it was like this, and like the recitation of Hawshab.

﴿صِراطٍ مُّسْتَقِيمٍ﴾ (to a straight path). ʿAli said: it is the Qur'an. It is also said: Islam.

﴿ألا إلى اللَّهِ تَصِيرُ الأُمُورُ﴾ (Unquestionably, to God all affairs are returned): He informed using the imperfect, and what is meant is continuity, like the saying: "Zayd gives and withholds," meaning that this is his habit, not that it refers literally to a future event. That is, all the affairs of creation are returned to Him, the Exalted, on the Day of Resurrection, and He judges between them with justice. This was specified for the Day of Resurrection because no one can claim anything for himself on that day. This is what al-Farraʾ said.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 42, verse 45–53 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And those who believe will say: "Indeed, the losers are those who have lost themselves and their families on the Day of Resurrection. Unquestionably, the wrongdoers are in lasting torment."﴾ ﴿They will have no allies to help them against Allah. And whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no way.﴾ ﴿Respond to your Lord before there comes a Day from Allah that cannot be turned back. You will have no refuge that Day, nor will you have any denial.﴾ ﴿But if they turn away, We did not send you as a guardian over them; your duty is only to convey. Indeed, when We let man taste mercy from Us, he rejoices in it; but if an evil befalls them because of what their hands have sent forth, then indeed man is ungrateful.﴾ ﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. He creates what He wills. He bestows females upon whom He wills and bestows males upon whom He wills.﴾ ﴿Or He pairs them, males and females, and He makes whom He wills barren. Indeed, He is All-Knowing, All-Powerful.﴾ ﴿It is not for any human that Allah should speak to him except by inspiration, or from behind a veil, or by sending a messenger who inspires by His permission what He wills. Indeed, He is Most High, All-Wise.﴾ ﴿And thus We have revealed to you an inspired Spirit by Our command. You did not know what the Book was, nor what faith was; but We made it a light by which We guide whom We will of Our servants. And indeed, you guide to a straight path,﴾ ﴿the path of Allah, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. Unquestionably, to Allah all matters are returned.﴾.

(p-٥٢٥) The apparent meaning is that "qāla" (said) is past both in wording and in meaning, i.e., "And those who believed said" in the life of this world, and "yawm al-qiyāmah" (the Day of Resurrection) is an object (ma'mūl) of "khasirū" (lost). It is also possible that the meaning of "qāla" is "yaqūlu" (says), and "yawm al-qiyāmah" is the object of "law yaqūlū" (if they said), i.e., they will say on that Day when they witness what has befallen the disbelievers and their families.

The apparent meaning is that "ahlīhim" refers to those who were their families in the world. If they are with them in the Fire, then they have lost them, meaning they gain nothing from them; and if they are in Paradise because they were believers, like the wife of Pharaoh (Āsiyah), then they likewise gain nothing from them. It was also said: their "ahl" (families) are the houses of the ḥūr (companions) that had been prepared for them had they believed. The apparent meaning is that His saying: ﴿Indeed, the wrongdoers are in lasting torment﴾ is from the words of the believers; and it was said: it is a new statement (isti'nāf) of information from Allah, exalted is He.

﴿Before there comes a Day﴾: it was said: it is the day of the arrival of death; and the apparent meaning is that it is the Day of Resurrection. "Min Allāh" (from Allah) is connected to a deleted element indicated by what has preceded, i.e., that Day will not come back with anything that Allah has decreed concerning it. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "min Allāh" is a complement of "lā maradd" (no turning back). End.

This is not the better view, for if it were its complement, it would be a governed noun and would be declined with tanwīn. It was also said: "min Allāh" is connected to "ya'tiya" (comes): before there comes from Allah a Day that no one can turn back.

(What you have, no refuge) you may take refuge in, by which you escape the punishment; and (nor have you any denial) of any of your deeds that bring you into the Fire. "Nakīr" is the verbal noun of "ankara" (to deny) by non-analogical form.

It was said: it may be an active participle of intensive form, but this is distant, because "nakara" does not have this meaning of distinguishing.

(But if they turn away) the verse: it is consolation for the Messenger and reassurance for him, and removal of his concern for them. "Al-insān" (man) is intended as a genus, and therefore ﴿if an evil befalls them﴾ came. The answer of the conditional came as ﴿indeed man﴾ and did not come as "fa-innahu" nor "fa-innahum," to indicate that this kind is marked by ingratitude for blessings, as He said: ﴿Indeed, man is greatly unjust, ungrateful﴾ [Ibrahim: 34], ﴿Indeed, man is to his Lord ungrateful﴾ [al-'Adiyat: 6].

When He mentioned that he disbelieves the blessings, He followed that with the fact that to Him belongs the dominion of the higher and lower worlds, that He does what He wills, and alerted to His great power, and that all existing things arise from His will. So He mentioned that He grants some females, and to some males, and to some both, and makes some barren so that they bear no child.

Ishaq ibn Bishr said: this verse was revealed concerning the prophets, then it became general. Lot was a father of daughters, to whom no males were born; Abraham was the opposite; Muhammad ﷺ and [Ibrahim]... both were born to both kinds; Yahya was barren. End.

Shu'ayb was also mentioned along with Lot, and 'Isa along with Yahya. Allah, exalted is He, placed the granting of daughters first, to comfort them and honor them, so that their protection and kindness to them would be given attention.

In a hadith: "Whoever is tested with any of these daughters and treats them well, they will be a shield for him from the Fire."

Wathilah ibn al-Asqa' said: among the blessings of a woman is that she is early with a female before a male, because Allah, exalted is He, began with females.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: (If you ask): Why did He place females before males, though males precede them, and then return and place males first? And why did He define the males after indefinitely mentioning the females? (I answer): Because He mentioned the trial at the end of the first verse. And the ingratitude of man is his forgetting the previous mercy he had received.

Then He reminded him by mentioning His dominion and His will, and the mention of the division of children, so He placed females first, because the context of speech is that He does what He wills, not what man wills; so the mention of females, who are among what man does not will, was more important, and importance necessitates precedence.

The trial: the genus that the Arabs used to count as a trial; He mentioned the trial and delayed the males. When He delayed them for this reason, He compensated for their delay, and they are more deserving of precedence by their definiteness; for definiteness is distinction and renown, as if He said: He grants to whom He wills both groups, the known ones mentioned who are not hidden from you. Then after that He gave each of the two kinds its share of precedence and delay; and the definiteness of placing them first was not due to their precedence, but to another requirement, so He said: ﴿males and females﴾, as He said: ﴿Indeed, We created you from a male and a female﴾ [al-Hujurat: 13], ﴿and made of him the pair, the male and the female﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 39]. End.

It was also said: He began with females, then followed with males, to move him from grief to joy. It was also said: so that he would know that there is no objection to Allah, so that he would be content. (p-٥٢٦) When He grants him a male, he knows that it is an increase and grace from Allah and a kindness to him.

It was also said: He placed them first as an indication that when weakness and need are theirs, Allah's care is greater.

Mujahid said: it is that a woman gives birth to a boy, then gives birth to a girl. Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah said: that she gives birth to twins, a boy and a girl. Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi said: "aw yuzawwijuhum dhukrānan wa-inātha" (or He pairs them, males and females). Our scholars said: he means Adam; Hawwa' used to bear him twins in every birth, a male and a female; he would marry the male of one birth to the female of the other birth. End.

When He mentioned the granting regarding females and the granting regarding males, He dispensed with mentioning it in His saying: ﴿or He pairs them, males and females﴾. Since barrenness is not praiseworthy, He said: ﴿and makes whom He wills barren﴾, and it is the counterpart of the one to whom a child is born. Since the hermaphrodite is among those whose existence causes grief, Allah, exalted is He, did not mention it. They said: the creation was constant, male and female, until in the first Jahiliyyah the hermaphrodite occurred. 'Amir ibn al-Zarib, the oldest and most experienced of the Arabs, was asked about its inheritance, and he did not know what to say and deferred them.

When night fell on him, he began to turn over, and his thoughts carried him away. His servant noticed his state and asked him, and he said: "I am bewildered by a matter about which I do not know what to say." She said to him: "What is it?" He said: "A person who has a penis and a vulva; what is its state in inheritance?" The slave-woman said to him: "Give it inheritance from where it urinates." He understood her and in the morning presented it to them, and they agreed to it.

Islam came in accordance with that, and 'Ali, may Allah honor his face, judged by it. Indeed, He is All-Knowing of the interests of the servants, All-Powerful over the bringing into being of whatever He wills.

There was among the disbelievers a dispute about the meaning of Allah's speaking to Musa, so Quraysh and the Jews went to anthropomorphism regarding it, and this verse was revealed. It was also said: Quraysh used to say: "Will you not speak to Allah and look at Him, if you are a truthful prophet, as Musa spoke to Him and looked at Him?" The Messenger, peace be upon him, said to them: "Musa did not look at Allah," and then this verse was revealed: ﴿It is not for any human that Allah should speak to him﴾, clarifying the form of Allah's speaking to His servants, i.e., it is not fitting and not possible for a human that anything be revealed to him except one of the modes of revelation, including inspiration.

Mujahid said: or the breathing into the heart. Al-Naqqash said: or a revelation in a dream. Al-Nakha'i said: among the prophets there was one to whom it was written on the ground, or by making him hear His speech without the speaker's direction or place being known to him, as with Musa, peace be upon him. This is the meaning of ﴿from behind a veil﴾, i.e., from concealment from the speaker; He is not limited, nor is He imagined in the mind as being in a place, and it is not like a veil in what is seen. Or by sending to him an angel who speaks to him with revelation from Allah, exalted is He. This was stated by Ibn 'Atiyyah.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: It is not valid for any human that Allah should speak to him except in three ways:

Either by way of revelation, which is inspiration and casting into the heart and in a dream, as He revealed to the mother of Musa and to Ibrahim, peace be upon him, regarding the slaughter of his son.

"And Allah inspired me that they have ordered
Ibn Abi Awfa, so I rose against a man."
That is: He inspired me and cast it into my heart.

﴿إنَّهُ عَلِيٌّ﴾, meaning He is Exalted above the attributes of created beings, ﴿حَكِيمٌ﴾: His actions proceed according to what wisdom requires. He speaks through an intermediary and without one.

﴿وكَذَلِكَ أوْحَيْنا﴾, meaning: Just as that decisive revelation, We revealed to you. For the Prophet (ﷺ) had gathered all three modes: the inspiration cast into the heart and the dream; God's direct speaking to him in reality on the night of the Ascension (al-Isrāʾ); and the sending of a messenger to him, who was Jibril (Gabriel). It is also said: just as We revealed to the prophets before you. ﴿أوْحَيْنا إلَيْكَ رُوحًا مِن أمْرِنا﴾ (We revealed to you a spirit by Our command). Ibn ʿAbbas said: prophethood. al-Suddi said: revelation. Qatadah said: mercy. al-Kalbi said: a book. al-Rabiʿ said: Jibril. It is also said: the Qur'an. He called what was revealed to him "spirit" because life comes through it from ignorance.

Malik ibn Dinar said: O people of the Qur'an, what has the Qur'an sown in your hearts? For the Qur'an is the spring of the hearts, just as grass is the spring of the earth.

﴿ما كُنْتَ تَدْرِي ما الكِتابُ ولا الإيمانُ﴾ (You did not know what the Book was, nor faith): this is a statement affirming the magnitude of the favor, and he (ﷺ) knew better than anyone its value. He coordinated ﴿ولا الإيمانُ﴾ (nor faith) with ﴿ما الكِتابُ﴾ (what the Book was). Its meaning is: the faith that is perceived through hearing, because there are aspects of faith that are known only through revelation.

As for the oneness of God, His freedom from deficiencies, and knowledge of His exalted attributes, all the prophets, upon them be blessings and peace, knew these things, and they are protected from making any error concerning them. Knowledge of these things preceded their receiving revelation. The word "faith" (īmān) is applied to prayer in His saying: ﴿وما كانَ اللَّهُ لِيُضِيعَ إيمانَكُمْ﴾ (God would never waste your faith) [al-Baqarah: 143], since prayer is part of what faith includes.

Whoever studies the biographies of the prophets from (p-528) their upbringing to their mission will be certain that they were protected from every defect, and that they were monotheists devoted to God from the time they grew up.

God the Exalted said concerning Yahya (John), peace be upon him: ﴿وآتَيْناهُ الحُكْمَ صَبِيًّا﴾ (And We gave him wisdom while still a child) [Maryam: 12]. Maʿmar said: he was two or three years old.

From Abu al-ʿAliyah: "You did not know before the revelation that you would recite the Qur'an, nor how you would call people to faith."

al-Qadi said: "Faith" (al-īmān) here means the obligations and rulings. He said: He was a believer in the oneness of God before that, then the obligations were revealed, which he had not known before, so he increased in faith through being charged with them.

al-Qushayri said: it is permissible to apply the term "faith" to the details of the Sharia. al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: it is elliptical, with an omitted noun, meaning: nor the people of faith, from among those who believed, such as Abu Talib, al-ʿAbbas, or others. ʿAli ibn ʿIsa said: that was when you were in the cradle.

It is also said: "What the Book was" means: were it not for Our favor upon you, and "nor faith" means: were it not for Our guidance to you. It is also said: meaning, you were among an unlettered people who did not know faith or the Book, so you took what you brought to them from someone among them who knew these things.

﴿ما الكِتابُ﴾ is an interrogative clause, a subject and predicate, and it occupies the position of an object governed by تَدْرِي (you knew), and it is suspended (muʿallaqah) in that position.

﴿ولَكِنْ جَعَلْناهُ نُورًا﴾ (But We made it a light): the pronoun may refer to "spirit" (rūḥan) mentioned earlier, to "the Book," or to "faith," and the nearest mention is the most likely. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: it refers to the Book. End of quotation.

It is also said that it refers to both the Book and faith together, since their purpose is one, and this is like His saying: ﴿واللَّهُ ورَسُولُهُ أحَقُّ أنْ يُرْضُوهُ﴾ (God and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him) [al-Tawbah: 62].

The majority recited لَتَهْدِي (you guide), the imperfect of هَدى in the active voice. Hawshab recited it in the passive voice, responding to the Prophet's (ﷺ) request: ﴿اهْدِنا الصِّراطَ المُسْتَقِيمَ﴾ (Guide us to the straight path) [al-Fatihah: 6]. Ibn al-Sumayqaʿ recited لَتُهْدِي with a ḍammah on the tāʾ and a kasrah on the dāl. It is reported from al-Jahdari that it was like this, and like the recitation of Hawshab.

﴿صِراطٍ مُّسْتَقِيمٍ﴾ (to a straight path). ʿAli said: it is the Qur'an. It is also said: Islam.

﴿ألا إلى اللَّهِ تَصِيرُ الأُمُورُ﴾ (Unquestionably, to God all affairs are returned): He informed using the imperfect, and what is meant is continuity, like the saying: "Zayd gives and withholds," meaning that this is his habit, not that it refers literally to a future event. That is, all the affairs of creation are returned to Him, the Exalted, on the Day of Resurrection, and He judges between them with justice. This was specified for the Day of Resurrection because no one can claim anything for himself on that day. This is what al-Farraʾ said.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 42, verse 45–53 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And those who believe will say: "Indeed, the losers are those who have lost themselves and their families on the Day of Resurrection. Unquestionably, the wrongdoers are in lasting torment."﴾ ﴿They will have no allies to help them against Allah. And whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no way.﴾ ﴿Respond to your Lord before there comes a Day from Allah that cannot be turned back. You will have no refuge that Day, nor will you have any denial.﴾ ﴿But if they turn away, We did not send you as a guardian over them; your duty is only to convey. Indeed, when We let man taste mercy from Us, he rejoices in it; but if an evil befalls them because of what their hands have sent forth, then indeed man is ungrateful.﴾ ﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. He creates what He wills. He bestows females upon whom He wills and bestows males upon whom He wills.﴾ ﴿Or He pairs them, males and females, and He makes whom He wills barren. Indeed, He is All-Knowing, All-Powerful.﴾ ﴿It is not for any human that Allah should speak to him except by inspiration, or from behind a veil, or by sending a messenger who inspires by His permission what He wills. Indeed, He is Most High, All-Wise.﴾ ﴿And thus We have revealed to you an inspired Spirit by Our command. You did not know what the Book was, nor what faith was; but We made it a light by which We guide whom We will of Our servants. And indeed, you guide to a straight path,﴾ ﴿the path of Allah, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. Unquestionably, to Allah all matters are returned.﴾.

(p-٥٢٥) The apparent meaning is that "qāla" (said) is past both in wording and in meaning, i.e., "And those who believed said" in the life of this world, and "yawm al-qiyāmah" (the Day of Resurrection) is an object (ma'mūl) of "khasirū" (lost). It is also possible that the meaning of "qāla" is "yaqūlu" (says), and "yawm al-qiyāmah" is the object of "law yaqūlū" (if they said), i.e., they will say on that Day when they witness what has befallen the disbelievers and their families.

The apparent meaning is that "ahlīhim" refers to those who were their families in the world. If they are with them in the Fire, then they have lost them, meaning they gain nothing from them; and if they are in Paradise because they were believers, like the wife of Pharaoh (Āsiyah), then they likewise gain nothing from them. It was also said: their "ahl" (families) are the houses of the ḥūr (companions) that had been prepared for them had they believed. The apparent meaning is that His saying: ﴿Indeed, the wrongdoers are in lasting torment﴾ is from the words of the believers; and it was said: it is a new statement (isti'nāf) of information from Allah, exalted is He.

﴿Before there comes a Day﴾: it was said: it is the day of the arrival of death; and the apparent meaning is that it is the Day of Resurrection. "Min Allāh" (from Allah) is connected to a deleted element indicated by what has preceded, i.e., that Day will not come back with anything that Allah has decreed concerning it. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "min Allāh" is a complement of "lā maradd" (no turning back). End.

This is not the better view, for if it were its complement, it would be a governed noun and would be declined with tanwīn. It was also said: "min Allāh" is connected to "ya'tiya" (comes): before there comes from Allah a Day that no one can turn back.

(What you have, no refuge) you may take refuge in, by which you escape the punishment; and (nor have you any denial) of any of your deeds that bring you into the Fire. "Nakīr" is the verbal noun of "ankara" (to deny) by non-analogical form.

It was said: it may be an active participle of intensive form, but this is distant, because "nakara" does not have this meaning of distinguishing.

(But if they turn away) the verse: it is consolation for the Messenger and reassurance for him, and removal of his concern for them. "Al-insān" (man) is intended as a genus, and therefore ﴿if an evil befalls them﴾ came. The answer of the conditional came as ﴿indeed man﴾ and did not come as "fa-innahu" nor "fa-innahum," to indicate that this kind is marked by ingratitude for blessings, as He said: ﴿Indeed, man is greatly unjust, ungrateful﴾ [Ibrahim: 34], ﴿Indeed, man is to his Lord ungrateful﴾ [al-'Adiyat: 6].

When He mentioned that he disbelieves the blessings, He followed that with the fact that to Him belongs the dominion of the higher and lower worlds, that He does what He wills, and alerted to His great power, and that all existing things arise from His will. So He mentioned that He grants some females, and to some males, and to some both, and makes some barren so that they bear no child.

Ishaq ibn Bishr said: this verse was revealed concerning the prophets, then it became general. Lot was a father of daughters, to whom no males were born; Abraham was the opposite; Muhammad ﷺ and [Ibrahim]... both were born to both kinds; Yahya was barren. End.

Shu'ayb was also mentioned along with Lot, and 'Isa along with Yahya. Allah, exalted is He, placed the granting of daughters first, to comfort them and honor them, so that their protection and kindness to them would be given attention.

In a hadith: "Whoever is tested with any of these daughters and treats them well, they will be a shield for him from the Fire."

Wathilah ibn al-Asqa' said: among the blessings of a woman is that she is early with a female before a male, because Allah, exalted is He, began with females.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: (If you ask): Why did He place females before males, though males precede them, and then return and place males first? And why did He define the males after indefinitely mentioning the females? (I answer): Because He mentioned the trial at the end of the first verse. And the ingratitude of man is his forgetting the previous mercy he had received.

Then He reminded him by mentioning His dominion and His will, and the mention of the division of children, so He placed females first, because the context of speech is that He does what He wills, not what man wills; so the mention of females, who are among what man does not will, was more important, and importance necessitates precedence.

The trial: the genus that the Arabs used to count as a trial; He mentioned the trial and delayed the males. When He delayed them for this reason, He compensated for their delay, and they are more deserving of precedence by their definiteness; for definiteness is distinction and renown, as if He said: He grants to whom He wills both groups, the known ones mentioned who are not hidden from you. Then after that He gave each of the two kinds its share of precedence and delay; and the definiteness of placing them first was not due to their precedence, but to another requirement, so He said: ﴿males and females﴾, as He said: ﴿Indeed, We created you from a male and a female﴾ [al-Hujurat: 13], ﴿and made of him the pair, the male and the female﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 39]. End.

It was also said: He began with females, then followed with males, to move him from grief to joy. It was also said: so that he would know that there is no objection to Allah, so that he would be content. (p-٥٢٦) When He grants him a male, he knows that it is an increase and grace from Allah and a kindness to him.

It was also said: He placed them first as an indication that when weakness and need are theirs, Allah's care is greater.

Mujahid said: it is that a woman gives birth to a boy, then gives birth to a girl. Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah said: that she gives birth to twins, a boy and a girl. Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi said: "aw yuzawwijuhum dhukrānan wa-inātha" (or He pairs them, males and females). Our scholars said: he means Adam; Hawwa' used to bear him twins in every birth, a male and a female; he would marry the male of one birth to the female of the other birth. End.

When He mentioned the granting regarding females and the granting regarding males, He dispensed with mentioning it in His saying: ﴿or He pairs them, males and females﴾. Since barrenness is not praiseworthy, He said: ﴿and makes whom He wills barren﴾, and it is the counterpart of the one to whom a child is born. Since the hermaphrodite is among those whose existence causes grief, Allah, exalted is He, did not mention it. They said: the creation was constant, male and female, until in the first Jahiliyyah the hermaphrodite occurred. 'Amir ibn al-Zarib, the oldest and most experienced of the Arabs, was asked about its inheritance, and he did not know what to say and deferred them.

When night fell on him, he began to turn over, and his thoughts carried him away. His servant noticed his state and asked him, and he said: "I am bewildered by a matter about which I do not know what to say." She said to him: "What is it?" He said: "A person who has a penis and a vulva; what is its state in inheritance?" The slave-woman said to him: "Give it inheritance from where it urinates." He understood her and in the morning presented it to them, and they agreed to it.

Islam came in accordance with that, and 'Ali, may Allah honor his face, judged by it. Indeed, He is All-Knowing of the interests of the servants, All-Powerful over the bringing into being of whatever He wills.

There was among the disbelievers a dispute about the meaning of Allah's speaking to Musa, so Quraysh and the Jews went to anthropomorphism regarding it, and this verse was revealed. It was also said: Quraysh used to say: "Will you not speak to Allah and look at Him, if you are a truthful prophet, as Musa spoke to Him and looked at Him?" The Messenger, peace be upon him, said to them: "Musa did not look at Allah," and then this verse was revealed: ﴿It is not for any human that Allah should speak to him﴾, clarifying the form of Allah's speaking to His servants, i.e., it is not fitting and not possible for a human that anything be revealed to him except one of the modes of revelation, including inspiration.

Mujahid said: or the breathing into the heart. Al-Naqqash said: or a revelation in a dream. Al-Nakha'i said: among the prophets there was one to whom it was written on the ground, or by making him hear His speech without the speaker's direction or place being known to him, as with Musa, peace be upon him. This is the meaning of ﴿from behind a veil﴾, i.e., from concealment from the speaker; He is not limited, nor is He imagined in the mind as being in a place, and it is not like a veil in what is seen. Or by sending to him an angel who speaks to him with revelation from Allah, exalted is He. This was stated by Ibn 'Atiyyah.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: It is not valid for any human that Allah should speak to him except in three ways:

Either by way of revelation, which is inspiration and casting into the heart and in a dream, as He revealed to the mother of Musa and to Ibrahim, peace be upon him, regarding the slaughter of his son.

From Mujahid: Allah revealed the Psalms to Dawud, peace be upon him, in his chest. 'Abid ibn al-Abras said:
"And Allah inspired me that they have ordered
Ibn Abi Awfa, so I rose against a man."
That is: He inspired me and cast it into my heart.

Or by making him hear His speech, which He creates in some bodies, without the hearer seeing who is speaking to him, since He in His essence is not seen.

His saying: ﴿from behind a veil﴾ is a parable: just as a king who is veiled speaks to some of his intimates, and he is behind a veil, so he hears his voice and does not see his person; and this is like how Allah spoke to Musa and speaks to the angels. Or by sending to him a messenger from the angels, who conveys revelation to him, as He spoke to the prophets other than Musa. End.

This follows the way of the Mu'tazilah in the impossibility of seeing Allah and the negation of true speech from Allah.

All three of these categories are truly called revelation, but the first was specially named "revelation" here, because what falls into the heart by way of inspiration falls all at once, so it is better to specify the term "revelation" for it.

It was said: "wahyan" (by inspiration) is as He revealed to the messengers through angels. ﴿Or He sends a messenger﴾, i.e., a prophet, as He spoke to the nations of the prophets through their tongues; this was related by al-Zamakhsharī, who omitted the explanation of ﴿or from behind a veil﴾, and its meaning in this view is: as He spoke to Muhammad and Musa, peace be upon them.

(p-٥٢٧) The majority read "ḥijāb" in the singular; Ibn Abi 'Abalah read "ḥujub" in the plural. The majority read both verbs in the accusative, coordinating "aw yursila" with the implied element to which "min warā' ḥijāb" is connected; its estimate: "aw yukallimahu min warā' ḥijāb," and this implied element is coordinated with "waḥyan." The meaning: except by inspiration, or by hearing from behind a veil, or by sending a messenger, who then inspires to the prophet to whom he is sent, by Allah's permission, what He wills. It is not permissible to coordinate "aw yursila" with "an yukallimahu Allāh," because the meaning would be corrupted.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: "Waḥyan" and "an yursila" are two verbal nouns functioning as adverbial accusatives of circumstance (ḥāl), because "an yursila" means "irsālan"; and "min warā' ḥijāb" is a adverbial phrase also functioning as a circumstance, like His saying: ﴿and upon their sides﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 191]. The estimate: "It is not valid that He speaks to anyone except inspiring, or making him hear from behind a veil, or sending." End.

As for the maṣdar (verbal noun) occupying the position of a ḥāl (circumstantial clause), this is not a general rule. The Arabs only used it in certain fixed expressions. Likewise, it is not permissible to say جاءَ زَيْدٌ بُكاءً (Zayd came weeping), meaning باكِيًا (weeping). al-Mubarrad allowed it by analogy where the maṣdar denotes a type of the verb, as in جاءَ زَيْدٌ مَشْيًا أوْ سُرْعَةً (Zayd came walking or hurrying). Sibawayh prohibited the construction of أنْ with the verb, which is interpreted as a maṣdar, occupying the position of a ḥāl. So it is not permissible to say جاءَ زَيْدٌ أنْ يَضْحَكَ, meaning ضَحِكًا in place of ضاحِكًا (laughing). Accordingly, treating وَحْيًا (revelation) as a maṣdar in the position of a ḥāl is among the things that are not analogically valid. And أنْ يُرْسِلَ, meaning إرْسالًا in place of مُرْسِلًا (sending), is forbidden by the explicit statement of Sibawayh.

Nafi' and the people of Medina recited ﴿أوْ يُرْسِلَ رَسُولًا فَيُوحِيَ﴾ with raising (rafʿ) in both places. This is explained either as an implied subject, "he sends," or as governed by what precedes it, مِن وراءِ (from behind), since the implied sense is: "or he speaks from behind a veil." وَحْيًا is a maṣdar in the position of a ḥāl, and the implied element is conjoined to it, أوْ يُرْسِلَ (or sends). The meaning is: "except by revealing, or speaking from behind a veil, or sending."

Attributing speech to God through His sending a messenger is a metaphor (majāz), as when you say: "The king proclaimed to the people such-and-such," while in fact the proclaimer was the town crier circulating in the markets. The act performed through an intermediary is treated as if it were performed directly.

Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: In this verse there is evidence that a message (risālah) is a kind of speech, and that a person who swears not to speak to someone, and then sends a messenger to him, while not intending direct address at the time of his oath, has not broken his oath. End of quotation.

﴿إنَّهُ عَلِيٌّ﴾, meaning He is Exalted above the attributes of created beings, ﴿حَكِيمٌ﴾: His actions proceed according to what wisdom requires. He speaks through an intermediary and without one.

﴿وكَذَلِكَ أوْحَيْنا﴾, meaning: Just as that decisive revelation, We revealed to you. For the Prophet (ﷺ) had gathered all three modes: the inspiration cast into the heart and the dream; God's direct speaking to him in reality on the night of the Ascension (al-Isrāʾ); and the sending of a messenger to him, who was Jibril (Gabriel). It is also said: just as We revealed to the prophets before you. ﴿أوْحَيْنا إلَيْكَ رُوحًا مِن أمْرِنا﴾ (We revealed to you a spirit by Our command).
