From Abu al-ʿAliyah: "You did not know before the revelation that you would recite the Qur'an, nor how you would call people to faith."

al-Qadi said: "Faith" (al-īmān) here means the obligations and rulings. He said: He was a believer in the oneness of God before that, then the obligations were revealed, which he had not known before, so he increased in faith through being charged with them.

al-Qushayri said: it is permissible to apply the term "faith" to the details of the Sharia. al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: it is elliptical, with an omitted noun, meaning: nor the people of faith, from among those who believed, such as Abu Talib, al-ʿAbbas, or others. ʿAli ibn ʿIsa said: that was when you were in the cradle.

It is also said: "What the Book was" means: were it not for Our favor upon you, and "nor faith" means: were it not for Our guidance to you. It is also said: meaning, you were among an unlettered people who did not know faith or the Book, so you took what you brought to them from someone among them who knew these things.

﴿ما الكِتابُ﴾ is an interrogative clause, a subject and predicate, and it occupies the position of an object governed by تَدْرِي (you knew), and it is suspended (muʿallaqah) in that position.

﴿ولَكِنْ جَعَلْناهُ نُورًا﴾ (But We made it a light): the pronoun may refer to "spirit" (rūḥan) mentioned earlier, to "the Book," or to "faith," and the nearest mention is the most likely. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: it refers to the Book. End of quotation.

It is also said that it refers to both the Book and faith together, since their purpose is one, and this is like His saying: ﴿واللَّهُ ورَسُولُهُ أحَقُّ أنْ يُرْضُوهُ﴾ (God and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him) [al-Tawbah: 62].

The majority recited لَتَهْدِي (you guide), the imperfect of هَدى in the active voice. Hawshab recited it in the passive voice, responding to the Prophet's (ﷺ) request: ﴿اهْدِنا الصِّراطَ المُسْتَقِيمَ﴾ (Guide us to the straight path) [al-Fatihah: 6]. Ibn al-Sumayqaʿ recited لَتُهْدِي with a ḍammah on the tāʾ and a kasrah on the dāl. It is reported from al-Jahdari that it was like this, and like the recitation of Hawshab.

﴿صِراطٍ مُّسْتَقِيمٍ﴾ (to a straight path). ʿAli said: it is the Qur'an. It is also said: Islam.

﴿ألا إلى اللَّهِ تَصِيرُ الأُمُورُ﴾ (Unquestionably, to God all affairs are returned): He informed using the imperfect, and what is meant is continuity, like the saying: "Zayd gives and withholds," meaning that this is his habit, not that it refers literally to a future event. That is, all the affairs of creation are returned to Him, the Exalted, on the Day of Resurrection, and He judges between them with justice. This was specified for the Day of Resurrection because no one can claim anything for himself on that day. This is what al-Farraʾ said.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 42, verse 45–53 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And those who believe will say: "Indeed, the losers are those who have lost themselves and their families on the Day of Resurrection. Unquestionably, the wrongdoers are in lasting torment."﴾ ﴿They will have no allies to help them against Allah. And whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no way.﴾ ﴿Respond to your Lord before there comes a Day from Allah that cannot be turned back. You will have no refuge that Day, nor will you have any denial.﴾ ﴿But if they turn away, We did not send you as a guardian over them; your duty is only to convey. Indeed, when We let man taste mercy from Us, he rejoices in it; but if an evil befalls them because of what their hands have sent forth, then indeed man is ungrateful.﴾ ﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. He creates what He wills. He bestows females upon whom He wills and bestows males upon whom He wills.﴾ ﴿Or He pairs them, males and females, and He makes whom He wills barren. Indeed, He is All-Knowing, All-Powerful.﴾ ﴿It is not for any human that Allah should speak to him except by inspiration, or from behind a veil, or by sending a messenger who inspires by His permission what He wills. Indeed, He is Most High, All-Wise.﴾ ﴿And thus We have revealed to you an inspired Spirit by Our command. You did not know what the Book was, nor what faith was; but We made it a light by which We guide whom We will of Our servants. And indeed, you guide to a straight path,﴾ ﴿the path of Allah, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. Unquestionably, to Allah all matters are returned.﴾.

(p-٥٢٥) The apparent meaning is that "qāla" (said) is past both in wording and in meaning, i.e., "And those who believed said" in the life of this world, and "yawm al-qiyāmah" (the Day of Resurrection) is an object (ma'mūl) of "khasirū" (lost). It is also possible that the meaning of "qāla" is "yaqūlu" (says), and "yawm al-qiyāmah" is the object of "law yaqūlū" (if they said), i.e., they will say on that Day when they witness what has befallen the disbelievers and their families.

The apparent meaning is that "ahlīhim" refers to those who were their families in the world. If they are with them in the Fire, then they have lost them, meaning they gain nothing from them; and if they are in Paradise because they were believers, like the wife of Pharaoh (Āsiyah), then they likewise gain nothing from them. It was also said: their "ahl" (families) are the houses of the ḥūr (companions) that had been prepared for them had they believed. The apparent meaning is that His saying: ﴿Indeed, the wrongdoers are in lasting torment﴾ is from the words of the believers; and it was said: it is a new statement (isti'nāf) of information from Allah, exalted is He.

﴿Before there comes a Day﴾: it was said: it is the day of the arrival of death; and the apparent meaning is that it is the Day of Resurrection. "Min Allāh" (from Allah) is connected to a deleted element indicated by what has preceded, i.e., that Day will not come back with anything that Allah has decreed concerning it. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "min Allāh" is a complement of "lā maradd" (no turning back). End.

This is not the better view, for if it were its complement, it would be a governed noun and would be declined with tanwīn. It was also said: "min Allāh" is connected to "ya'tiya" (comes): before there comes from Allah a Day that no one can turn back.

(What you have, no refuge) you may take refuge in, by which you escape the punishment; and (nor have you any denial) of any of your deeds that bring you into the Fire. "Nakīr" is the verbal noun of "ankara" (to deny) by non-analogical form.

It was said: it may be an active participle of intensive form, but this is distant, because "nakara" does not have this meaning of distinguishing.

(But if they turn away) the verse: it is consolation for the Messenger and reassurance for him, and removal of his concern for them. "Al-insān" (man) is intended as a genus, and therefore ﴿if an evil befalls them﴾ came. The answer of the conditional came as ﴿indeed man﴾ and did not come as "fa-innahu" nor "fa-innahum," to indicate that this kind is marked by ingratitude for blessings, as He said: ﴿Indeed, man is greatly unjust, ungrateful﴾ [Ibrahim: 34], ﴿Indeed, man is to his Lord ungrateful﴾ [al-'Adiyat: 6].

When He mentioned that he disbelieves the blessings, He followed that with the fact that to Him belongs the dominion of the higher and lower worlds, that He does what He wills, and alerted to His great power, and that all existing things arise from His will. So He mentioned that He grants some females, and to some males, and to some both, and makes some barren so that they bear no child.

Ishaq ibn Bishr said: this verse was revealed concerning the prophets, then it became general. Lot was a father of daughters, to whom no males were born; Abraham was the opposite; Muhammad ﷺ and [Ibrahim]... both were born to both kinds; Yahya was barren. End.

Shu'ayb was also mentioned along with Lot, and 'Isa along with Yahya. Allah, exalted is He, placed the granting of daughters first, to comfort them and honor them, so that their protection and kindness to them would be given attention.

In a hadith: "Whoever is tested with any of these daughters and treats them well, they will be a shield for him from the Fire."

Wathilah ibn al-Asqa' said: among the blessings of a woman is that she is early with a female before a male, because Allah, exalted is He, began with females.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: (If you ask): Why did He place females before males, though males precede them, and then return and place males first? And why did He define the males after indefinitely mentioning the females? (I answer): Because He mentioned the trial at the end of the first verse. And the ingratitude of man is his forgetting the previous mercy he had received.

Then He reminded him by mentioning His dominion and His will, and the mention of the division of children, so He placed females first, because the context of speech is that He does what He wills, not what man wills; so the mention of females, who are among what man does not will, was more important, and importance necessitates precedence.

The trial: the genus that the Arabs used to count as a trial; He mentioned the trial and delayed the males. When He delayed them for this reason, He compensated for their delay, and they are more deserving of precedence by their definiteness; for definiteness is distinction and renown, as if He said: He grants to whom He wills both groups, the known ones mentioned who are not hidden from you. Then after that He gave each of the two kinds its share of precedence and delay; and the definiteness of placing them first was not due to their precedence, but to another requirement, so He said: ﴿males and females﴾, as He said: ﴿Indeed, We created you from a male and a female﴾ [al-Hujurat: 13], ﴿and made of him the pair, the male and the female﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 39]. End.

It was also said: He began with females, then followed with males, to move him from grief to joy. It was also said: so that he would know that there is no objection to Allah, so that he would be content. (p-٥٢٦) When He grants him a male, he knows that it is an increase and grace from Allah and a kindness to him.

It was also said: He placed them first as an indication that when weakness and need are theirs, Allah's care is greater.

Mujahid said: it is that a woman gives birth to a boy, then gives birth to a girl. Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah said: that she gives birth to twins, a boy and a girl. Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi said: "aw yuzawwijuhum dhukrānan wa-inātha" (or He pairs them, males and females). Our scholars said: he means Adam; Hawwa' used to bear him twins in every birth, a male and a female; he would marry the male of one birth to the female of the other birth. End.

When He mentioned the granting regarding females and the granting regarding males, He dispensed with mentioning it in His saying: ﴿or He pairs them, males and females﴾. Since barrenness is not praiseworthy, He said: ﴿and makes whom He wills barren﴾, and it is the counterpart of the one to whom a child is born. Since the hermaphrodite is among those whose existence causes grief, Allah, exalted is He, did not mention it. They said: the creation was constant, male and female, until in the first Jahiliyyah the hermaphrodite occurred. 'Amir ibn al-Zarib, the oldest and most experienced of the Arabs, was asked about its inheritance, and he did not know what to say and deferred them.

When night fell on him, he began to turn over, and his thoughts carried him away. His servant noticed his state and asked him, and he said: "I am bewildered by a matter about which I do not know what to say." She said to him: "What is it?" He said: "A person who has a penis and a vulva; what is its state in inheritance?" The slave-woman said to him: "Give it inheritance from where it urinates." He understood her and in the morning presented it to them, and they agreed to it.

Islam came in accordance with that, and 'Ali, may Allah honor his face, judged by it. Indeed, He is All-Knowing of the interests of the servants, All-Powerful over the bringing into being of whatever He wills.

There was among the disbelievers a dispute about the meaning of Allah's speaking to Musa, so Quraysh and the Jews went to anthropomorphism regarding it, and this verse was revealed. It was also said: Quraysh used to say: "Will you not speak to Allah and look at Him, if you are a truthful prophet, as Musa spoke to Him and looked at Him?" The Messenger, peace be upon him, said to them: "Musa did not look at Allah," and then this verse was revealed: ﴿It is not for any human that Allah should speak to him﴾, clarifying the form of Allah's speaking to His servants, i.e., it is not fitting and not possible for a human that anything be revealed to him except one of the modes of revelation, including inspiration.

Mujahid said: or the breathing into the heart. Al-Naqqash said: or a revelation in a dream. Al-Nakha'i said: among the prophets there was one to whom it was written on the ground, or by making him hear His speech without the speaker's direction or place being known to him, as with Musa, peace be upon him. This is the meaning of ﴿from behind a veil﴾, i.e., from concealment from the speaker; He is not limited, nor is He imagined in the mind as being in a place, and it is not like a veil in what is seen. Or by sending to him an angel who speaks to him with revelation from Allah, exalted is He. This was stated by Ibn 'Atiyyah.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: It is not valid for any human that Allah should speak to him except in three ways:

Either by way of revelation, which is inspiration and casting into the heart and in a dream, as He revealed to the mother of Musa and to Ibrahim, peace be upon him, regarding the slaughter of his son.

From Mujahid: Allah revealed the Psalms to Dawud, peace be upon him, in his chest. 'Abid ibn al-Abras said:
"And Allah inspired me that they have ordered
Ibn Abi Awfa, so I rose against a man."
That is: He inspired me and cast it into my heart.

Or by making him hear His speech, which He creates in some bodies, without the hearer seeing who is speaking to him, since He in His essence is not seen.

His saying: ﴿from behind a veil﴾ is a parable: just as a king who is veiled speaks to some of his intimates, and he is behind a veil, so he hears his voice and does not see his person; and this is like how Allah spoke to Musa and speaks to the angels. Or by sending to him a messenger from the angels, who conveys revelation to him, as He spoke to the prophets other than Musa. End.

This follows the way of the Mu'tazilah in the impossibility of seeing Allah and the negation of true speech from Allah.

All three of these categories are truly called revelation, but the first was specially named "revelation" here, because what falls into the heart by way of inspiration falls all at once, so it is better to specify the term "revelation" for it.

It was said: "wahyan" (by inspiration) is as He revealed to the messengers through angels. ﴿Or He sends a messenger﴾, i.e., a prophet, as He spoke to the nations of the prophets through their tongues; this was related by al-Zamakhsharī, who omitted the explanation of ﴿or from behind a veil﴾, and its meaning in this view is: as He spoke to Muhammad and Musa, peace be upon them.

(p-٥٢٧) The majority read "ḥijāb" in the singular; Ibn Abi 'Abalah read "ḥujub" in the plural. The majority read both verbs in the accusative, coordinating "aw yursila" with the implied element to which "min warā' ḥijāb" is connected; its estimate: "aw yukallimahu min warā' ḥijāb," and this implied element is coordinated with "waḥyan." The meaning: except by inspiration, or by hearing from behind a veil, or by sending a messenger, who then inspires to the prophet to whom he is sent, by Allah's permission, what He wills. It is not permissible to coordinate "aw yursila" with "an yukallimahu Allāh," because the meaning would be corrupted.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: "Waḥyan" and "an yursila" are two verbal nouns functioning as adverbial accusatives of circumstance (ḥāl), because "an yursila" means "irsālan"; and "min warā' ḥijāb" is a adverbial phrase also functioning as a circumstance, like His saying: ﴿and upon their sides﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 191]. The estimate: "It is not valid that He speaks to anyone except inspiring, or making him hear from behind a veil, or sending." End.

As for the maṣdar (verbal noun) occupying the position of a ḥāl (circumstantial clause), this is not a general rule. The Arabs only used it in certain fixed expressions. Likewise, it is not permissible to say جاءَ زَيْدٌ بُكاءً (Zayd came weeping), meaning باكِيًا (weeping). al-Mubarrad allowed it by analogy where the maṣdar denotes a type of the verb, as in جاءَ زَيْدٌ مَشْيًا أوْ سُرْعَةً (Zayd came walking or hurrying). Sibawayh prohibited the construction of أنْ with the verb, which is interpreted as a maṣdar, occupying the position of a ḥāl. So it is not permissible to say جاءَ زَيْدٌ أنْ يَضْحَكَ, meaning ضَحِكًا in place of ضاحِكًا (laughing). Accordingly, treating وَحْيًا (revelation) as a maṣdar in the position of a ḥāl is among the things that are not analogically valid. And أنْ يُرْسِلَ, meaning إرْسالًا in place of مُرْسِلًا (sending), is forbidden by the explicit statement of Sibawayh.

Nafi' and the people of Medina recited ﴿أوْ يُرْسِلَ رَسُولًا فَيُوحِيَ﴾ with raising (rafʿ) in both places. This is explained either as an implied subject, "he sends," or as governed by what precedes it, مِن وراءِ (from behind), since the implied sense is: "or he speaks from behind a veil." وَحْيًا is a maṣdar in the position of a ḥāl, and the implied element is conjoined to it, أوْ يُرْسِلَ (or sends). The meaning is: "except by revealing, or speaking from behind a veil, or sending."

Attributing speech to God through His sending a messenger is a metaphor (majāz), as when you say: "The king proclaimed to the people such-and-such," while in fact the proclaimer was the town crier circulating in the markets. The act performed through an intermediary is treated as if it were performed directly.

Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: In this verse there is evidence that a message (risālah) is a kind of speech, and that a person who swears not to speak to someone, and then sends a messenger to him, while not intending direct address at the time of his oath, has not broken his oath. End of quotation.

﴿إنَّهُ عَلِيٌّ﴾, meaning He is Exalted above the attributes of created beings, ﴿حَكِيمٌ﴾: His actions proceed according to what wisdom requires. He speaks through an intermediary and without one.

﴿وكَذَلِكَ أوْحَيْنا﴾, meaning: Just as that decisive revelation, We revealed to you. For the Prophet (ﷺ) had gathered all three modes: the inspiration cast into the heart and the dream; God's direct speaking to him in reality on the night of the Ascension (al-Isrāʾ); and the sending of a messenger to him, who was Jibril (Gabriel). It is also said: just as We revealed to the prophets before you. ﴿أوْحَيْنا إلَيْكَ رُوحًا مِن أمْرِنا﴾ (We revealed to you a spirit by Our command). Ibn ʿAbbas said: prophethood. al-Suddi said: revelation. Qatadah said: mercy. al-Kalbi said: a book. al-Rabiʿ said: Jibril. It is also said: the Qur'an. He called what was revealed to him "spirit" because life comes through it from ignorance.

Malik ibn Dinar said: O people of the Qur'an, what has the Qur'an sown in your hearts? For the Qur'an is the spring of the hearts, just as grass is the spring of the earth.

﴿ما كُنْتَ تَدْرِي ما الكِتابُ ولا الإيمانُ﴾ (You did not know what the Book was, nor faith): this is a statement affirming the magnitude of the favor, and he (ﷺ) knew better than anyone its value. He coordinated ﴿ولا الإيمانُ﴾ (nor faith) with ﴿ما الكِتابُ﴾ (what the Book was). Its meaning is: the faith that is perceived through hearing, because there are aspects of faith that are known only through revelation.

As for the oneness of God, His freedom from deficiencies, and knowledge of His exalted attributes, all the prophets, upon them be blessings and peace, knew these things, and they are protected from making any error concerning them. Knowledge of these things preceded their receiving revelation. The word "faith" (īmān) is applied to prayer in His saying: ﴿وما كانَ اللَّهُ لِيُضِيعَ إيمانَكُمْ﴾ (God would never waste your faith) [al-Baqarah: 143], since prayer is part of what faith includes.

Whoever studies the biographies of the prophets from (p-528) their upbringing to their mission will be certain that they were protected from every defect, and that they were monotheists devoted to God from the time they grew up.

God the Exalted said concerning Yahya (John), peace be upon him: ﴿وآتَيْناهُ الحُكْمَ صَبِيًّا﴾ (And We gave him wisdom while still a child) [Maryam: 12]. Maʿmar said: he was two or three years old.

From Abu al-ʿAliyah: "You did not know before the revelation that you would recite the Qur'an, nor how you would call people to faith."

al-Qadi said: "Faith" (al-īmān) here means the obligations and rulings. He said: He was a believer in the oneness of God before that, then the obligations were revealed, which he had not known before, so he increased in faith through being charged with them.

al-Qushayri said: it is permissible to apply the term "faith" to the details of the Sharia. al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: it is elliptical, with an omitted noun, meaning: nor the people of faith, from among those who believed, such as Abu Talib, al-ʿAbbas, or others. ʿAli ibn ʿIsa said: that was when you were in the cradle.

It is also said: "What the Book was" means: were it not for Our favor upon you, and "nor faith" means: were it not for Our guidance to you. It is also said: meaning, you were among an unlettered people who did not know faith or the Book, so you took what you brought to them from someone among them who knew these things.

﴿ما الكِتابُ﴾ is an interrogative clause, a subject and predicate, and it occupies the position of an object governed by تَدْرِي (you knew), and it is suspended (muʿallaqah) in that position.

﴿ولَكِنْ جَعَلْناهُ نُورًا﴾ (But We made it a light): the pronoun may refer to "spirit" (rūḥan) mentioned earlier, to "the Book," or to "faith," and the nearest mention is the most likely. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: it refers to the Book. End of quotation.

It is also said that it refers to both the Book and faith together, since their purpose is one, and this is like His saying: ﴿واللَّهُ ورَسُولُهُ أحَقُّ أنْ يُرْضُوهُ﴾ (God and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him) [al-Tawbah: 62].

The majority recited لَتَهْدِي (you guide), the imperfect of هَدى in the active voice. Hawshab recited it in the passive voice, responding to the Prophet's (ﷺ) request: ﴿اهْدِنا الصِّراطَ المُسْتَقِيمَ﴾ (Guide us to the straight path) [al-Fatihah: 6]. Ibn al-Sumayqaʿ recited لَتُهْدِي with a ḍammah on the tāʾ and a kasrah on the dāl. It is reported from al-Jahdari that it was like this, and like the recitation of Hawshab.

﴿صِراطٍ مُّسْتَقِيمٍ﴾ (to a straight path). ʿAli said: it is the Qur'an. It is also said: Islam.

﴿ألا إلى اللَّهِ تَصِيرُ الأُمُورُ﴾ (Unquestionably, to God all affairs are returned): He informed using the imperfect, and what is meant is continuity, like the saying: "Zayd gives and withholds," meaning that this is his habit, not that it refers literally to a future event. That is, all the affairs of creation are returned to Him, the Exalted, on the Day of Resurrection, and He judges between them with justice. This was specified for the Day of Resurrection because no one can claim anything for himself on that day. This is what al-Farraʾ said.

﴿Before there comes a Day﴾: it was said: it is the day of the arrival of death; and the apparent meaning is that it is the Day of Resurrection. "Min Allāh" (from Allah) is connected to a deleted element indicated by what has preceded, i.e., that Day will not come back with anything that Allah has decreed concerning it. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "min Allāh" is a complement of "lā maradd" (no turning back). End.

This is not the better view, for if it were its complement, it would be a governed noun and would be declined with tanwīn. It was also said: "min Allāh" is connected to "ya'tiya" (comes): before there comes from Allah a Day that no one can turn back.

(What you have, no refuge) you may take refuge in, by which you escape the punishment; and (nor have you any denial) of any of your deeds that bring you into the Fire. "Nakīr" is the verbal noun of "ankara" (to deny) by non-analogical form.

It was said: it may be an active participle of intensive form, but this is distant, because "nakara" does not have this meaning of distinguishing.

(But if they turn away) the verse: it is consolation for the Messenger and reassurance for him, and removal of his concern for them. "Al-insān" (man) is intended as a genus, and therefore ﴿if an evil befalls them﴾ came. The answer of the conditional came as ﴿indeed man﴾ and did not come as "fa-innahu" nor "fa-innahum," to indicate that this kind is marked by ingratitude for blessings, as He said: ﴿Indeed, man is greatly unjust, ungrateful﴾ [Ibrahim: 34], ﴿Indeed, man is to his Lord ungrateful﴾ [al-'Adiyat: 6].

When He mentioned that he disbelieves the blessings, He followed that with the fact that to Him belongs the dominion of the higher and lower worlds, that He does what He wills, and alerted to His great power, and that all existing things arise from His will. So He mentioned that He grants some females, and to some males, and to some both, and makes some barren so that they bear no child.

Ishaq ibn Bishr said: this verse was revealed concerning the prophets, then it became general. Lot was a father of daughters, to whom no males were born; Abraham was the opposite; Muhammad ﷺ and [Ibrahim]... both were born to both kinds; Yahya was barren. End.

Shu'ayb was also mentioned along with Lot, and 'Isa along with Yahya. Allah, exalted is He, placed the granting of daughters first, to comfort them and honor them, so that their protection and kindness to them would be given attention.

In a hadith: "Whoever is tested with any of these daughters and treats them well, they will be a shield for him from the Fire."

Wathilah ibn al-Asqa' said: among the blessings of a woman is that she is early with a female before a male, because Allah, exalted is He, began with females.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: (If you ask): Why did He place females before males, though males precede them, and then return and place males first? And why did He define the males after indefinitely mentioning the females? (I answer): Because He mentioned the trial at the end of the first verse. And the ingratitude of man is his forgetting the previous mercy he had received.

Then He reminded him by mentioning His dominion and His will, and the mention of the division of children, so He placed females first, because the context of speech is that He does what He wills, not what man wills; so the mention of females, who are among what man does not will, was more important, and importance necessitates precedence.

The trial: the genus that the Arabs used to count as a trial; He mentioned the trial and delayed the males. When He delayed them for this reason, He compensated for their delay, and they are more deserving of precedence by their definiteness; for definiteness is distinction and renown, as if He said: He grants to whom He wills both groups, the known ones mentioned who are not hidden from you. Then after that He gave each of the two kinds its share of precedence and delay; and the definiteness of placing them first was not due to their precedence, but to another requirement, so He said: ﴿males and females﴾, as He said: ﴿Indeed, We created you from a male and a female﴾ [al-Hujurat: 13], ﴿and made of him the pair, the male and the female﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 39]. End.

It was also said: He began with females, then followed with males, to move him from grief to joy. It was also said: so that he would know that there is no objection to Allah, so that he would be content. (p-٥٢٦) When He grants him a male, he knows that it is an increase and grace from Allah and a kindness to him.

It was also said: He placed them first as an indication that when weakness and need are theirs, Allah's care is greater.

Mujahid said: it is that a woman gives birth to a boy, then gives birth to a girl. Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah said: that she gives birth to twins, a boy and a girl. Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi said: "aw yuzawwijuhum dhukrānan wa-inātha" (or He pairs them, males and females). Our scholars said: he means Adam; Hawwa' used to bear him twins in every birth, a male and a female; he would marry the male of one birth to the female of the other birth. End.

When He mentioned the granting regarding females and the granting regarding males, He dispensed with mentioning it in His saying: ﴿or He pairs them, males and females﴾. Since barrenness is not praiseworthy, He said: ﴿and makes whom He wills barren﴾, and it is the counterpart of the one to whom a child is born. Since the hermaphrodite is among those whose existence causes grief, Allah, exalted is He, did not mention it. They said: the creation was constant, male and female, until in the first Jahiliyyah the hermaphrodite occurred. 'Amir ibn al-Zarib, the oldest and most experienced of the Arabs, was asked about its inheritance, and he did not know what to say and deferred them.

When night fell on him, he began to turn over, and his thoughts carried him away. His servant noticed his state and asked him, and he said: "I am bewildered by a matter about which I do not know what to say." She said to him: "What is it?" He said: "A person who has a penis and a vulva; what is its state in inheritance?" The slave-woman said to him: "Give it inheritance from where it urinates." He understood her and in the morning presented it to them, and they agreed to it.

Islam came in accordance with that, and 'Ali, may Allah honor his face, judged by it. Indeed, He is All-Knowing of the interests of the servants, All-Powerful over the bringing into being of whatever He wills.

There was among the disbelievers a dispute about the meaning of Allah's speaking to Musa, so Quraysh and the Jews went to anthropomorphism regarding it, and this verse was revealed. It was also said: Quraysh used to say: "Will you not speak to Allah and look at Him, if you are a truthful prophet, as Musa spoke to Him and looked at Him?" The Messenger, peace be upon him, said to them: "Musa did not look at Allah," and then this verse was revealed: ﴿It is not for any human that Allah should speak to him﴾, clarifying the form of Allah's speaking to His servants, i.e., it is not fitting and not possible for a human that anything be revealed to him except one of the modes of revelation, including inspiration.

Mujahid said: or the breathing into the heart. Al-Naqqash said: or a revelation in a dream. Al-Nakha'i said: among the prophets there was one to whom it was written on the ground, or by making him hear His speech without the speaker's direction or place being known to him, as with Musa, peace be upon him. This is the meaning of ﴿from behind a veil﴾, i.e., from concealment from the speaker; He is not limited, nor is He imagined in the mind as being in a place, and it is not like a veil in what is seen. Or by sending to him an angel who speaks to him with revelation from Allah, exalted is He. This was stated by Ibn 'Atiyyah.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: It is not valid for any human that Allah should speak to him except in three ways:

Either by way of revelation, which is inspiration and casting into the heart and in a dream, as He revealed to the mother of Musa and to Ibrahim, peace be upon him, regarding the slaughter of his son.

From Mujahid: Allah revealed the Psalms to Dawud, peace be upon him, in his chest. 'Abid ibn al-Abras said:
"And Allah inspired me that they have ordered
Ibn Abi Awfa, so I rose against a man."
That is: He inspired me and cast it into my heart.

Or by making him hear His speech, which He creates in some bodies, without the hearer seeing who is speaking to him, since He in His essence is not seen.

His saying: ﴿from behind a veil﴾ is a parable: just as a king who is veiled speaks to some of his intimates, and he is behind a veil, so he hears his voice and does not see his person; and this is like how Allah spoke to Musa and speaks to the angels. Or by sending to him a messenger from the angels, who conveys revelation to him, as He spoke to the prophets other than Musa. End.

This follows the way of the Mu'tazilah in the impossibility of seeing Allah and the negation of true speech from Allah.

All three of these categories are truly called revelation, but the first was specially named "revelation" here, because what falls into the heart by way of inspiration falls all at once, so it is better to specify the term "revelation" for it.

It was said: "wahyan" (by inspiration) is as He revealed to the messengers through angels. ﴿Or He sends a messenger﴾, i.e., a prophet, as He spoke to the nations of the prophets through their tongues; this was related by al-Zamakhsharī, who omitted the explanation of ﴿or from behind a veil﴾, and its meaning in this view is: as He spoke to Muhammad and Musa, peace be upon them.

(p-٥٢٧) The majority read "ḥijāb" in the singular; Ibn Abi 'Abalah read "ḥujub" in the plural. The majority read both verbs in the accusative, coordinating "aw yursila" with the implied element to which "min warā' ḥijāb" is connected; its estimate: "aw yukallimahu min warā' ḥijāb," and this implied element is coordinated with "waḥyan." The meaning: except by inspiration, or by hearing from behind a veil, or by sending a messenger, who then inspires to the prophet to whom he is sent, by Allah's permission, what He wills. It is not permissible to coordinate "aw yursila" with "an yukallimahu Allāh," because the meaning would be corrupted.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: "Waḥyan" and "an yursila" are two verbal nouns functioning as adverbial accusatives of circumstance (ḥāl), because "an yursila" means "irsālan"; and "min warā' ḥijāb" is a adverbial phrase also functioning as a circumstance, like His saying: ﴿and upon their sides﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 191]. The estimate: "It is not valid that He speaks to anyone except inspiring, or making him hear from behind a veil, or sending." End.

As for the maṣdar (verbal noun) occupying the position of a ḥāl (circumstantial clause), this is not a general rule. The Arabs only used it in certain fixed expressions. Likewise, it is not permissible to say جاءَ زَيْدٌ بُكاءً (Zayd came weeping), meaning باكِيًا (weeping). al-Mubarrad allowed it by analogy where the maṣdar denotes a type of the verb, as in جاءَ زَيْدٌ مَشْيًا أوْ سُرْعَةً (Zayd came walking or hurrying). Sibawayh prohibited the construction of أنْ with the verb, which is interpreted as a maṣdar, occupying the position of a ḥāl. So it is not permissible to say جاءَ زَيْدٌ أنْ يَضْحَكَ, meaning ضَحِكًا in place of ضاحِكًا (laughing). Accordingly, treating وَحْيًا (revelation) as a maṣdar in the position of a ḥāl is among the things that are not analogically valid. And أنْ يُرْسِلَ, meaning إرْسالًا in place of مُرْسِلًا (sending), is forbidden by the explicit statement of Sibawayh.

Nafi' and the people of Medina recited ﴿أوْ يُرْسِلَ رَسُولًا فَيُوحِيَ﴾ with raising (rafʿ) in both places. This is explained either as an implied subject, "he sends," or as governed by what precedes it, مِن وراءِ (from behind), since the implied sense is: "or he speaks from behind a veil." وَحْيًا is a maṣdar in the position of a ḥāl, and the implied element is conjoined to it, أوْ يُرْسِلَ (or sends). The meaning is: "except by revealing, or speaking from behind a veil, or sending."

Attributing speech to God through His sending a messenger is a metaphor (majāz), as when you say: "The king proclaimed to the people such-and-such," while in fact the proclaimer was the town crier circulating in the markets. The act performed through an intermediary is treated as if it were performed directly.

Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: In this verse there is evidence that a message (risālah) is a kind of speech, and that a person who swears not to speak to someone, and then sends a messenger to him, while not intending direct address at the time of his oath, has not broken his oath. End of quotation.

﴿إنَّهُ عَلِيٌّ﴾, meaning He is Exalted above the attributes of created beings, ﴿حَكِيمٌ﴾: His actions proceed according to what wisdom requires. He speaks through an intermediary and without one.

﴿وكَذَلِكَ أوْحَيْنا﴾, meaning: Just as that decisive revelation, We revealed to you. For the Prophet (ﷺ) had gathered all three modes: the inspiration cast into the heart and the dream; God's direct speaking to him in reality on the night of the Ascension (al-Isrāʾ); and the sending of a messenger to him, who was Jibril (Gabriel). It is also said: just as We revealed to the prophets before you. ﴿أوْحَيْنا إلَيْكَ رُوحًا مِن أمْرِنا﴾ (We revealed to you a spirit by Our command). Ibn ʿAbbas said: prophethood. al-Suddi said: revelation. Qatadah said: mercy. al-Kalbi said: a book. al-Rabiʿ said: Jibril. It is also said: the Qur'an. He called what was revealed to him "spirit" because life comes through it from ignorance.

Malik ibn Dinar said: O people of the Qur'an, what has the Qur'an sown in your hearts? For the Qur'an is the spring of the hearts, just as grass is the spring of the earth.

﴿ما كُنْتَ تَدْرِي ما الكِتابُ ولا الإيمانُ﴾ (You did not know what the Book was, nor faith): this is a statement affirming the magnitude of the favor, and he (ﷺ) knew better than anyone its value. He coordinated ﴿ولا الإيمانُ﴾ (nor faith) with ﴿ما الكِتابُ﴾ (what the Book was). Its meaning is: the faith that is perceived through hearing, because there are aspects of faith that are known only through revelation.

As for the oneness of God, His freedom from deficiencies, and knowledge of His exalted attributes, all the prophets, upon them be blessings and peace, knew these things, and they are protected from making any error concerning them. Knowledge of these things preceded their receiving revelation. The word "faith" (īmān) is applied to prayer in His saying: ﴿وما كانَ اللَّهُ لِيُضِيعَ إيمانَكُمْ﴾ (God would never waste your faith) [al-Baqarah: 143], since prayer is part of what faith includes.

Whoever studies the biographies of the prophets from (p-528) their upbringing to their mission will be certain that they were protected from every defect, and that they were monotheists devoted to God from the time they grew up.

God the Exalted said concerning Yahya (John), peace be upon him: ﴿وآتَيْناهُ الحُكْمَ صَبِيًّا﴾ (And We gave him wisdom while still a child) [Maryam: 12]. Maʿmar said: he was two or three years old.

From Abu al-ʿAliyah: "You did not know before the revelation that you would recite the Qur'an, nor how you would call people to faith."

al-Qadi said: "Faith" (al-īmān) here means the obligations and rulings. He said: He was a believer in the oneness of God before that, then the obligations were revealed, which he had not known before, so he increased in faith through being charged with them.

al-Qushayri said: it is permissible to apply the term "faith" to the details of the Sharia. al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: it is elliptical, with an omitted noun, meaning: nor the people of faith, from among those who believed, such as Abu Talib, al-ʿAbbas, or others. ʿAli ibn ʿIsa said: that was when you were in the cradle.

It is also said: "What the Book was" means: were it not for Our favor upon you, and "nor faith" means: were it not for Our guidance to you. It is also said: meaning, you were among an unlettered people who did not know faith or the Book, so you took what you brought to them from someone among them who knew these things.

﴿ما الكِتابُ﴾ is an interrogative clause, a subject and predicate, and it occupies the position of an object governed by تَدْرِي (you knew), and it is suspended (muʿallaqah) in that position.

﴿ولَكِنْ جَعَلْناهُ نُورًا﴾ (But We made it a light): the pronoun may refer to "spirit" (rūḥan) mentioned earlier, to "the Book," or to "faith," and the nearest mention is the most likely. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: it refers to the Book. End of quotation.

It is also said that it refers to both the Book and faith together, since their purpose is one, and this is like His saying: ﴿واللَّهُ ورَسُولُهُ أحَقُّ أنْ يُرْضُوهُ﴾ (God and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him) [al-Tawbah: 62].

The majority recited لَتَهْدِي (you guide), the imperfect of هَدى in the active voice. Hawshab recited it in the passive voice, responding to the Prophet's (ﷺ) request: ﴿اهْدِنا الصِّراطَ المُسْتَقِيمَ﴾ (Guide us to the straight path) [al-Fatihah: 6]. Ibn al-Sumayqaʿ recited لَتُهْدِي with a ḍammah on the tāʾ and a kasrah on the dāl. It is reported from al-Jahdari that it was like this, and like the recitation of Hawshab.

﴿صِراطٍ مُّسْتَقِيمٍ﴾ (to a straight path). ʿAli said: it is the Qur'an. It is also said: Islam.

﴿ألا إلى اللَّهِ تَصِيرُ الأُمُورُ﴾ (Unquestionably, to God all affairs are returned): He informed using the imperfect, and what is meant is continuity, like the saying: "Zayd gives and withholds," meaning that this is his habit, not that it refers literally to a future event. That is, all the affairs of creation are returned to Him, the Exalted, on the Day of Resurrection, and He judges between them with justice. This was specified for the Day of Resurrection because no one can claim anything for himself on that day. This is what al-Farraʾ said.
